blocks.text: The number of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in Australia before colonisation was dramatically underestimated, according to new research that suggests many more of them were killed.
Modelling by a national research group puts the population levels before the 1788 first fleet arrived at 2.2 million, compared with early estimates of 250,000 people.
The research, by the Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence for Indigenous and Environmental Histories and Futures (CIEHF), has been published in the peer-reviewed Nature Human Behaviour.

The authors wrote that, historically, population estimates have been poor “due to lethal diseases, frontier and structural violence, and absence of systematic censuses” and that it’s “invaluable to truth-telling and reconciliation” to try to rectify that.
They warn readers that the content of the study is confronting and possibly distressing.

The modelling showed there had to be millions of excess deaths from smallpox and other diseases, massacres, and the other results of colonisation such as dispossession and malnutrition, according to co-author Prof Corey Bradshaw, a global ecology professor at Flinders University.

His previous research found that an 1789 smallpox outbreak alone killed as many as 220,000 Aboriginal people. There were also other smallpox epidemics, as well as outbreaks of measles, influenza, tuberculosis, typhoid and other diseases.
Bradshaw said he would bet his career that massacre databases were underestimated by an “order of magnitude”.

“If you’re a frontier farmer, a colonialist that came out to a new area, and you were trying to remove people from ‘your’ land, you’re not going to write extensively about how many people you killed to do that,” he said.

“There’s another component here that’s essentially greed and racism – the entire concept of terra nullius was based on not many people being here. If there’s a systematic desire to take land [fewer people means a] better justification for imperialism.”

Australia was colonised on the basis of terra nullius, that it belonged to no one. That concept was overthrown with the high court’s Mabo decision, when it was recognised that First Nations people had been here for tens of thousands of years.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people were not properly counted in the census until 1971, after the 1967 referendum. A that point, 115,953 people identified as Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander.
In 2021, 812,728 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people were counted in the census, a figure revised upwards to 983,257 with post-census recounts.
The 2.2 million figure, as well as a new estimate of 2.06 million excess deaths between 1788 and 1861, means the population was reduced to about 7% of its original size.

“We are not talking about a marginal consequence of colonisation but a demographic catastrophe at the heart of the Australian story,” distinguished professor Larissa Behrendt said. A Euahleyai/Gamillaroi woman, she is also the chair of the CIEHF’s advisory committee.

Early on after colonisation, various people estimated how many Aboriginal people were in their region. For example, governor Arthur Phillip estimated Gadigal people of the Eora nation came to about 1,500.

The first continent-wide estimate by social anthropologist Alfred Radcliffe-Brown put the number between 250,000 and 300,000, but mainly used observations from after the impacts of colonisation had been felt.
after newsletter promotion

Radcliffe-Brown was aware that was an underestimate, but many researchers since have relied on that count as a baseline. Again, often recognising that it would be an undercount because of historical reasons and because changes in who identified/was identified as Aboriginal.

In 1983, economic historian Noel Butlin estimated the population at about 900,000. Later he increased that to between 1.1 million and 1.3 million. In 1987, archaeologists John Mulvaney and J. Peter White argued it was more likely 750,000.
There have been many and varied estimates since, usually based on historical and ethnographic information.

The Australian team used different approaches to model the population. They looked at archaeological items to reconstruct how many people would have been there at a particular time, reconstructed the climate and the productivity of the land to infer how many people it could sustain, and looked at genetic data to work back in time based on known DNA mutation rates.
They also reviewed, but did not rely on, ethnographic estimates.

“The findings highlight the scale of demographic catastrophe experienced by Indigenous Australians due to colonisation, with the implications being a heightened understanding of intergenerational trauma and to inform future policy that assists Indigenous people,” said co-author and distinguished professor Lynette Russell of the Monash University Indigenous Studies Centre and CIEHF.

The authors wrote that Australia must prioritise reconciliation, engagement and policymaking with Indigenous people who still suffer intergenerational trauma and that the broader community should embrace the rich culture that survived these events.

The lead author, James Cook University associate professor Alan Williams, said the “devastating findings” highlight the impacts of invasion. But they also demonstrate the “remarkable survival, resilience and recovery over the past century of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Island people”.
Behrendt said the research “tells us something extraordinary”.
“Our survival is one of Australian history’s most remarkable stories,” she said.

articles.title: N.S. families thought they buried their loved ones. Officials are now investigating
articles.summary: Nova Scotia officials are investigating after the new owners of a funeral home in the Annapolis Valley discovered the cremated remains of a “significant number” of people in storage, CBC News has…

image.caption: Kristina Sweeney says she was shocked to learn an urn was discovered with what's believed to be her mother's cremated remains. Sweeney's mother, Elizabeth Pelton, died in 2024 and a funeral was held at that time. (David Laughlin/CBC)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia·Exclusive

Nova Scotia officials are investigating after the new owners of a funeral home in the Annapolis Valley discovered the cremated remains of a “significant number” of people in storage, CBC News has learned. Several families were recently told ashes belonging to their dead loved ones had been found.
New funeral home owner discovers ‘significant number’ of human ashes in storage
· CBC News
· Posted: Sep 15, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago

The province and the Nova Scotia regulator of funeral directors are investigating after the new owners of an Annapolis Valley funeral home discovered the cremated remains of a “significant number” of people in storage, CBC News has learned.

It comes as several Nova Scotia families who used the services of Serenity Funeral Home say they were shocked and horrified to receive calls letting them know that ashes belonging to their dead loved ones had been found.
“I kind of started internally freaking out because I buried my mom in 2024,” said Kristina Sweeney.
“I don't even think the shock has worn off yet … I thought I buried my mom, all of her. I put her in the ground by myself.”

Sweeney wasn't the only one contacted by East Coast Memorial, which recently purchased the buildings from Serenity Funeral Home. Serenity’s head office and crematorium was located in the small community of Coldbrook. The company also had other locations in the Annapolis Valley.

Michelle Carey and her sister Amanda Sabean used Serenity when they buried what they believed were the cremated remains of their father, Hendrik (Hank) Sabean, in the spring of 2018. On Sept. 8, Carey was informed by East Coast Memorial that her father’s full remains were found in storage.
“Having to, you know, bury him and to do this all over again. It's really hard,” said Carey.
The sisters are also left wondering whose remains they buried.
“There’s a family out there that's missing remains of their family member,” said Sabean.

In an email, Andrew George, the owner of the new business East Coast Memorial, explained that his company discovered “a significant number of cremated remains that had been left in storage, some for many, many years.”

George said he and his staff are carefully reviewing the home’s information to “make every reasonable effort to locate and contact families so that these loved ones could be returned to their families or otherwise laid to rest appropriately.”
‘Dozens’ of other urns found, daughter told
Sweeney said when her mother, Elizabeth Pelton, died in 2024 at the age of 60, her body was cremated. Sweeney chose a green urn, which she received and buried.

This month, the employee of East Coast Memorial who returned what’s believed to be the rest of her mother’s ashes gave her a green urn with a different pattern. It had been identified with a sticky note label as her mother’s. Sweeney said the employee told her that there were “dozens” of other urns found.
Another family told CBC their loved one’s remains were delivered to them in a cardboard box.

Sweeney wrote a post on Facebook about her experience and started receiving responses from other families. They recounted similar experiences, believing that they had received and buried their loved ones. Then they were contacted by East Coast Memorial years later suggesting otherwise.
“Every single person I've spoken to was under the impression that they had taken care of all the remains,” Sweeney said. “They were either buried or they took the urn home.”

George said his company is still assessing all the cases and doing its due diligence “as thoroughly as possible for each family,” and so he isn’t able to say exactly how many persons’ remains were found.
Former owner responds

When CBC reached Tony Facey, a former owner of Serenity Funeral Home for 12 years until December 2025, he confirmed there was a “whole stack” of cremated remains dating back as far as 25 years that had never been claimed by families. He said unclaimed remains is a wider issue all funeral homes are dealing with, and this has been an ongoing discussion at the regulatory board. Facey declined an interview.
The president of the Funeral Service Association of Nova Scotia, Kollin Weatherbee, said he’s never heard of a funeral home keeping decades of unclaimed remains.
“It is unusual that a funeral home would hold a portion of someone's ashes without the family knowing,” he said.
Weatherbee added that if a funeral home held ashes for a family, it would only be for a matter of weeks.
And in situations where a next of kin can’t be identified or reached, he said the public trustee usually gets involved within the first 12 days of a death.
Provincial inspectors visit
The province licenses and regulates funeral homes through Service Nova Scotia, while an arm’s-length board licenses and regulates funeral home directors.

The province learned of the stored ashes on Sept. 9 when it was contacted by that board and George, the owner of East Coast Memorial. It assigned two provincial inspectors to visit the crematorium the next day to learn more.

Adam Tipert, the chair of the Nova Scotia Board of Registration of Embalmers and Funeral Directors, told CBC in an email the board is taking the concerns “very seriously” and will collaborate with Service Nova Scotia in its investigation as more information emerges.
The province and the board also conducted an investigation at Serenity Funeral Home in 2018, when the location in Berwick mixed up the bodies of two women. A funeral director had his licence revoked.
That case eventually led to a change in the legislation surrounding funeral homes in 2025.

items: Family horrified after funeral home mixes up bodies, cremates wrong one
New law coming aimed at preventing body mix-ups at funeral homes

blocks.text: A provincial spokesperson said Serenity was routinely inspected in 2022, and some non-compliant administrative matters were resolved.
Following the sale to East Coast Memorial, Serenity is no longer licensed to operate funeral homes in Nova Scotia.
George said right now he is keeping focused on doing what is right for the families.

“We do not want to speculate about decisions or practices that occurred before our involvement,” he said, adding that his company will treat the remains with respect and dignity, as they were “received into our care when we acquired Serenity.”
George said his company is making plans for a community burial ceremony for any remains that can’t be reunited with a family, or if the families direct his company to do so.
Hank Sabean’s daughters still have many unanswered questions, especially since their father had been so clear about his own funeral arrangements and being laid to rest with his family.
“He had strong morals and values, and I know that he would think that this is so wrong that this could happen,” said Carey.
Kristina Sweeney said her mother would also be “really, really disgusted.”
“I felt like my mom and I had been violated,” she said. “I expect when someone passes away that, and I'm sure most people do, they're treated with dignity and respect.”

articles.title: China tightens travel rules over tech security
articles.summary: Beijing says the new rules, which could also apply to foreign and Taiwanese nationals, are aimed at safeguarding "national security."

image.caption: The restrictions come amid a technological arms race between China and the USImage: Wang Yu/Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: Sweeping travel restrictions on Chinese citizens came into effect on Tuesday, including exit bans for people considered to have endangered China's "industrial or technological security."
The new exit-and-entry rules, which were passed in July, apply to citizens deemed to have violated technology import and export regulations, particularly in the field of artificial intelligence.
The State Council in Beijing said the new rules were formulated to "safeguard national sovereignty, security, and development interests."
The regulations apply not only to people within China but also to Chinese citizens deemed to have committed criminal acts abroad.
In such cases, citizens could be "prohibited from leaving the country for a period of six months to three years from the date of their return to China," said the State Council.
Travel bans give Beijing 'wide remit'
The restrictions come as China remains locked in a technological arms race with the United States, with both countries accusing each other of stealing locally developed AI models in recent months.
And analysts warn that the full scope of the new rules will only become clear once they start being implemented.

Security and criminal activities "can be vaguely defined and easily adjusted," said Chong Ja Ian, an analyst from the National University of Singapore, telling the AFP news agency that Beijing has given itself a "wide remit."
Hong Kong activist pleads guilty to foreign collusion
Will China's new travel bans affect foreigners?
Under the new regulations, foreign nationals could also be denied entry to China for up to five years if found to have made false statements in ​visa applications.
Foreign governments have often reported instances of citizens being denied permission to leave China due ⁠to security-related ​investigations.
Analyst Chong highlighted the recent case of US citizen Min Zin who the US government said was detained improperly in Yunnan province in June.
"The case of Min Zin is a reminder that the range of people [that Beijing] could restrict from exiting could be quite wide – and potentially arbitrary," he said.

blocks.caption: Analysts warn it could take some time before the full scope of the new rules becomes clearImage: Tetiana Chernykova/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: Chinese travel bans: Taiwan warns citizens
The new rules could have particular implications for Taiwanese nationals who work in the tech sector and who travel between Taiwan and China.
Authorities in Taipei have warned citizens to take extra care on visits to China, which considers people from Taiwan to be Chinese citizens.
Beijing has dismissed any such concerns, claiming the rules provide better legal protection for Taiwanese.

Dylan Loh, an associate professor at Singapore's Nanyang Technological University, told AFP the travel restrictions "send a message" that China will take action to prevent "leaks in security or national interest-sensitive areas."
AI's expanding power alarms China's intelligence agency

articles.title: Lito Lapid asks: Do gov't workers really tell the whole truth in SALNs?
articles.summary: Do politicians or government workers really tell the whole truth in their SALNs? Senator-judge Lito Lapid put that question to an Office of the Ombudsman official on Tuesday as he underscored the…

blocks.text: Published September 15, 2026 4:53pm

Do politicians or government workers really tell the whole truth in their SALNs? Senator-judge Lito Lapid put that question to an Office of the Ombudsman official on Tuesday as he underscored the document’s importance in holding public officials accountable.

Lapid posed the question to lawyer Karen Batu, the Ombudsman Records Division officer-in-charge, whom the prosecution presented as a witness on Tuesday to testify on Vice President Sara Duterte’s SALN submissions.

“Meron po kasi ako napanood na isang abogado na in-interview sa TV. Ang sabi niya, ewan ko lang po kung tama ito, walang politiko o magsa-submit ng SALN na nagtatrabaho sa gobyerno na totoo," he said.
(I saw a lawyer being interviewed on TV. I don't know if this is true, but he said there is no politician or government employee who submits a truthful SALN.)
"Ang sabi niya, isang kalokohan ‘yan kung magsasabi sila ng totoo. Tama po ba ’yun?” Lapid asked the witness.
(He said it would be foolish for them to tell the truth. Is that correct?)
Looking slightly flustered, Batu chuckled before replying, “Kami po, ako po, nagsa-submit po ako ng totoong SALN ko, Your Honor.”
(I myself submit a truthful SALN, Your Honor.)
Lapid said that many ordinary Filipinos who do not work in government may not fully understand the significance of filing a SALN.
“Alam niyo po, sa tagal ng discussion natin, maraming nakikinig na mga kababayan natin na hindi naiintindihan kung ano ang SALN. ’Yung magsasaka, mga tricycle driver, mga mangingisda," he said.
(You know, amid our discussions, many of our countrymen who are listening do not really understand what SALN is--the farmers, the tricycle drivers, the fisherfolk.)

"Discussion tayo nang discussion dito, ’di natin alam... Halimbawa kami, ang nakakaintindi lang sa SALN, kami lang po, kami mga politiko, ’yung nagtatrabaho sa gobyerno, ’yun lang po nakakaintindi sa SALN,” he said.
(We keep discussing this, but many do not understand. For example, only us politicians and those who work in government understand what a SALN means.)
Lapid then asked Batu about the penalty for a government official who neglects to file a SALN even once.

Batu said this would constitute a violation of Republic Act No. 6713, or the Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees, which includes provisions on the filing of SALNs.
“Para malaman po ng ating mga kababayan na ang SALN ay masyadong mabigat sa amin. Lalo-lalo na po kung hindi kami nagdeklara nang tama,” Lapid said.
(I just want our countrymen to know that the SALN is a big deal for us, especially if we fail to declare it correctly.)
Batu testifed on Article 2 of the Articles of Impeachment, which alleges that Duterte accumulated unexplained wealth through:

items: failure to fully and truthfully disclose all of her and her spouse’s assets, liabilities and net worth in their SALNs, including her SALNs for 2022, 2023 and 2024; and
failure to divest herself of, and instead willfully continued, her business interests during her tenure as vice president in 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025.

articles.title: Marcos unhappy with 2026 BARMM election killings
articles.summary: Malacañang on Tuesday lamented the recorded deaths in the first-ever elections of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), saying that President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr.…

blocks.text: Published September 15, 2026 4:51pm

Malacañang on Tuesday lamented the recorded deaths in the first-ever elections of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), saying that President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. was unhappy with the killings.

This developed even as the Commission on Elections (Comelec) described the BARMM polls as generally peaceful, save for a few isolated incidents of violence. At least four people were killed and 19 others wounded, with most of the victims logged in a shootout in Cotabato City on the eve of the elections.

"Kahit isang tao lang po ang nasaktan hindi po ikasasaya ng Pangulo, kahit sabihin po natin generally peaceful and orderly iyong nangyaring eleksyon kahapon basta po mayroong kahit isa na nasaktan hindi po magiging maganda ang pakiramdam ninuman, lalung-lalo na ng Pangulo," Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Atty. Claire Castro said.

(Even if just one person was hurt, the President would not be happy with it, even if you say that the elections yesterday were generally peaceful and orderly, as long as even one person was hurt, no one would be happy with it, especially the President.)
Nonetheless, Castro said the BARMM election was still a success.
"Sa pananaw po ng administrasyon ay naging maganda naman po ang naging eleksyon kahapon sa BARMM," Castro said.
(In the views of the administration, the elections in BARMM still went well.)
Citing reports from the Philippine National Police and the COMELEC, Castro said the election turnout was still high.
Aside from the incidents of violence, the Palace official said the election was still generally orderly and peaceful. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Netherlands: Suspected sabotage disrupts train services
articles.summary: A major outage has hit parts of the Dutch railway system after objects were found placed across lines, authorities say. The company responsible for rail infrastructure says it suspects deliberate…

image.caption: The disruption began during Tuesday's morning rush hourImage: Vincent Jannink/ANP/IMAGO

blocks.text: Train services in various parts of the Netherlands have been severely disrupted, with ProRail, the company that maintains the nation's rail infrastructure, saying that sabotage was possibly at play.
National railway company NS said that train services around the central cities of Zwolle, Deventer and Amersfoort have been affected since the morning rush hour.

blocks.caption: The national railway company said it is not clear when services can resumeImage: Vincent Jannink/ANP/IMAGO

blocks.text: What do we know about the causes of the disruption?

In a statement, rail authority ProRail said that "[m]aterials deliberately placed on the tracks have been found at several locations. This is causing track-circuit failures. It appears to be a case of sabotage."
The ‌objects caused failures ‌across ​the network, affecting several level crossings, which disrupted ​road traffic, Pro Rail said.
ProRail ​workers ​were clearing the ​objects and ‌working to restore safe conditions, it ​added.
Though the company itself did not say what the "materials" were, a ProRail spokesperson told the daily de Volkskrant that "pipes had been found attached to the line" in several places.
This caused the disruptions, as the railway security systems can register a train's presence on a line because of an object placed on it and thus block access for other trains.
The spokesperson told the paper that one train had even collided with one of the pipes laid on the tracks, but that no accident or injuries had occurred.

blocks.caption: The disruption originated at 13 locations on tracks in the central NetherlandsImage: Vincent Jannink/ANP/IMAGO

blocks.text: Important event in The Hague
It remains unknown whether the incident has to do with so-called Prinsjesdag, the day the Dutch government presents its annual budget to parliament, where the reigning monarch gives a speech.
On the day, thousands of people go to The Hague to watch the royal family ride through the city in horse-drawn carriages.

articles.title: Rodrigo Duterte camp challenges experts' report, seeks 'greater medical certainty'
articles.summary: Former President Rodrigo Duterte"s defense team has asked the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III to allow the parties to question the experts about their findings and conclusions…
articles.byline: JAY-VEE MARASIGAN PANGAN, ANDY PEÑAFUERTE III

blocks.text: Former President Rodrigo Duterte’s defense team has asked the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III to allow the parties to question the experts about their findings and conclusions regarding his fitness to stand trial.

In a filing on September 14, Duterte’s counsel Peter Haynes questioned the court-appointed medical experts’ still-confidential reports, which the Office of the Prosecutor interprets as demonstrating the former president’s “reduced effort and unreliability during assessments.”
The specifics of these reports have been redacted in the filings of the defense and the Office of the Prosecutor.
Haynes said the examinations showed “significant memory impairment that prevents him from retaining recent information and reliably accessing memories.”

“This makes it difficult for him to engage meaningfully with the charges, the alleged incidents, the tens of thousands of disclosed items of evidence, let alone give proper instructions to his Lead Counsel, whose name he only sometimes remembers,” Haynes added.
“As a result, the Defense will, in reality, be preparing the case without meaningful input from the accused.”

The defense also asked the Trial Chamber to seek “greater medical certainty” and direct the experts “to complete ancillary examinations” to ascertain “the nature and extent of Mr. Duterte’s cognitive impairments.”

“This would allow the experts to confirm or exclude, once and for all, the possibility that his performance was the result of his failing to apply himself fully and would allow the Trial Chamber to interpret their final assessments on a properly informed basis," Haynes said.
Panel report 'incomplete and inadequate'

Haynes argued that “the Panel’s assessment is incomplete and inadequate,” and that “the Panel has left the Trial Chamber and parties in a situation of significant uncertainty as to how the cognitive difficulties identified in Mr. Duterte should be properly interpreted.”

According to the defense, the three court-appointed experts recorded “largely consistent” results depicting “serious deficits” that could limit Duterte’s ability to participate effectively in the proceedings, with some scores indicating impairment ranging from “moderate to severe.”

The experts, however, considered that the results could not be relied upon as an accurate measure of his cognitive condition because of the “possibility that his performance was the result of his failing to apply himself fully.”

Haynes further argued that the experts themselves could not determine whether it was due to “malingering or a lack of motivation” or “from a genuine inability to carry out and complete the tests as a consequence of an underlying neurological condition.”
The defense pointed to a qualification made by one of the experts.

“Professor [REDACTED] expressly made clear that his reference to underperformance was valid only ‘in the absence’ of any neurological disorders,” Haynes added, saying that Duterte’s condition has not yet been established.
According to Duterte’s lawyers, that qualification is significant because the experts have not definitively ruled out an underlying neurological condition that could explain his test results.
The defense argued that further examinations should have been conducted before the Chamber relies on the experts’ conclusion that Duterte retains the capacities to stand trial.

"Setting aside the issue of underperformance, the Defense struggles to understand how the Panel could have concluded that Mr. Duterte retains all the capacities necessary to participate meaningfully in the trial, when the answers he provided during the interviews – and, even more significantly, the medical records made available to them – reasonably point to a different conclusion," Haynes said.

Haynes said interviews conducted by the unnamed professors with Duterte, 81, showed, among other things, that he believed he was living in 2007 or 2008; that he was unable to correctly identify members of his own family, particularly his grandchildren; that he believed his last election had taken place 46 years ago and that he was 84 or 85 years old; and that he could not accurately recall which relatives had recently visited him or who the current President of the United States was.

"There is a direct link between these kinds of consistent memory lapses on fundamental questions, and Mr. Duterte’s ability to provide instructions or assist in the preparation of his defense, given that they make it impossible for his Counsel to place confidence in the information he provides about past events," Haynes said.

"These lapses also undermine Mr. Duterte’s ability to testify in his own defense. Where he cannot remember when he was last elected in the Philippines, for example, any finding that Mr. Duterte could give accurate testimony in his own defense would accordingly be unreasonable."
Prosecution: Duterte fitness reassessment unnecessary
The defense’s filing comes as the Trial Chamber III considers Duterte’s fitness to stand trial, an issue his lawyers have also linked to his continued detention.

Acting Prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang has already submitted to the Trial Chamber III that it is unnecessary to reassess Duterte’s fitness at this stage. However, if the Chamber orders such, the Prosecution asks that it “should be carried out by the same Panel to ensure continuity.”
The prosecution has also notified the Chamber of the expert panels’ “practical suggestions” to facilitate the former president’s “effective participation”.
The practicality and implementation of these measures, which the prosecution considers “reasonable”, are still subject to the Trial Chamber’s review.
The Trial Chamber III will convene on Wednesday, September 16, from 10:30 a.m. local time (4:30 p.m. in the Philippines) for the third status conference hearing.
It has yet to publish a document regarding Duterte’s attendance before the court.
The former president last appeared publicly via a video stream on March 14, 2025, during his initial appearance hearing before the ICC Pre-Trial Chamber I.
Duterte’s trial for crimes against humanity in connection with his administration’s war on drugs is scheduled to begin on November 30. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Macacua ally secures parliament seat for BFP in Cotabato City 3rd District
articles.summary: Tomanda Antok will keep his post in the Bangsamoro Parliament, despite being stripped of his position in the Bangsamoro Islamic Armed Forces a week before the BARMM polls

blocks.text: BFP. Bangsamoro Federalist Party founding chairman Tomanda Antok.
Antok's Facebook page
Tomanda Antok will keep his post in the Bangsamoro Parliament, despite being stripped of his position in the Bangsamoro Islamic Armed Forces a week before the BARMM polls

items: Tomanda Antok, chairman of the Bangsamoro Federalist Party, won a key parliament seat in Cotabato City with 49.92% of the votes, defeating rival candidates including one from the United Bangsamoro Justice Party.
Antok's victory is significant as it strengthens the faction of interim chief minister Abdulraof Macacua, providing an additional vote for the election of the BARMM chief minister.

Antok will serve a special five-year transition term in the Bangsamoro Parliament, which consists of 32 district representatives, and his win follows a leadership rift within the Moro Islamic Liberation Front.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Tomanda Antok, founding chairman of the Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP), won a key parliament seat in one of the three districts of Cotabato City, the regional government center and capital of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).
Antok obtained 9,223 or 49.92 % of the votes, according to Cotabato City’s certificates of canvass from the Commission on Elections’ website.

He is an ally of interim chief minister and current BFP chair Abdulraof Macacua. This means that Antok will not only keep his position as a member of the Bangsamoro Parliament, but that Macacua’s faction has secured one more vote for the eventual election of the BARMM chief minister.

Antok defeated two other candidates for Cotabato City’s 3rd District seat, including the bet of the BFP’s rival party, the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF).
The UBJP’s Hashim Baluno Manticayan used to be deputy minister of the BARMM Ministry of Science and Technology. He lost to Antok by a mere 253 votes, after getting 8,970 or 48.55 % of the votes.
Former Barangay Poblacion 3 official Reynaldo Largo Canen of the Bangsamoro Empowerment and Social Transformation Party ranked last with 283 or 1.53 % of the votes.
Antok’s win over a UBJP bet is especially significant because of his history with the MILF and its political party.

Macacua, Antok, and their allies in the BFP had been stripped of their positions in the Bangsamoro Islamic Armed Forces (BIAF) just a week before the BARMM polls. A news release by the MILF’s information committee owed it to “a leadership rift years in the making.”

It apparently began when President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. unceremoniously replaced Al Haj Murad Ebrahim as interim chief minister with then-MILF army chief Abdulraof Macacua in March 2025. (READ: MILF central committee frowns on BARMM leadership change)

Tensions only grew as Macacua began making decisions as chief minister without consulting the MILF. In the end, Macacua and several other high-ranking MILF officials, including Antok, defected from the UBJP to the BFP.
Macacua and his cohorts had been suspended from their positions in the BIAF for months before they were eventually removed — though they remain members of the MILF.
Antok was a general staff member of the BIAF at the time of his removal.

Like other newly elected parliament members, Antok will serve a special five-year transition term from October 30, 2026, to June 30, 2031. He will be one of the 32 district representatives making up 40% of the 80-seat Bangsamoro Parliament. – Rappler.com

blocks.text: Published September 15, 2026 4:32pm

The Department of Justice (DOJ) has issued a subpoena to Senator Robin Padilla in connection with the complaint filed against him by the Philippine National Police (PNP) for obstruction of justice over Senator Ronald Bato Dela Rosa’s departure from the Semate premises amid an ICC warrant against him.

According to a post on X (formerly Twitter) by Nimfa Ravello of Super Radyo dzBB, the DOJ subpoenaed Padilla to appear before the panel of prosecutors and to submit his counter-affidavit on September 25, Friday, and October 9, Friday.
In a Facebook post, Padilla said, “A subpoena has arrived.”
The PNP-Criminal Investigation and Detection Group filed a complaint against Padilla and others in May for allegedly helping Dela Rosa escape.

Dela Rosa is the subject of an arrest warrant for “alleged criminal responsibility as an indirect co-perpetrator” in the crimes against humanity of murder from July 3, 2016, until the end of April 2018, wherein at least 32 persons died.

Authorities attempted to serve the warrant against him on May 11, leading to a chase inside the Senate building. He was later placed under protective custody by the upper chamber and slipped out of the Senate premises on May 14.
He has not appeared in public since.
Padilla, for his part, previously said that he did not help Dela Rosa escape, saying the former police chief only asked to hitch a ride with him out of the Senate building on May 14.
He is also facing an obstruction of justice complaint before the Office of the Ombudsman. –NB, GMA News

Air India's CEO has been summoned after three Italian nationals "skipped" immigration at Delhi airport and left the country

blocks.text: Here are the latest developments from India on Tuesday, September 15:
September 15, 2026
Meta to report child sexual abuse material to India's cybercrime portal: reports
Meta has agreed to report child safety-related matters, including child sexual abuse cases, to law enforcement agencies in India, Indian media reported on Tuesday, citing government sources.
News agency PTI quoted a Meta spokesperson as saying the cases would now be reported to the cybercrime portal managed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre.
The US tech giant has come under fire in India in recent months over alleged paid advertisements promoting AI-generated child sexual abuse material on its Facebook and Instagram platforms.

"Meta has agreed to report child safety-related matters to the appropriate law enforcement agencies. It is a first step towards making the platforms safe for children and much more needs to be done," news agency ANI quoted unnamed government sources as saying.
The Indian government is engaging with other online platforms to ensure that they identify and remove such content proactively, news agency PTI cited government sources as saying.
ANI and PTI also quoted sources saying that the government would take action against platforms that fail to take proactive measures to ensure online child safety.
The news agencies were told by the sources that online safety of children is a "fundamental principle" for any social media platform operating in India and was "non-negotiable."
Meta under scrutiny in India
In July, an investigative report by the BBC found that Instagram had been running paid advertisements promoting child sexual abuse material in India.
India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) later ordered Instagram to disable all ads and content promoting and facilitating access to such material.
The ministry also demanded a detailed explanation on the issue and held several rounds of discussions with top Meta executives.

Last week, India's National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) summoned the managing director and head of Meta India over its inquiry into alleged ads related to child sexual exploitative and abuse material.

Meanwhile, a US-based nonprofit Tech Transparency Project (TTP) published a report saying that it had found more than 300 ads with child sexual abuse material that ran on Facebook and Instagram this year.
It said that 84 of the ads ran in India — 78 of them after the Indian government directive to Meta to remove any Instagram ads promoting child sexual abuse material.

articles.title: BFP spox keeps BARMM Parliament seat, wins in Cotabato’s 2nd District
articles.summary: Naguib Sinarimbo secures a parliament seat under the BFP and hands the MILF’s UBJP — a party he co-founded — a decisive defeat

blocks.text: BARMM. BARMM Member of Parliament Naguib Sinarimbo
Naguib Sinarimbo's Facebook page
Naguib Sinarimbo secures a parliament seat under the BFP and hands the MILF’s UBJP — a party he co-founded — a decisive defeat

items: Naguib Sinarimbo of the Bangsamoro Federalist Party won a parliamentary seat in Cotabato City with 77.91% of the votes, defeating his rival from the United Bangsamoro Justice Party.

Sinarimbo has a long history of involvement in the governance of the Bangsamoro region, having previously served as the region's executive secretary and played a key role in the peace negotiations with the MILF.
He will serve a special five-year transition term in the Bangsamoro Parliament, which consists of 32 district representatives.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – A key figure in the Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP) has captured one of the three parliamentary district seats of Cotabato City, the regional government center and capital of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).
BFP spokesperson Naguib Sinarimbo topped in the district’s race with 31,114 or 77.91 % of the votes, based on Cotabato City’s total certificates of canvass from the Commission on Elections’ website.

This means he will hold onto the parliament seat he was first appointed to in 2025 as part of the Bangsamoro Transition Authority (BTA). (READ: Once an MILF ally, ex-BARMM minister returns with Malacañang’s backing before polls)

For decades, Sinarimbo has been deeply involved in the formation of the Bangsamoro region and its governance. Sinarimbo was even instrumental in founding the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP), the Moro Islamic Liberation Front’s (MILF) regional political party and the BFP’s most contentious rival in the 2026 polls.
Now, Sinarimbo has handed his former party a decisive defeat. UBJP bet Zahrumin Andong Midtimbang, who is former Bagua 1 barangay chairman, ranked second with 8,411 or 21.06 % of the votes.

Two other candidates joined the four-way race in Cotabato City’s 2nd District. Ex-soldier and former Cotabato City councilor Madatu Brahim Datumanong from the Bangsamoro Party placed third with 246 or 0.62 % of the votes, while former Cotabato City councilor and independent candidate Christina Tan Chua landed in last place with 167 or 0.42 %votes.

In the former Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, Sinarimbo was the region’s executive secretary from 2009 to 2011. He also played a key role in forming the BARMM by negotiating the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro, which is the final peace accord signed between the Philippine government and the MILF in 2014.

When the BARMM was formed, Sinarimbo became the region’s spokesperson and minister of the interior and local government. He later stepped down from the regional government amid a wave of courtesy resignations ordered by then-interim chief minister Ahod Balawag “Al Haj Murad” Ebrahim.

But a few months after he left the regional government, in 2024, he joined the Serbisyong Inklusibo–Alyansang Progresibo (SIAP), a party aligned with the Adiongs of Lanao del Sur. A year later, in 2025, he was given a parliamentary seat in the BTA as a presidential appointee.
SIAP later formed a coalition with two other parties called the BARMM Grand Coalition, but Sinarimbo eventually left SIAP to join the BFP ahead of the 2026 polls.

Like other newly elected parliament members, Sinarimbo will serve a special five-year transition term from October 30, 2026, to June 30, 2031. He will be one of the 32 district representatives making up 40% of the 80-seat Bangsamoro Parliament. – Rappler.com

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Former Commission on Elections (Comelec) chairman Sheriff Abas topped the race for Cotabato City’s 1st District seat in the Bangsamoro Parliament, after the first-ever Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) parliamentary elections on Monday, September 14.

He obtained 12,334 or 57.75 % of the votes, securing one seat for his political party, the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), according to Cotabato City’s certificates of canvass from the Commission on Elections’ website.
Abas is the nephew of UBJP second nominee Mohagher Iqbal, former BARMM education minister and the MILF’s longest-serving peace negotiator.
Prior to being Comelec chairman from 2017 to 2022, he was Comelec commissioner starting in 2015. Abas is the first Mindanaoan and first Muslim to serve as the commission’s chairman.
Abas’ win in the BARMM polls comes two days after he was issued a show-cause order over his alleged involvement in a vote-buying incident. He has since denied the allegation, calling it “fake news.”
He defeated two other candidates to capture one of the three districts of Cotabato City, BARMM’s capital and seat of government.

After placing second in the polls, Romeo Kabuntalan Sema has failed to keep his parliament seat as part of the appointed Bangsamoro Transition Authority — a position he has held since 2019. He got 8,676 or 40.63 % of the votes.
Sema is also the vice chairman of the Moro National Liberation Front’s (MNLF) central committee for political affairs and former BARMM labor minister.

He is related to MNLF chairman and incumbent labor minister Muslimin Sema, who also heads the Bangsamoro Party. This is despite Romeo running under the Mahardika Party, led by the opposing faction of MNLF founder Nur Misuari.
Placing third is former seaman Danilo Ramos Liggayo, who was the bet of the Bangsamoro Empowerment and Social Transformation Party. He got 346 or 1.62 % of the votes.
Liggayo served under the Office of the President for Mindanao while Fidel Ramos was Philippine president.

Like other newly elected parliament members, Abas will serve a special five-year transition term from October 30, 2026, to June 30, 2031. He will be one of the 32 district representatives making up 40% of the 80-seat Bangsamoro Parliament. – Rappler.com

articles.summary:
Party leader claims proposed new retrospective laws are unfair and Reform would retaliate with a crackdown on union funding if elected

Good morning. Ministers already think that the new…

blocks.text: Party leader claims proposed new retrospective laws are unfair and Reform would retaliate with a crackdown on union funding if elected
LIVE Updated now
Key events

items: 21m agoFarage says a Reform UK government would stop unions funding Labour if they block £72m donations

blocks.text: Farage says a Reform UK government would stop unions funding Labour if they block £72m donations

Good morning. Ministers already think that the new laws on political donations, as set out in the version of the representation of the people bill which left the Commons earlier this month, will be enough to block some or all of the donations worth £72m to Reform UK announced at the weekend. But they are still planning further amendments to the legislation, when peers debate their own amendments to the bill, to make the restrictions even tighter. Pippa Crerar, Jessica Elgot and Kiran Stacey have the details here in our overnight splash.

blocks.caption: Guardian splash Photograph: Guardian

blocks.text: Kiran and Henry Dyer also have written a good explainer about the rules.

Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, has hit back. In an article for the Daily Telegraph, he claims that the proposed new laws – which are retrospective in the sense that they will apply from March 2026, when ministers first announced their intention to legislate, not from the moment when the bill gets royal assent, later this year or early next year – are unfair. If the crackdown goes ahead, Reform UK will stop Labour getting money from the trade unions if it wins the next election, he says.

double quotation markThe Unite union alone has given the Labour party over £50m over the course of the last few years. They’ve got the Employment Rights Act, not to mention big pay rises for bus drivers. If anybody is giving money to do political bidding, it’s the trade unions. So I would just warn the Labour party here and now: If you try and ban our donors, we in government would certainly ban funding from the trade unions. I don’t want to go down that route. But it’s something we would be prepared to do. Once again, let me be clear. Neither Ben Delo nor Christopher Harborne will be getting membership of the House of Lords. They won’t be getting favours, they won’t be influencing policy. It isn’t happening. Because unlike the uniparty we are not for sale.

Until recently the trade unions were opposed to caps on the amount individuals can donate to political parties because they feared that would lead to a rightwing government limiting what unions can donate to Labour. The £72m donations to Reform UK have prompted a bit of a rethink, and union leaders are expected to issue a statement later.
Here is the agenda for the day.
Morning: Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, chairs a political cabinet. Andy Burnham has cancelled engagements today following the death of his father.
9.30am: The Department for Work and Pensions publishes figures relating to personal independence payment claims and universal credit health claims.
11.30am: Alex Norris, the justice secretary, takes questions in the Commons.
Noon: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.

After 12.30pm: Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, is expected to make a Commons statement following the publication of the inquiry report into how the nurse Lucy Letby was able to repeatedly kill babies at the Countess of Chester hospital.
2.45pm: Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, takes questions from the Commons home affairs committee.
3.45pm: Haigh addresses the TUC conference, standing in for Burnham.

Also today, in Piddlington, a small Oxfordshire village, residents are holding a symbolic independence referendum, as a protest against plans to house more than 1,000 asylum seekers in a former military base nearby.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

articles.title: Not political persecution: Palace says no basis for Harry Roque asylum plea
articles.summary: Following reports that former presidential spokesperson Harry Roque"s asylum bid was denied, the Palace reiterated that there was no basis for his petition, saying that he was not politically…

blocks.text: Published September 15, 2026 4:15pm

Following reports that former presidential spokesperson Harry Roque’s asylum bid was denied, the Palace reiterated that there was no basis for his petition, saying that he was not politically persecuted.

Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla on Tuesday said in a press conference that Roque’s asylum bid had been denied, but said he would need to further confirm details. Roque would later deny Remulla’s claim.

Asked about the matter in a press conference, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said that she has not been able to speak to President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. about the development. However, she reiterated the Palace’s previous position on Roque’s bid.

“Even before…sinasabi naman po na ang paniniwala ng PCO (Presidential Communications Office) ay wala pong batayan ang ginawang request ni Harry Roque, na sinasabing political persecution lang ang ginagawa sa kanya,” Castro said.
(Even before…the PCO has been stating its belief that Harry Roque’s request had no basis, that what was being done to him was political persecution.)
Castro said the case against Roque was clear. The former presidential spokesperson was not just facing a qualified human trafficking case, but he also has tax evasion and land-grabbing cases.

“So, hindi ito political persecution, records ang nagsasalita dito, ebidensiya ang nagsusumigaw,” Castro said. (So, this is not political persecution, these are records talking, the evidence is shouting.)
Roque is currently sought by authorities for his alleged role in human trafficking operations involving a Philippine Offshore Gaming Operators (POGO) hub in Porac, Pampanga. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Why top AI researchers are warning about human extinction
articles.summary: Could artificial intelligence pose an existential threat to humanity? Some leading researchers are warning against an unregulated race toward AI superintelligence.

image.caption: Some researchers argue that artificial general intelligence could pose unforeseeable risksImage: Marc Asensio/NurPhoto/IMAGO

blocks.text: Dramatic warnings about the existential risks posed by artificial intelligence to humanity are nothing new.
As early as in the 1940s, the renowned scientist and science fiction author Isaac Asimov explored potential risks and unintended consequences of intelligent machines.
In 1991, Hollywood blockbuster "Terminator 2" imagined a dystopian 2029 in which an out-of-control military AI called Skynet directs killer robots in a war against humanity.
If the warnings of several of the biggest names in AI are to be believed, a similar scenario could become a reality — even before 2029.

blocks.caption: The opening sequence of 'Terminator 2' depicts a dystopian future where AI has spiraled out of control and turned against humanityImage: Columbia/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Growing calls for strict regulation
"The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade," AI researcher Jacob Coxon posted on X last week, without exactly explaining how it might happen.
"No other human activity poses this level of danger," he added.

Coxon also revealed that he had quit his job at Anthropic, a US-based AI company, in protest against what he saw as an irresponsible race among AI companies to develop an ever better, self-improving superintelligence.

He warned that algorithms could begin to analyze and improve their own source code independently, which could shrink development cycles from several months to just a few minutes and thus make them uncontrollable.

Coxon is not an isolated voice. Nobel Prize-winning physicist Geoffrey Hinton, often called the "Godfather of AI," has been warning for years about the serious consequences of artificial superintelligence.

In 2023, he left his job at Google to publicly warn of the dangers of AI technologies he helped pioneer. Yoshua Bengio, a pioneer of artificial neural networks and deep learning, has also expressed concern about current developments and called for government regulation.

As recently as July 2026, more than 1,000 employees of leading AI companies warned in an open letter of an imminent loss of control if the race for "superintelligence" were not subject to significantly stricter regulations.
Caught in an unregulated race?
Despite the growing warnings, US President Donald Trump's administration has clearly shifted its AI policy toward minimizing regulatory hurdles and accelerating AI development.

In his X post, Jacob Coxon indirectly criticized the consequences of this policy: "At OpenAI, many have not deeply internalized the civilizational stakes. At Anthropic, the stakes are well-understood, but they are locked in a race to get there first — they believe no one else will act responsibly, so they must do it themselves, despite the risk."
Coxon, who had moved from OpenAI to Anthropic in early 2026, is familiar with both corporate cultures.
In an interview with The Wall Street Journal, he said that under the "most aggressive scenarios," things could spiral out of control as early as the end of 2027.
America's AI boom: Who pays the price?
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, for his part, is currently calling for a coordinated, industry-wide slowdown in development to buy time to address the risks and prevent any misuse of AI.

In a lengthy essay shared on X over the weekend, he wrote that in six to 12 months, AI agents "could be capable ​of taking over the entire internet" and potentially cause "hundreds of billions of dollars in damage" without proper guardrails.
Both Elon Musk, who runs xAI, and Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, said they agree with Amodei.
The alignment problem

In recent years, numerous experts have voiced concern about the rapid AI advances, particularly the development of artificial general intelligence, which refers to systems that not only solve individual tasks but also match or exceed human intellectual capabilities in nearly all areas.
Sophisticated AI models, for instance, may pursue goals in ways that diverge from human intentions, something AI security researchers refer to as the "alignment problem."
On top of that, even developers can't always fully understand how AI makes certain decisions.
And so, it's no surprise that Coxon's former colleague Evan Hubinger came to his defense.

"Jacob is correct here — we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," Hubinger, who himself is the team lead for alignment stress tests at Anthropic, wrote on X.

In his post, Hubinger made clear that Anthropic hasn't yet found a solution to the alignment problem and warned that an AI model might begin to resist being shut down, because that would limit its ability to achieve its programmed goal.
Exaggerated hysteria?
Other AI experts, however, consider such doomsday scenarios to be extremely unlikely.
Among the most prominent critics of the so-called "AI doomers" is Meta's chief scientist, Yann LeCun. In October 2024, he dismissed such concerns as "complete nonsense."
Still other experts note that developing AI systems requires enormous amounts of computing power, energy, data and infrastructure.

They argue that an AI model cannot simply take over the world pointing out that it would first need to rely on servers, power grids, communication systems and physical resources that are controlled by humans.
China's humanoid robots put to the test
Does the real danger lie elsewhere?
In fact, many experts see the short-term risks not so much in the extinction of humanity as in the numerous indirect consequences of AI systems that already exist even without superintelligence.
These include disinformation campaigns on an unprecedented scale and the related manipulation of democratic processes, an expansion of mass surveillance, and job losses across numerous industries.

Just last week, Anthropic revealed that there had been several attempts by users to misuse its Claude AI models for research that could support biological weapons development. The company said it had banned the accounts involved.
In August, Meta, Anthropic and OpenAI caused a stir when they announced that their AI systems had unintentionally carried out autonomous hacking activities.
Following reports of further AI hacking attacks during testing, even top US AI frontier labs are now expressing willingness to slow down the development of the technology.
This piece was originally published in German.

articles.title: COVID-19 benefit repayment is hurting low-income Canadians, report says

image.caption: The Canada Revenue Agency reported that as of last November, it was owed more than $10 billion in COVID-19 benefits paid out to those who were ineligible. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Over six years after the COVID-19 pandemic began, the federal government is still trying to track down billions of dollars sent to Canadians who were later found to be ineligible for benefits. According to a new report, much of that burden still rests on low-income Canadians.
Think-tank says collecting debts from ineligible recipients is costly, ineffective
Over six years after the COVID-19 pandemic started, the federal government is still trying to track down billions of dollars sent to Canadians who were later found to be ineligible for benefits.

According to a report from Maytree, a think-tank and advocacy group that studies poverty, those recollection efforts disproportionately affect low-income Canadians who can't pay, and ultimately cost more than they recover.
It calls for an end to the government's efforts to recover pandemic benefits.

In total, Ottawa distributed about $14 billion in COVID-related benefits to individuals who didn't meet the Canada Revenue Agency's income requirements. Most of that sum was provided under the Canada emergency response benefit (CERB) and later the Canada recovery benefit (CRB).

By the end of last November, the CRA reported that $10 billion was outstanding, over $8 billion of which was owed on CERB and CRB payouts. CBC News reached out to the CRA for updated figures, but the agency was unable to provide them after more than two weeks of requests.

items: CRA says it's owed $10 billion in COVID-related benefits sent to ineligible recipients

blocks.text: "This is not a story about fraud," the report says. "It is a story about what happens when a government moves fast, makes mistakes and then hands the bill to the people least able to pay it."
John Stapleton, co-author of the Maytree report and a social policy expert, says his group acknowledges some people knowingly applied for benefits they shouldn't have received.
"We're not asking them to absolve those people," he said. "[But] there's some people out there that got caught in this net who are really suffering as a result."
In Budget 2025, Ottawa provided $123 million to support the government's collection of its pandemic response benefits over two years, starting in 2026-27.
According to Stapleton and Tyler Meredith, a senior fellow at the Munk School of Public Policy and a fellow at Maytree, many Canadians who still owe a debt on pandemic benefits are low-income.
"By the time you asked them to repay that benefit, they would have already, frankly, used that money," Meredith said.
Meredith was the head of economic and fiscal policy under former prime minister Justin Trudeau and a main architect of the federal government's economic response to the COVID-19 pandemic.
"It was always clear, I would argue, that the intent of the program was to be for people who had lost income," Meredith said.
While he said the government needed to provide certainty to Canadians that support was there if they needed it, the program was misunderstood as a form of universal income.

items: CRA reversed $246M in pandemic benefit debts after thousands contested eligibility status
Canadians told to pay back CERB say eligibility requirements were unclear

blocks.text: "Most people don't check the fine print," Meredith said.

CERB was in place from March to October 2020. Applicants had to have earned at least $5,000 in income in the last 12 months, lost income as a result of the pandemic and not been receiving EI in order to be eligible. They received $2,000 every four weeks.
CERB 'didn't have a plan for recovery'
Meredith said the government didn't have a plan to recover ineligible benefit payouts when it was initially launching its pandemic relief programs.
"Our goal, in all of the programs we were designing, was to have something that was like 80 to 85 per cent ready, knowing that we would amend and adjust the program as we went," Meredith said.
"We just didn't have time to wait."

According to Meredith, the government's initial plan was to deliver benefits by traditional means like through the quarterly GST tax credit — now the groceries and essentials benefit — or Canada's employment insurance system. But Meredith said the EI system would have been overwhelmed as millions of Canadians were set to lose work during the pandemic.
Because of this, the government drafted the Canada Emergency Response Benefit Act to create a new system, legislation Meredith said was put together in "a matter of a couple days."

items: Federal COVID-19 vaccine, benefits rollout swift but wasteful: AG
More than 1,000 Canadians take CRA to court over pandemic payments — and some win

blocks.text: The government allows for interest-free repayment over time.

But CERB's legislation "doesn't have a mechanism inside it to say the government is permitted, or CRA's officials are permitted, to entertain some form of settlement," Meredith said. "From their point of view, their hands are tied."

"The Federal Court has confirmed that the CRA is required to apply the eligibility criteria established by legislation and does not have discretion to depart from those requirements," the CRA told CBC News in a written statement.

The CRA said it is not legally obligated to pursue all ineligible CERB payments. According to Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC), the CRA can allow payment deferrals if a client is facing financial hardship. If it determines that hardship is permanent, the CRA can recommend a debt for writeoff to ESDC.
Can Ottawa dissolve the debt?

But Meredith says simply writing off the remaining debt owed by those ineligible for benefits is "not a realistic option" and "probably politically unpalatable for any government, at any point in time."

He pointed to the government's use of partial forgiveness on loans from the Canada emergency business account program (CEBA) as a possible guide, and suggested it develop an option to "spread out repayment costs over a much longer period of time."

items: Businesses need to pay CEBA loans or lose free money — because the deadline isn't changing

blocks.text: In its report, Maytree outlined a plan to wind down the collection of pandemic benefits along a suggested timeline. It also recommended the Office of the Parliamentary Budget Officer examine the cost of the government's collection efforts.
Other recommendations include amending the Income Tax Act to give the CRA discretion to make deals on the remaining debt and for the CRA to resolve over 1,200 outstanding cases by the end of 2026.
"I think it's incumbent upon government to set out a framework," Meredith said.

"Up to now, they've largely avoided making or entertaining any of that, both because there will eventually be some fiscal costs associated with doing so, but also because, I think the reality is people have harsh attitudes towards this.… If you used a program that you shouldn't have, they don't think that you're deserving usually of amnesty."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
David Cummings is a reporter for CBC News.

articles.title: Make NHS and MoD uniforms in UK, fashion firms urge Burnham
articles.summary: More than 1,200 people including Ben Fogle sign letter saying buying British will help preserve manufacturing firms

blocks.text: London fashion week is only days away, but one industry organisation has turned its attention to clothing that is a little less catwalk-worthy – the uniforms worn by British defence forces and NHS staff.
On Wednesday afternoon, the thinktank Fashion Roundtable will hand deliver a letter to No 10 urging Andy Burnham to commit to manufacturing these uniforms in the UK.

Signed by more than 1,200 people – including the adventurer Ben Fogle and The British Sewing Bee’s Patrick Grant – the organisation’s letter says that public procurement such as this could be vital to preserving the UK’s manufacturing industry.

“The biggest lever we have to support skills retention, inclusive growth and regional resilience is awarding public procurement contracts for textile goods to suppliers who manufacture onshore in the UK,” the thinktank said.
According to a Fashion Roundtable economist’s estimate, about £120m is spent a year by the NHS and Ministry of Defence on uniforms, with 55% of them currently manufactured overseas.

The benefit of domestic manufacturing to an economy has already been demonstrated. The Covid inquiry concluded that nearly £10bn of public money was wasted on the flawed way it went about buying personal protective equipment (PPE), much of it manufactured in China. By contrast, Scotland, which invested £102.7m in PPE and produced 88% of it domestically in 2021, generated £66.7m of additional economic value and 1,400 jobs.

Kate Hills, the founder of the manufacturing organisation Make It British, said making these items in the UK could allow companies breathing space. “These sort of contracts would give manufacturers confidence to employ more people, to look at the long term rather than feel like they’re surviving day to day,” she added.

blocks.caption: Some British army uniforms are made in China, but the US manufactures domestically by law. Photograph: Ben Birchall/PA

blocks.text: The US is an example where contracts for military uniforms are manufactured by companies within the country by law – thanks to the Berry amendment, which was passed in 1941. In 2025, the market for the industry reached $1.62bn (£1.19bn).

Hills hopes Burnham might commit to this change – partly thanks to his own taste for UK-made apparel: he buys suits from Manchester-based brand Private White VC, for example. The Labour leader has argued that government procurement should do more to support UK manufacturers rather than prioritising the lowest-cost overseas suppliers.
“Maybe he is the prime minister that sees the value of products that are actually made here,” Hills said.
after newsletter promotion

Grant invested in Blackburn-based military outfitters Cookson & Clegg in 2015 – with their last military contract, making uniforms for the British army, stopping in 2009. They now make the designs for his label Community Clothing, with almost 2,000 employees. He agreed that this legislation would be a boost. “Manufacturing requires steady state business with good visibility [and] long-term demand,” he said. “That’s the kind of thing that government procurement can do.”

He said he would “absolutely” like to bid for these contracts but even if they were for British companies, the process is “unfeasibly complicated … unless you’re a 20,000-employee operation with an enormous clerical department … Something needs to happen on that side, too.”

There has been concern raised over army uniforms being made in China. In July, Iain Duncan Smith dubbed it a security concern, telling the Telegraph it was “tantamount to having our uniforms made by Nazi Germany in the 1930s”.

Grant is also concerned. “We are currently producing a lot of stuff in countries that we do not have the most stable relationships with,” he said. “If something bad were to happen, we would have no resilience at all in our supply chains.”

The entrepreneur said this kind of legislation would go some way to future-proofing employment, by creating jobs for people to make things that will always be needed. “We have to try to think about where jobs are going to come from in the version of our society that we’re going to have in 10 years’ time when AI really starts to kick in,” he added. “Why not just get ahead of it?”

articles.title: Denmark summons Russia’s ambassador after warship fires flares at Danish army helicopter – Europe live
articles.summary:
Danish PM says action was ‘reckless’ as Moscow-attributed security incidents continue to intensify across Europe

Separately, Dutch authorities are investigating a major outage that…

blocks.text: Morning opening: Russia-attributed security incidents intensify across Europe

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa
Denmark has summoned Russia’s ambassador after a Russian warship fired two emergency flares at a Danish army’s helicopter in the Baltic Sea in the latest of incidents attributed to Moscow.
The incident took place during what Denmark said was “a routine” monitoring of the frigate.

“Reckless action from Russia towards Danish military during a routine overflight yesterday. Russian actions are meant to intimidate and divide. They will not succeed. We will not waver,” prime minister Mette Frederiksen said.

blocks.caption: Denmark's prime minister Mette Frederiksen, leader of Denmark's Social Democrats. Photograph: Henning Bagger/Ritzau Scanpix/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Denmark’s foreign minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said the frigate’s behaviour was “completely unacceptable.”
The incident took place amid worsening security situation in Europe.
Separately, Nato fighter jets stationed on the alliance’s eastern flank shot down a drone – believed to be flying from Belarus – over Lithuania last night.
“With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region,” Lithuania’s president Gitanas Nausėda said.
Meanwhile, Poland discovered remains of a suspected Russian drone near its Baltic Sea coast, just a day after a Russian drone hit a train on Ukraine’s border with Poland on Sunday.
It’s Tuesday, 15 September 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.
Key events

items: 4m agoLithuania briefs EU, Nato allies about drone incident, minister says
27m agoSuspected sabotage disrupts Dutch trains
30m agoDanish incident further proof of Russia's 'aggressive' behaviour, former Danish defence minister warns
32m agoMorning opening: Russia-attributed security incidents intensify across Europe

blocks.text: Lithuania briefs EU, Nato allies about drone incident, minister says
Meanwhile, Lithuanian defence minister Kęstutis Budrys said he informed Nato allies about last night’s drone incident, with discussions now ongoing on how to strengthen the alliance’s eastern flank.

blocks.caption: Military police and response vehicles stand parked near the site where a NATO fighter jet shot down a drone near Pratkunai village, Lithuania. Photograph: Lithuanian Army/Reuters

blocks.text: He said Lithuania will be “requesting discussions on these topics both in the EU and Nato, because it is obvious that we all still have a lot of homework to do,” Lithuanian public broadcaster LRT reported.
The drone was shot down by Italian fighter jets taking part in a Nato mission, Italy’s defence ministry confirmed.
Suspected sabotage disrupts Dutch trains
Separately, Dutch authorities are investigating a major outage that affected parts of the country’s railway system, suspecting a possible sabotage after objects were placed on tracks.

blocks.caption: Passenger information at Zwolle station. No trains are running in parts of the country due to a disruption that originated at 13 locations on the tracks in the central Netherlands. Photograph: ANP/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The objects caused failures across the network, affecting several level crossings which ‌disrupted road traffic, Dutch rail infrastructure operator Pro Rail said ​in a statement.
It explained that as a result, “our computer system identifies a section of track as occupied, even though there is no train present.”
“Because safety always comes first, signals automatically turn red. As a result, trains must stop or slow down. Level crossings can also malfunction,” it said.
It did not comment on who could be behind the incident.
Danish incident further proof of Russia's 'aggressive' behaviour, former Danish defence minister warns
Former Danish defence minister Troels Lund Poulsen warned that the frigate incident was a further proof of Russia’s “extremely aggressive” behaviour seeking to “provoke potential conflicts.”
“We should be very aware of that,” he said in comments reported by Danish broadcaster DR.
Defence minister Jeppe Bruus called an all-party meeting on the incident this morning to give political leaders a more detailed read on what happened, DR said.
