articles.title: UK must heed warnings from AI experts, minister says
articles.summary:
Louise Haigh will set out benefits of AI to TUC conference while vowing government will take safety seriously

Ministers must “heed the warnings” from industry leaders about the threat posed…

blocks.text: Ministers must “heed the warnings” from industry leaders about the threat posed by AI as it looks to capitalise on the technology, the first secretary, Louise Haigh, will say on Tuesday.

Labour MPs and peers have called for the government to further cooperate with international partners to build regulation for the technology, after three Anthropic researchers warned that artificial intelligence could kill off humanity within the decade.

Over the weekend, Anthropic urged its competitors and governments to coordinate a global slowdown in AI development. It was backed by many of its rivals including OpenAI, Google DeepMind and X’s Elon Musk.

Haigh will say at a speech at TUC Congress on Tuesday that there are huge potential benefits for health and public services from the use of AI, but that the government would look seriously at the public safety and national security threats with international partners.

On Monday night, one of the founders of Anthropic, Jack Clark, suggested that an artificial intelligence “kill switch” held by a third party may need to be mandatory for companies, saying it was something society “might want to eventually pass rules around”.
One of Anthropic’s biggest rivals and the operator of ChatGPT, OpenAI, has also urged the government to capitalise on renewed fears over AI safety and impose legislation reining in the technology.
“We support stronger UK rules for the handful of companies, including OpenAI, developing the most powerful AI systems,” said OpenAI’s head of policy in Europe, Tom Duff Gordon.
However, the tech company said legislation should be narrowly focused on the most advanced AI labs and not startups working on less powerful systems.

Haigh, whose speech will also lay out priorities for public control of transport, water and energy, will tell trade unions: “AI has enormous potential to transform our public services, make our businesses stronger and deliver new scientific breakthroughs.”

But she will say that the government must “heed the warnings of those who are at the forefront of developing this technology” and “be ready to work with international partners” to prioritise public safety and national security.

MPs and peers on the parliamentary committee for human rights on Monday called for a new regulatory framework for AI in the UK, including an independent oversight body and legislation to protect the public.

blocks.caption: Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, calls on the AI industry to coordinate a slowdown. Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters

blocks.text: It said AI posed a number of threats, from public face-scanning to explicit deepfakes and flagging disciplinary action for workers without reasonable cause.
Alex Sobel, the Labour chair of the human rights committee, said the world was unprepared for dealing with the “potentially dire” consequences of a rapidly developing technology.
“Nowhere in the world, including the UK, has a current legislative and regulatory approach to AI that is fit for purpose,” he said.

A government spokesperson said the UK took the risks from advanced AI “extremely seriously” and recognised the need to keep pace with the evolving technology, including working closely with AI companies and other countries.
after newsletter promotion

“We should not assume that the existing framework will always be sufficient as AI capabilities develop. Any future measures will be evidence-based and focused on the risks we need to address,” said the spokesperson.

But the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, on Tuesday morning said people should not get “hyperbolic” about the risks of AI. He said he did not think it would be particularly helpful to discuss a potential AI “kill switch”, as he felt that had little practical meaning.

He told BBC Radio4’s Today programme: “This is extremely powerful technology, and I think we should never be complacent or naive about the impact it might have. People will be worried by some of the things they’ve heard in the last few weeks, and I think we’ve got to be careful not to get hyperbolic about this either.
“Of course, there are risks, but let’s be frank: there are some tremendous upsides for people as well. Whether it’s public services, healthcare, the contribution to the economy.

“If you regulate it in a way where you’re no longer having access to those frontier developments, that would obviously make us less safe. So I think you’ve got to be proportionate and understanding about this in how we seek to regulate going forward.”

Last Friday, more than 70 MPs and peers urged Andy Burnham to back a ban on the creation of artificial superintelligence (ASI) and lead an international movement to stop its development. The letter came at the end of a week of chilling warnings about the technology, in which experts estimated a 10% chance ASI would wipe out humans.

Among the signatories were former government ministers, along with the former head of the civil service Robin Butler, senior Labour MPs including John McDonnell, and leading Conservative, Liberal Democrat and Scottish National party MPs.
They urged the prime minister to throw the government’s weight behind a bill, tabled in the Commons on Tuesday, that would prohibit ASI.
Sobel, the Labour MP behind the bill, said they wanted Burnham to foster “a clear framework where superintelligent AI cannot be created”.

articles.title: Chocolate faces more climate shocks as study highlights risk of extreme rainfall
articles.summary: As West African cocoa farmers feel the pain of drought, aging trees and competition for farmland, new research out of Harvard says extreme rain is an under-appreciated danger — often hammering…

image.caption: The road to chocolate starts with these beans, and they face many threats including too much rain during the wet season, says a new study. (Francis Kokoroko/Reuters)

blocks.text: As stores around the country trot out hyper-bright boxes of bite-sized chocolate for Halloween, a new peer-reviewed study says there's an underappreciated threat that cocoa production faces.
"People have tended to focus on heat and drought as the main climate risks, and those do matter," said Anna Lea Albright, who led this research as an environmental fellow at Harvard University.
"But what we found is that the strongest weather risk to cocoa is actually heavy rainfall."

Cocoa prices have shot up in recent years and consumers have felt it. Today, a tonne of cocoa hovers around $6,000 US, from a relatively long period of trading around $2,000 to $3,000 US per tonne since 2014. In 2024, the price shot up to over $12,000 US. That was triggered by multiple factors including heavy flooding in West Africa, where more than two million farmers help make it the world's biggest cocoa-growing region.
Boo! Chocolate prices are haunting Halloween shoppers
Leslie Agyare, founder of Three Mountains Cocoa, which works with thousands of farmers in a mountainous region of Ghana, says the rainfall has been a real challenge this year.
"Just imagine, you manage your whole crop, then it's raining so much and you can't harvest because the rains are just too much," Agyare told CBC News from London, England.

But even as climate change, driven by humanity's burning of fossil fuels, is expected to make extreme rainfall events worse, the authors say there are ways to mitigate the impact on this crop that billions of people enjoy.
The risks of rain

The study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, focused on Ghana, the world's second largest producer of cocoa. Using newly available district-level data on production, the authors compared that to rainfall and temperature data.

"When we did that pairing, extreme rainfall during flowering stood out as limiting yields, much more so than temperature during those months," Albright told CBC News from Paris. While cocoa trees need this moisture during the wet season, too much of it can damage the sensitive flowers and young pods.

Wet conditions, Albright says, can also lead to more fungal infections — such as black pod disease — that are spread by splashing rain. The connection between extreme rain and lower yields was also found when the team looked at other cocoa-producing countries, Ecuador and Indonesia.
The research also found a clear climate signal, as warmer air holds more moisture.
"In the satellite record, in rain gauges, we see [evidence] over the past few decades that the heaviest rain events during the wet season are indeed becoming more intense," Albright said.
It's worth noting that in West Africa, El Niño typically reduces the risk of extreme rain but raises the chance of drought, which the region is expecting.
"Now there is a dry period — when they need the rain, there is no rain," Agyare said.
Losing ground

While underappreciated, extreme rainfall's impact on crops isn't a new danger. The study also points out non-climactic risks like aging trees and illegal gold mining, which the UN Food and Agriculture Organization says is part of multiple threats to cocoa production.

Still, Sophia Carodenuto, environmental governance expert and associate professor at the University of Victoria, appreciates the study's findings, but says the key question remains about what farmers can do about it.

"You cannot stop rain, especially extreme rainfall," Carodenuto said, acknowledging the authors hinted at potential interventions involving fungicide and better drainage to mitigate spread of fungal diseases.
For Agyare, the solution requires serious infrastructure investment.
"For some areas that we work with, once it rains, the farmers are trapped in that area," he said. "These are kids that can't go to school. These are families that are stuck."
Many farmers also don't have reservoirs to save some of that rainwater for later use. But a major issue, Agyare says, is a system that puts too much work on the farmer.

"In Ghana, they have two issues. The farmers farm, then they do all the post-harvest themselves," he said, suggesting that splitting the post-harvest duties with other labourers would allow farmers to focus on growing only.
This would allow for collection and processing to be done in a centralized area, avoiding the losses that come from farmers drying their beans on the land and losing them during torrential rains.
A cocoa-free future?
These climate shocks, experts say, are making the job of cocoa farming unattractive in West Africa, and a lot harder.

"I think smallholder farmers are going to be a thing of the past," Agyare said, adding that children don't want to get into what their parents are doing and prefer to find opportunities in the cities.

Carodenuto questions whether adapting to the changing climate will eventually be too much, forcing people out of the job. That will add to the price volatility, which won't just edge out farmers, but push chocolate producers to ditch cocoa in chocolate altogether.

"It's been [a] completely crazy spike in price that I think was a major instigator for a lot of the innovation around cocoa-free chocolate," she told CBC News from Graz, Austria, adding that alternative chocolate is being promoted as less vulnerable, with a more resilient supply chain.

Earlier this year, the world's largest food company, Nestlé, entered the space, partnering with a German cocoa-free chocolate startup. That company makes ChoViva, an alternative that uses sunflower seeds, which Carodenuto says is attractive in terms of supply chain control because it's grown in Europe.
Even a significant rise in price, she says, won't result in a better future for the people who grow and harvest cocoa.
"Chocolate, especially the type of chocolate that you give out for trick-or-treating at Halloween, it's been so historically underpriced," Carodenuto said.
"And who's been footing that bill? It has been smallholder farmers in West Africa."

articles.title: El Salvador court hands down first life sentence for femicide
articles.summary: The landmark conviction comes 42 days after the killing of a woman in Santa Ana who prosecutors said was stalked and harassed by her neighbor.

image.caption: The conviction comes after El Salvador lifted a ban on life imprisonment for murderers, rapists and terrorists earlier this yearImage: Camilo Freedman/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: A court in El Salvador has sentenced a 39-year-old man to life in prison for aggravated femicide, a statement from the prosecutor's office said.
It marks the first time in the country's history that a life sentence has been imposed for femicide.
"Just 42 days after the crime, the Attorney General's Office of the Republic of El Salvador (FGR) obtained a life sentence for aggravated femicide," authorities announced in a post on X.

The defendant was found guilty of stabbing his neighbor to death in the western city of Santa Ana in August. According to prosecutors, Eduardo had been "constantly harassing the victim" before the attack.
The landmark conviction follows a number of recent legal reforms promoted by the country's right-wing president, Nayib Bukele.

blocks.caption: Rights activists accuse the Bukele's government of widespread abusesImage: Alex Brandon/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Bukele's tough-on-crime policies

In April, El Salvador's legislature approved reforms allowing life imprisonment for severe crimes, including homicide, rape, femicide, and terrorism. Previously, the maximum prison sentence was 60 years, with the possibility of reductions for good behavior.

The reform is part of President Bukele's broader strategy to combat crime and insecurity. In 2023, Bukele inaugurated the Terrorism Confinement Center (CECOT), a mega-prison that has been widely criticized by human rights organizations.

Bukele governs under a state of emergency, and his war on gangs has led to the imprisonment of more than 90,000 people while significantly reducing crime and homicide rates. However, UN experts and NGOs have raised concerns about human rights violations, including crimes against humanity, amid the crackdown.

blocks.caption: Gender-based killings went up in El Salvador during the coronavirus pandemicImage: Camilo Freedman/SOPA Images/Zumapress/picture alliance

blocks.text: A longstanding problem

El Salvador has one of the highest rates of femicide in the world. In the 2010s, the rate of killings frequently exceeded 12 femicides per 100,000 women. In 2016 alone, more than 500 women were killed.
According to feminist organizations, COVID-19 lockdowns worsened the situation by exposing more women to domestic violence and limiting access to support services.

articles.title: Iran and America: A tale of two lands and the pistachio between them
articles.summary: The pistachios sold across the US have a surprising history: California's trees trace their roots to Iran. Now both regions face the same threat: their farmland is sinking as groundwater disappears.

image.caption: Pistachios like these sold across the US trace their roots back to IranImage: Svetlanasf/Pond5 Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: Hand-width cracks crisscross Armin's pistachio orchard in southeastern Iran, damaging irrigation pipes and swallowing precious water as the ground beneath him sinks.

"You look, and the earth has opened its mouth, and the water just pours in," Armin says. He has seen the cracks spread rapidly over the past five years, and worries his children may not be able to work the land as his father and grandfather did before him.

Armin, whose real name DW has chosen not to reveal for security reasons, lives in the arid region of Rafsanjan. For generations, farmers there have cultivated the pistachio tree for its small green edible seed used in everything from ice cream to the viral Dubai chocolate.

The region has long covered much of the world's demand for pistachios, but a combination of drought and groundwater extraction for irrigation has made Rafsanjan one of the fastest-sinking areas in Iran. One study found parts of the ground are dropping by up to 37 centimetres a year (14 inches) annually. And that is impacting production.

It's a similar picture in California, where some pistachio farmers are also seeing their ground sink. Joe Coelho's family has cultivated the crop since 2000, and he says while his farm in Fresno is not directly affected, "growers are very aware of the risk."
Some areas nearby are facing serious water problems, he says, adding that "subsidence is absolutely a serious issue in parts of the San Joaquin Valley."

blocks.caption: A pistachio orchard in California's Central Valley, now the world's largest producing regionImage: Photosoundsplanet/Pond5 Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: The same pistachio and the same problems

The link between growers in the two countries goes back to the 1960s when US famers started building a pistachio industry. They did it using an Iranian variety — the pistachio that now dominates most Californian orchards is called Kerman, named after a city near Armin's farm.

California has recently overtaken Iran as the world's largest producer, with most of the crop grown in the Central Valley, where Coelho has his orchard. And though it is one of the world's most productive farming regions, there are places where the ground is sinking by as much as 20 centimeters a year.
Like in Iran, the problem is that more water is being pumped from underground aquifers for crop irrigation than is flowing back in.

"As surface water reliability has declined, growers have relied more heavily on groundwater," Coelho told DW, adding that he has witnessed the land change. "In certain areas, the soil does not have the same structure or water movement it once had."
Pistachio orchards in the Central Valley use around 4% of the valley's crop water. In Rafsanjan, more than nine in ten liters of groundwater go to pistachio orchards.
As groundwater levels drop from overpumping, spaces within the aquifer collapse and the earth above begins to sink in a process called land subsidence.

"Land subsidence in Iran is a man-made hazard, not a natural one like an earthquake," says Ali Beitollahi, who leads subsidence research at Iran's Road, Housing and Urban Development Research Center. "Much of the damage cannot be undone. When an aquifer collapses, it can never hold as much water again as before."

Older farmers in Rafsanjan remember reaching water at depths of just 20 meters, says Armin. Today, many have to drill down to 300 meters. Some farmlands near Armin's are dead or dying, he says, while other orchards have been abandoned as wells dried up.

It's another blow to the struggling farmers, who says the boom driven by food trends like Dubai chocolate never reaches them because international sanctions and global competition have stripped Iran of the markets it once held as the world's biggest pistachio producer.
"We used to be known for quality," he says. "Now we are known for the low price."

blocks.caption: Ripening pistachios in Wasco, California, where growers, like farmers in Rafsanjan, are pumping more groundwater than flows back in and watching their land sinkImage: Ashley Cooper/Pond5 Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: Two pistachio regions, two different responses
The biggest difference between the two regions is how they are responding to the crisis.
In California, the Sustainable Groundwater Management Act (SGMA), passed in 2014, requires water agencies to balance pumping and recharge in groundwater basins by 2040.

Managed aquifer recharge is one method the state is using to do so. It entails allowing water to recharge aquifers in rainy years, by flooding farmlands for instance, as a store for drought. Coelho, who is also the director of sustainability at American Pistachio Growers, is taking part in a pilot project that does just that.

SGMA has seen some progress. According to California's Department of Water Resources, groundwater levels have risen in four out of 10 monitored wells. But large parts of the Central Valley are still sinking.
Helen Dahlke, professor of integrated hydrologic sciences at the University of California, Davis, says recharge alone is not likely to offset decades of overexploitation of groundwater.

"Agriculture is by far the largest consumptive use of water in the Central Valley, so bringing groundwater basins into balance will likely require aligning crop water demand with the long-term water available under a warmer and more variable climate."

In Iran, awareness of groundwater management and subsidence has grown over the past decade among scientists but remains limited, says Ali Beitollahi. He worked on draft subsidence regulations that are currently awaiting government approval. Pointing to the example of Tokyo where subsidence rates fell dramatically after authorities restricted groundwater pumping, he believes the problem could be managed if the state were to act quickly. Though given the current political situation in Iran, swift action is unlikely.
Another urgent step, he says, "is changing how farmers water their fields immediately, and teaching them why it matters."

Most of Rafsanjan's orchards are still flood-irrigated, meaning large amounts of water are lost to evaporation before it reaches plant roots. Armin says he is trying to learn from US growers, but that many older farmers are set in their ways.

blocks.caption: Rows of pistachio trees in California's Central Valley, where in some areas the ground is sinking by as much as 20 centimeters a yearImage: Photosoundsplanet/Pond5 Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: The meaning of a pistachio
Across California's Central Valley, the pressures of a warming climate, drought, and diminishing groundwater are hard to ignore.
"We live with it every day," Coelho says, adding that California's pistachio farmers also need better water policy as well as better infrastructure and protection of water rights.
"Financial sustainability, water sustainability and environmental sustainability are connected," he told DW.
Armin doesn't see a future in pistachio farming. But when he looks at a single pistachio, he sees more than a crop competing for water or a snack on a shelf half a world away.
He sees the history and the present of his family and his region.
"This pistachio sometimes comes from a tree a hundred years old," he says. "It has paid for a wedding, for a child's education, for someone's happiness. Its money comes, and it creates a life."
How a Swiss farmer reshapes his fields to fight drought

articles.title: Ex-Google DeepMind researcher adds to warnings that AI could ‘kill all humans’
articles.summary: Bilal Chughtai writes. 'I earnestly believe that AI has the potential to kill us all, and that we might be running out of time to avoid this outcome'

blocks.text: A former Google DeepMind employee on Monday, September 14, became the latest AI researcher to warn that the technology could “kill all humans,” saying time could be running out to avoid the outcome.

Public alarm about the potential danger posed by AI is growing, after Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon said last week he had resigned, in part because the “people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger then responded to Coxon’s comments, saying he was correct and that he believed there was a greater than 10% chance that AI could kill all humans within the next decade.

“I recently resigned from Google DeepMind, where I worked on AGI safety and alignment research,” Bilal Chughtai wrote on X. “I earnestly believe that AI has the potential to kill us all, and that we might be running out of time to avoid this outcome.”
Chughtai, who co-authored research papers while at Google DeepMind, worked there as a research engineer and left the company in July 2026, according to his LinkedIn profile.
Google did not respond to a request for comment outside regular business hours.

Following recent concerns, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a slowdown in the pace of advanced AI development over the weekend, winning rare backing from SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and sparking a debate over AI “doomerism.”
Chughtai also said that navigating AI safely was possible but would require coordination “to avoid this manic race between AI companies.”
“We need to pace AI development to a speed that society can handle, where emerging risks can be addressed before extreme harm is realised,” he added.
President Donald Trump, however, has dismissed the warnings, saying on social media the AI industry’s call for regulation is a “hoax.”

I recently resigned from Google DeepMind, where I worked on AGI safety and alignment research. At Google, I witnessed AI development first hand. I too am extremely concerned by the default trajectory of this technology. I earnestly believe that AI has the potential to kill us…— bilal 🔶 (@bilalchughtai_) September 14, 2026

articles.title: Jaguar Land Rover in talks to sell Defender to Nato countries
articles.summary: Carmaker builds on relationship with British armed forces by seeking to cash in on Europe’s rearmament drive

blocks.text: Jaguar Land Rover is in talks with Nato countries about selling them the newly revamped Defender military vehicle, as the UK-based carmaker seeks to tap into Europe’s defence spending boom.

It is also among carmakers bidding for a UK defence ministry contract worth £900m to replace an ageing fleet of Land Rovers that have been out of production since 2016, competing with General Motors and the UK’s Ineos.

JLR, owned by India’s Tata Motors, has set up a new Defender defence division to explore new partnerships to supply vehicles for people and equipment transportation to defence sectors around the world.

The carmaker is trying to expand beyond its relationship with the British armed forces to exploit a spending boom by Nato countries racing to rearm, as it faces weaker demand elsewhere coupled with higher costs.

JLR insisted that the move, which was first reported by the Financial Times, was not related to its planned 4,000 job cuts globally, as part of an effort to save £1.7bn. It is slashing costs as it struggles with tough trading conditions, Donald Trump’s tariff wars and the fallout from a damaging cyber-attack last year.

As he unveiled three new variants of the Defender Wolf Series II, the next-generation military vehicle, Patrick McGillycuddy, the Defender managing director, said: “Through our newly established Defender defence division, we will offer Defender Wolf Series II to defence organisations worldwide, while also bidding for the UK Ministry of Defence light mobility vehicle tender.”

He said the new 4x4s were “exceptionally robust and versatile,” and added that their lightweight aluminium monocoque construction, with a stiffer body structure, means they can be adapted to the “wide range of roles and operational requirements demanded by military organisations”.

“It is a modern successor to the world-famous Defender Wolf and Land Rovers that have served the British armed forces for more than 70 years,” he said. The new Defender series is designed and engineered in the UK, with an engine built in Wolverhampton.

JLR also wants to break into the $80bn (£59bn) US pickup truck market with a local version of its Defender vehicle. The Defender pickup will be built in the US through a joint venture with Chrysler carmaker Stellantis, the Sunday Times reported at the weekend.
It is the most high-profile UK carmaker to pivot the newly booming defence sector as manufacturers grapple with a transition to electric vehicles and rising competition from Chinese rivals.

The site would switch production from cars to heavy-duty trucks that carry anti-missile systems for the maker of Israel’s Iron Dome, Arrow ‌and David’s ⁠Sling air and missile defence systems.

“These plans involve the potential manufacture of systems and components for air defence systems for Germany and Europe,” Volkswagen said, adding the cooperation could pave the way for further such deals.

articles.title: Europe launches two climate observation satellites
articles.summary: The European Space Agency has put two satellites into orbit to take a closer look at the impact of climate change. One of them will focus particularly on plant life.

image.caption: The two satellites were carried by a Vega-C rocket, seen here lifting off in French GuianaImage: Ronan Lietar/AFP

blocks.text: Two satellites designed to enhance the monitoring of extreme weather events linked to climate change have been successfully sent into orbit by the European Space Agency (ESA).

The Vega-C rocket carrying the Sentinel-3C and Flex satellites lifted off from the Kourou space center in French Guiana at 10:21 p.m. Monday (0121 GMT Tuesday), with the two spacecraft entering sun-synchronous orbit within two hours of lift-off.
What will the Flex satellite do?

The Flex (Fluorescence Explorer) satellite aims to provide data on the impact of heat waves on plant matter by monitoring the very faint fluorescence emitted by plants when they carry out photosynthesis.
That fluorescence gives an indication of how efficiently vegetation is converting sunlight and carbon dioxide into energy.
The measurements provided by the satellite will thus "help scientists assess plant health, ecosystem productivity and the effects of environmental stress and climate change," according to ESA.
The €350 million ($403.5 million) mission is planned to last three years.
The satellite will orbit the Earth 14 times a day, revisiting particular locations every 27 days.
What is the role of the Sentinel-3C satellite?
The Sentinel-3C satellite is to collect data from the marine environment, including temperature, wave height and ocean currents.
It will also monitor land use and land cover with the aim of optimizing yields to prevent food crises.
Sentinel-3C is part of Copernicus, the Earth observation component of the EU’s space program.
Simonetta Cheli, the director of Earth Observation Programmes at the ESA, described the missions as "essential" in helping with the "climate change we are experiencing."

articles.title: US confirms it has weapons in space
articles.summary: The US Space Force justified the weapons deployment by citing its two biggest geopolitical rivals — Russia and China.

image.caption: The Space Force, a relatively new branch of the US military, was created by US President Donald Trump in 2019Image: Cover-Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: The United States has weapons deployed in spatial orbit, the US Space Force said, confirming the existence of such capabilities for the first time.

"The US has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action," a US Space Force spokesperson said in a press release. The statement did not provide specifics on the weapons in question.

"Space control encapsulates the mission areas required to contest and control the space domain — employing kinetic and non-kinetic means to affect adversary capabilities," it said, adding that "these capabilities can be employed for offensive and defensive purposes."
US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink also confirmed the existence of US weapons in space, while speaking at the Air, Space and Cyber Conference on Monday.

The Space Force, the US military's arm dedicated to space, justified the weapons deployment by citing its two biggest geopolitical rivals — Russia and China. It said both countries pose a threat to American interests in space.

China "develops and operates space and counterspace capabilities as part of a military modernization strategy," while Russia "views space as a warfighting domain and believes space supremacy will be a decisive factor in future conflicts," the statement read.
AI and satellites: The new nuclear watchdogs?
The final frontier
The militarization of space is an issue as old as the race to space itself.
In 1967, the world's biggest superpowers and other nations signed the Outer Space Treaty addressing the single biggest concern — deployment of nuclear weapons in space.

Since then, Russia, US, India and China have been exploring ways to fight in space outside of that treaty. That includes targeting each other's satellites critical for military communication, navigation and surveillance.

articles.title: MV June Aster captain turns up five days after ferry fire off Coron
articles.summary: The captain of MV June Aster, missing since a fire tore through the ferry off Coron, Palawan and killed 76 people, showed up at the shipping company's office on Monday, September 14.

blocks.text: September 15, 2026 | 3:22pm

The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) recovered 30 bodies from MV June Aster, which were brought to the Port of Borac, on September 12, 2026 afternoon following the ferry fire off Coron, Palawan on September 9, 2026.

MANILA, Philippines — The captain of MV June Aster, missing since a fire tore through the ferry off Coron, Palawan and killed 76 people, showed up at the shipping company's office on Monday, September 14.

This was confirmed by the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) in a statement issued Tuesday, September 15, where it also said it now plans to gather more details from him about the fire that blazed MV June Aster and his whereabouts after the incident.
Capt. Roel Sarmiento went on his own to the Palawan office of Atienza Interisland Ferries Inc., the vessel's operator, on September 14, the PCG said Tuesday.
Dindo Macalinao, a human resources manager of the company, accompanied him.

PCG spokesperson Comm. Noemie Cayabyab said investigators will ask Sarmiento about "the circumstances surrounding the incident, including his whereabouts following the fire and what transpired before his appearance."
With Sarmiento accounted for, the PCG now counts 44 survivors, 76 recovered dead and 12 missing among the 132 people aboard.
Search and retrieval operations are still ongoing for the 12 missing.
The ticket manifest listed 134, but two people later said they did not board the ferry.
Authorities have not determined what caused the fire, though survivors told investigators they heard explosions from the cargo hold before the flames spread.
The fire started in a cargo hold carrying an electric vehicle, motorcycles and a forklift.
The ferry had passed a pre-departure inspection in Manila and a Vessel Safety Enforcement Inspection in March.
The Maritime Industry Authority has opened its own probe into the incident.

The June Aster left Baseco port in Manila at 8:13 p.m. on September 8 and was due in Coron at 6 p.m. the next day. Fire broke out around 6:45 p.m. on September 9, about 2.2 kilometers northeast of Barangay Marcilla.
Smoke and heat kept responders off the ship for almost 40 hours, until the PCG declared the fire out on the morning of September 11.

The former presidential spokesperson said that officials should verify their facts.

Following Remulla’s initial statement in the press briefing, GMA News Online sought further confirmation and details on the supposed denial of Roque’s asylum bid.

articles.title: Sara Duterte trial, Sept. 15: VP's net worth, business interests
articles.summary: Prosecutors zoomed in on key documents on Tuesday, Sept. 15, showing that Vice President Sara Duterte's declared net worth rose from P7.25 million in 2007 to P98.66 million in 2025.

blocks.text: September 15, 2026 | 2:59pm

MANILA, Philippines — Prosecutors zoomed in on key documents on Tuesday, Sept. 15, showing that Vice President Sara Duterte's declared net worth rose from P7.25 million in 2007 to P98.66 million in 2025.
The records also show she declared no cash on hand or in the bank from 2019 onward.

Karen Batu, officer-in-charge of the Ombudsman's Central Records Division, read the figures from Duterte's Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALNs). On cross-examination, the defense had Batu confirm that SALN forms have no separate line for cash and no column for the acquisition cost of business interests. Batu also said her office does not verify the veracity of what officials declare.

Tuesday was the second day of evidence presentation under Article II, which accuses Duterte of amassing unexplained wealth, making false SALN declarations and keeping her business interests as vice president.
Presiding Officer Sen. Chiz Escudero reiterated that SALNs filed before 2022 serve only as a baseline, since Duterte faces charges only for acts during her term.
Here are the three highlights from today's proceedings.
1. Declared net worth rose; cash declarations stopped in 2019
Batu read Duterte's declared net worth based on her own SALNs. It was P7.25 million in 2007, P65,04 million in 2021, her last filed SALN before becoming vice president, and P98.66 million in 2025.

Batu said Duterte declared cash on hand and in bank in her SALNs from 2007 to 2012 and from 2016 to 2018, in amounts from P2 million to about P6.37 million. She said the 2019 and 2020 SALNs declared none. "For SALNs 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025, no cash on hand or in bank was declared," Batu said.

Batu also read the business interests declared by Duterte and her husband, lawyer Manases Carpio. The 2024 SALN lists 10, including Metro City Chow Foods Corp. and Gencorp Industries Inc., among others.
Asked who swore to the SALNs, Batu said, "The vice president herself."
2. Escudero, defense cite gaps in SALN form

Counsel to the prosecution James Bryan Ibrahim Alih argued that Section 8 of Republic Act 6713, the Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees, requires personal property, including stocks, to be declared with its acquisition cost. "It has to be itemized," he said.

Under Escudero's questioning, Batu confirmed that the SALN form has no space for the acquisition cost of business interests. "You're correct in the law, but even if the official wanted to, where and how will he put it when we're supposed to fill out a prescribed form?" Escudero asked Alih.

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said the missing values for the acquisition cost, could mean Duterte's declared net worth is understated. "Without concluding anything, yes, it can be a possibility," Alih said.
On cross-examination, defense lawyer Justin Nicol Gular had Batu confirm that the CSC's 1994, 2013, 2015 and 2025 forms have no separate cash line and no business acquisition-cost column.

Asked about the 2025 rules, she said there was "no prohibition on lumping." Alih noted that the 2013 guidelines allow collective declaration for personal properties collectively acquired or of minimal value.
Alih told Sen. Risa Hontiveros, "I do not recall any law that would specifically say that it has to be separate."
Earlier, Batu told Sen. Joel Villanueva that in her own experience, cash was declared separately even before the 2025 rules.
3. Ombudsman does not review SALN contents; no record of Duterte's 2013 exit SALN
Batu said her office, as repository, checks only that SALNs use the correct form and are signed, dated and paginated. "But the contents, your honor, we do not review," she told Sen. Erwin Tulfo.
She said the Ombudsman's Field Investigation Office has no access to submitted SALNs unless it requests them for an investigation.
On cross, Batu said she has "no personal knowledge on the listed personal properties" beyond what the SALNs state.
She agreed she is not competent to say whether Duterte's SALNs are irregular. Escudero had ruled earlier that Batu was "not testifying as to the truth of the content stated therein."
Batu said the Ombudsman has no record of Duterte's 2013 and 2014 SALNs, as relayed to them by its Mindanao office. "For 2013, she has no exit SALN," Batu said.
Escudero noted that Duterte's term as Davao City mayor ended June 30, 2013.
Escudero said that as far as he knew, Duterte corrected her 2016 and 2019 SALNs by letter on minor matters. Batu said the Ombudsman's records show only one amendment, to the 2025 SALN, filed in June.

The court will hold no trial tomorrow, September 16. It will instead hear retired Chief Justices Artemio Panganiban and Reynato Puno and retired Associate Justice Adolfo Azcuna on the 16-vote conviction threshold. Retired Chief Justice Hilario Davide Jr. submitted a written memorandum.
Testimony from Gerardo del Rosario of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on companies linked to Duterte and Carpio was moved to September 21 and 22.
Batu said the SALNs presented in court were redacted to hide the names of Duterte's minor children.

articles.title: Ortega on Sara Duterte's call for Marcos to resign: 'Mauna siya'
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte should resign first before calling on President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to step down, House Deputy Speaker Paolo Ortega V of La Union said Tuesday.

blocks.text: Published September 15, 2026 2:42pm
Vice President Sara Duterte should resign first before calling on President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to step down, House Deputy Speaker Paolo Ortega V of La Union said Tuesday.

Ortega was responding to Duterte’s comments last weekend following her arraignment in the grave threat case she is facing over her alleged threat to kill Marcos, First Lady Liza Marcos and then-House Speaker Martin Romualdez.
Duterte said Marcos should resign because he had allegedly forsaken the voters who elected him by failing to provide sufficient government assistance amid massive flooding.
“Pinipilit niya ang President na mag-resign. Mauna na lang muna siya para mabawasan ‘yung mga hinaharap niyang problema ngayon,” Ortega said in a press conference.
(She is forcing the President to resign. She should do it first to reduce the problems she is facing now.)

Ortega was referring to the impeachment case filed against Duterte, which includes allegations of betrayal of public trust and culpable violation of the Constitution over her alleged threat to have President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Marcos and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez killed.
“Mauna lang siya mag-resign kasi siya ang nakaisip. She must set an example then,” Ortega added.
(She should do it first because she was the one who thought of it.)
Ortega also said the country should not be subjected to the Vice President’s whims.
“Hindi naman siya ang masusunod sa buong Pilipinas (She cannot order the entire nation around),” Ortega said.
GMA News Online has reached out to lawyer Paolo Panelo, Duterte's spokesperson, and will update this story once a response is received.

Under Article VII, Section 8 of the 1987 Constitution, if a sitting Philippine president resigns, the Vice President automatically becomes President and serves the unexpired portion of the President's term. — MCG, GMA News

articles.title: What would it take to make India’s cities better – and safer?
articles.summary:
After a five-storey building collapsed in Delhi, focus is on how urban areas can adapt to growing populations. Plus, Ahmedabad’s ace newspaper delivery driver goes viral

Recently, I may have…

blocks.text: Recently, I may have saved a woman’s life on the road. Somehow, this was something I had expected to happen.

On that day, I saw a truck leave a construction site with a tangled wire trailing behind. I frantically looked to see what the wire was attached to and spotted the scaffolding a few meters ahead. I shrieked and grabbed the hand of the woman walking in front of me just as the metal pipes came crashing down. We hugged for a brief second, and then walked our separate ways.

Mumbai (pictured top) is a city that is being made every day, and so much of the Bandra-Khar area that I inhabit is never not under construction. Since I moved here from Seoul earlier this year, I have learned to be hypervigilant every time I walk the streets.

I was reminded of that moment last week as news broke about the collapse of a five-storey building in Delhi, which killed seven people. Authorities had flagged safety concerns in the neighbourhood months earlier, the Hindustan Times reported, after 23 people died in a fire at another building.

As the world’s most populous country, India can feel like a place where life can be startlingly cheap, and people die every day in tragedies that could have been prevented. According to analysis of government data by the Times of India, between 2020 and 2004 nearly 33,000 deaths occurred due to building collapses, fires or people falling into pits and maintenance holes.

The collapse in Delhi has prompted questions, once again, about the state of urban infrastructure in India’s biggest cities. At a time when the country is undertaking a rapid infrastructure boom – new airports, high-speed expressways, luxury residential towers– daily life in cities like Delhi, Mumbai or Bengaluru appears to be deteriorating.

Indian cities are not walkable, they rank among the worst for air quality, construction is poorly regulated, seasonal flooding is common and waste management remains under pressure. These challenges are only going to increase; the World Bank expects India’s urban population to double, going up to 951 million, by 2050. More than half of the urban infrastructure the country will need by then has yet to be built, it said.

blocks.caption: The problem with India’s roads begins with on-street parking, believe some experts. Photograph: DB Pictures/Alamy

blocks.text: So, what would it take to make our cities better and safer? The experts I spoke to broadly agreed that Indian cities don’t lack rules as much as the political will and institutional machinery to enforce them.

For infrastructure veteran Vinayak Chatterjee, one solution lies in giving urban local bodies more power. He points to a constitutional amendment from 1992 that was meant to strengthen municipalities and give them greater responsibility over urban planning. “But it remains largely unimplemented – in spirit and will. It is a serious matter that affects the very fabric of our urban existence,” said Chatterjee, founder of the Infravision Foundation.

Rahul Goel, an expert on transportation safety and a professor at the Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi, believes the problem with India’s roads begins with on-street parking. “People are using public space for personal use. Everything becomes better when you remove on-street parking,” he said, arguing that freeing up roads would make pedestrians and cyclists safer, reduce traffic jams and make walking easier.

In other cities in the global south, from Bangkok to Manila to Cape Town, one cannot just park their car on the road to run errands, Goel said. He described it as a governance failure, saying there is a need to create more parking spaces and perhaps have civil defense personnel or municipal workers enforce fines.

“Our streets are self-run,” Goel said. “That’s why they are in complete disarray.” He pointed to the Delhi Metro as an example of a space where people follow rules and things are orderly. “When rules are enforced, people follow them.”

blocks.caption: People vacate buildings marked for demolition in Satya Niketan after the collapse of a five-storey building. Photograph: Vishal Kapoor/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The same gap between rules and enforcement is evident at construction sites.

India has detailed guidelines for construction approvals, including how traffic must be managed, what signage must be put up, and creating paths for pedestrians. But compliance remains a significant problem, says Geetam Tiwari, emeritus professor at Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi. In an audit of construction sites on highways, including bridges, Tiwari and her colleagues found widespread violations. Contractors had a financial incentive to complete projects quickly with payments being tied to the pace of construction, she said, adding that penalties for violations were low enough that it was cheaper to simply pay the fine than make fixes.

For unsafe buildings and unauthorised renovations, Tiwari said, the solution also requires bringing stakeholders together: resident associations, landlords, lessees and local authorities to conduct audits, raise awareness and penalise contractors who violate safety requirements. Actions, she said, that should not wait for the next tragedy.

In the aftermath of the Delhi case, the high court has directed authorities to inspect student accommodations for safety. Building owners have been arrested and several municipal officials in charge of the area have been suspended.

A similar governance deficit shows up when it comes to air pollution, another long-time challenge for Indian cities. Ronak Sutaria, founder and CEO of Respirer Living Sciences, has been working on one aspect of this issue: by developing affordable air-quality monitors for construction sites. Respirer’s air-quality monitors are now installed in 5,000 locations across 10 cities in India, helping authorities identify pollution hotspots. (Some cities, including Mumbai, require construction sites to monitor pollution levels.)

“A number of sites are getting alerts [from authorities] and are taking dust-suppression measures, for instance, to bring down [pollution] levels. So, the entire loop is sort of working,” Sutaria said.

Indian cities continue to grow, but the question is whether governance can keep pace. On that afternoon in Bandra, I recall thinking how lucky the woman and I were not to be grievously injured. But we shouldn’t have to rely on luck to survive.
What else we’re reading about

blocks.caption: Xi Jinping, far right, with Russia’s Vladimir Putin and India’s Narendra Modi at this year’s Brics summit. Photograph: Alexander Kazakov/Sputnik/Kremlin Pool/EPA

blocks.text: New Delhi declaration | The Brics summit held in New Delhi over the weekend adopted a declaration with Iran and the United Arab Emirates agreeing to a late-stage compromise on the language about the war in the Middle East. Chinese president, Xi Jinping, who visited India for the first time in almost seven years, announced that China would helm the group’s presidency for the next year.

Political donations | An investigation by the BBC’s Shubhangi Misra claimed that six unrecognised political parties registered in Gujarat received donations of £132m (Rs 1,700 crore) in 2023-24, higher than the income of national parties excluding the BJP. Despite fielding few candidates and evidence of little political activity, the high amounts expose glaring gaps in oversight of political finances.

Women’s health support | Two south Indian states, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, have recently announced policies aimed at supporting women through perimenopause and menopause. Karnataka plans to introduce a women’s health programme that will integrate menopause into the public health system. Tamil Nadu will assess the physical and mental health needs of perimenopausal women.
after newsletter promotion

Calling all emerging writers | Applications are open for South Asia Speaks, a wonderful platform for emerging writers from the region offering free, year-long mentorship and resources to develop a book-length project. The deadline is 30 September – find out more and apply here.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste

blocks.caption: Poet Parag Pawan’s book.

blocks.text: This week, write and professor Amitava Kumar (@amitavawriter), whose latest book, The Social Life of Trains, explores how railways helped shape India’s national identity, suggests the work of a poet he discovered on Instagram:

“Can I begin with a confession? I have been a professor of literature for more than three decades, but I don’t often understand poems. How lovely it is, then, to discover a poet whose lines are as clear and beautiful as the dawn! Recently, I came across the poems of a young Hindi poet named Parag Pawan. They spoke to me and, more importantly, they spoke to our moment. I immediately sat down to translate them into English.

A series of his poems could be translated as Poems for the Unemployed. One of the poems, sharp and precise, begins with the funny, acerbic lines: ‘On the topic of our unemployment / the prime minister gives speeches / but he doesn’t give us jobs. / He works for eighteen hours / while we believe that asking anyone to work / for more than eight hours / is exploitation.’”
Count it
A number worth knowing

blocks.caption: Umar Khalid, who has spent six years in an Indian jail without trial.

blocks.text: That’s the number of days Umar Khalid has spent in jail since his arrest on 13 September 2020 – without trial. Last week, the student activist wrote a searing account describing the daily drudgery of life in prison, published in The Quint. Earlier this year, in his first interview since being jailed, Khalid told the Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Peterson: “Humanity is a privilege that is not granted to people like me.”
Vibe check

blocks.caption: World’s fastest paper delivery service? Ayan Shaikh at work in Ahmedabad. Photograph: Instagram

blocks.text: As more people read news online, watching Ayan Shaikh (@paperboy_ayan) delivering newspapers with serious swag gave me great joy and some hope. The 22-year-old from Ahmedabad posts videos of it on Instagram, and it’s a feat to watch. Watch his papers swerve, reach gravity-defying heights and land with pinpoint accuracy and tell me his deliveries don’t rival Jasprit Bumrah.

Delivering papers was Shaikh’s first job after he dropped out of school. He spent four years mastering the techniques that would allow him to make faster deliveries to earn more money. The first video, filmed by his friend, had 20m views and a recent one has crossed 128m, more views than many Bollywood stars might command. He starts his day at 4:30am, making 300 deliveries in two hours, before he begins a second shift as a gig worker for quick commerce apps.

“I think people love [the videos] because I do it passionately … from my heart,” he said. “If you do things dedicatedly, anything is possible. It won’t work out once, twice, thrice, but it might on the fourth attempt.”
Get in touch

Do you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us at thisisindia@theguardian.com and we may include your response in a future issue.

articles.title: UBJP bet overtakes BARMM deputy speaker in Lanao del Sur 4th District race
articles.summary: The United Bangsamoro Justice Party’s Lampa Pandi is on the verge of defeating Bangsamoro Parliament Deputy Speaker Amenodin Sumagayan

blocks.text: WINNER. United Bangsamoro Justice Party candidate Lampa Pandi.
Pandi's Facebook page
The United Bangsamoro Justice Party’s Lampa Pandi is on the verge of defeating Bangsamoro Parliament Deputy Speaker Amenodin Sumagayan

COTABATO CITY, Philippines – Lampa Pandi, United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) candidate and ex-mayor of Poona Bayabao town in Lanao del Sur, is one step closer to winning the electoral race in his province’s 4th District.

Pandi has received 38,505 votes so far, according to 98.60% of total election returns as of Tuesday, September 15, 1:59 pm, a day after the first-ever Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) parliamentary polls.

He is on the verge of defeating Bangsamoro Parliament Deputy Speaker Amenodin Sumagayan, whose family holds power in the municipality of Taraka. Running as the candidate of the Serbisyong Inklusibo-Alyansang Progresibo Party, Sumagayan — a former mayor of Taraka — obtained 37,324 votes.
The bottom two candidates in the race are engineer Camal Abdul, the bet of the Progresibong Bangsamoro Party, and independent candidate Johari Comadug.

According to Pandi’s Facebook page, he was Poona Bayabao mayor from 2007 to 2016. He previously served as assistant and officer-in-charge regional health secretary of BARMM’s predecessor, the now-defunct Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao. – Rappler.com

articles.title: UBJP’s Gauraki to take Lanao del Sur 2nd District seat in BARMM Parliament
articles.summary: Hamza Gauraki is set to win against an Adiong-backed candidate, an independent bet, and a Progresibong Bangsamoro Party candidate in Lanao del Sur's 2nd District

blocks.text: BARMM POLLS. The bet of the United Bangsamoro Justice Party in Lanao del Sur's 2nd District is Hamza Gauraki, former mayor of Kapai.
Municipality of Kapai's Facebook page
Hamza Gauraki is set to win against an Adiong-backed candidate, an independent bet, and a Progresibong Bangsamoro Party candidate in Lanao del Sur's 2nd District

COTABATO CITY, Philippines – Hamza Gauraki, former mayor of Kapai town in Lanao del Sur, emerged as the victor for the province’s 2nd District in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao or BARMM parliamentary elections held on Monday, September 14.
Gauraki received 41,393 votes, according to 98.80% of total election returns as of Tuesday, September 15, 12:59 pm.
The former Kapai mayor is from the influential Gauraki political dynasty. His wife, Aidah, is the incumbent mayor of Kapai.
Gauraki ran under the banner of the United Bangsamoro Justice Party, which is led by Ahod “Al Haj Murad” Ebrahim, chairman of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front.
His closest competitor is Alexander Alonto Jr., the bet of the Adiong-led Serbisyong Inklusibo-Alyansang Progresibo Party, who has 36,477 votes. Alonto can no longer overtake Gauraki.
Other bets trailing in the four-way race are independent candidate Salahuden Edres and Samanudin Bazer from the Progresibong Bangsamoro Party. – Rappler.com

articles.title: ‘I was being polite’: prominent athlete continued texting Alan Jones after alleged assaults due to his reputation, trial hears
articles.summary:
Witness tells court he sent Jones friendly messages after two alleged assaults because he had been generous to him

  • Listen to the podcast

blocks.text: A prominent athlete who has accused Alan Jones of twice kissing him without consent has told a Sydney court he continued to text the broadcaster after the alleged assaults because Jones was powerful and had been generous to him.
The witness, who is appearing for a second day in the seventh week of a lengthy trial, agreed he had sent Jones friendly messages after the two alleged assaults.
He was asked by prosecutor Georgina Wright SC why he wished Jones a happy Christmas and new year after the defendant allegedly kissed him and pressed his genitalia against his leg.
“I was being polite,” he said. “I made reference [yesterday] to the challenges of the relationship between myself and the defendant.
“Someone that has a presence in the media, someone that has a reputation around what they do.
“Someone also who’s been generous to me at times in my life.
“That’s why I believe I am wishing them the best for Christmas even though an incident has occurred prior to this at their house.”
The former athlete, who is known as complainant M, is the third of six complainants to give evidence.
Jones, 85, has pleaded not guilty to 20 charges of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching.

Defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC took the witness through his evidence-in-chief about the flattering texts Jones sent him, which included: “If someone hasn’t told you, let me be the person who tells you that you’re special.”
M has told the court the “incredibly overwhelmingly complimentary” texts made him feel uncomfortable.
Bashir suggested some of the texts were reflective of the truth.
“You were an extraordinary athlete, weren’t you?” Bashir asked.
“Thank you,” M replied.
“You were something special, weren’t you?” Bashir asked.
“I believe I still am,” he said.
after newsletter promotion

M has testified that the two unwanted kisses, one at an event in 2015 and one at Jones’s Macquarie Street apartment in 2020 were a shock and not consensual: “I did not want to be kissed by him in that way.”
After the unwanted kiss near his lips at the event, the court heard Jones sent him a text that said: “You looked great. I love you. I hope you can feel my kisses, darling”.

M told the court on Tuesday he was seated in the harbourside apartment, and alone with Jones, when “the defendant was standing over the top of me beginning to kiss me. As it got closer to my lips I started to move into a standing position.”
“I felt there was something behind me when I tried to get away from the defendant that prevented me from doing so.”
He has testified that he said “OK mate” in a defiant tone, which indicated “get away from me” and he left abruptly.

M said his last communication with Jones was in 2022. When the Sydney Morning Herald published an investigation about sexual allegations against Jones in 2023, he told three friends that “something similar has happened to me”, and later went to police to report the alleged incidents.
Under cross-examination by Bashir, M agreed he had been friends with Jones for 20 years and that the broadcaster had “been a vocal supporter” of his and had helped him through “personal crises”.
“I had had a close relationship over a period of time,” he said. “It was both professional and there was a personal side.”
“He has helped me,” he agreed.
M agreed that he replied to some of Jones’s messages with “love, hugs and kisses”.

The former athlete is the first complainant to choose to give evidence in a closed court and come face to face with Jones in the Downing Centre court room. The media were given permission to cover the case from a separate location.
The trial before judge Glenn Walsh continues.

articles.title: Jean Nassif swears during Icac evidence and declares ‘no one can make me shut up’
articles.summary: Fugitive property developer beams in from Beirut bedroom to declare ‘I’m not corrupt’ and waves handwritten notes at counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer

blocks.text: Fugitive property developer Jean Nassif has declared he cannot be silenced as he ranted about “crook” politicians and proclaimed his innocence during an expletive-laden tirade at the New South Wales anti-corruption watchdog.
Nassif, 58, on Tuesday dialled into the Independent Commission Against Corruption inquiry via video link from his Beirut bedroom.

As part of its investigation into allegations against people associated with the NSW Liberals, Icac is examining whether Liberal figures anticipated receiving $2m in prohibited donations from Nassif, in exchange for political outcomes, including damage to the career of former NSW Liberal minister David Elliott and the removal of then-building commissioner David Chandler.
But as he was questioned on Tuesday by counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer SC, Nassif launched into a diatribe about Elliot and Chandler, NSW politics, and the state of the construction industry.

He claimed Elliot had delayed approvals to put pressure on him, accused the building commissioner of lying about defects in his buildings, and said he was “fed up with the budget and the way the government is ruled by corrupt politicians”.
Dwyer repeatedly urged Nassif to remain calm, asked him not to shout at her, and tried to pose further questions, but the property developer would not be stopped.
“I want to prove my point, if you don’t want me to prove myself, I’ll withdraw from all this nonsense,” he told the commission.

Showing handwritten notes to the camera, Nassif said: “I’m taking notes … so stop fucking putting words in my mouth. This is a public hearing, and I know what you’re doing. You want to show the public that I am corrupt. I’m not corrupt.”

blocks.caption: Jean Nassif beamed into an Icac inquiry from his Beirut bedroom. Photograph: Icac

blocks.text: The assistant commissioner Fabian Gleeson SC told Nassif to take a breath.
after newsletter promotion
“The purpose of this inquiry is to get to the truth of certain allegations,” Gleeson said.
“It’s not for you to attack other people. You can be passionate about that, but this is not the forum for those complaints.”
Nassif responded by saying: “No, no, no, no. There is no one [who] can make me shut up. If you guys are not going to accept the problem, I need to pull out now.”
Nassif initially appeared at Icac on Monday. The former Toplace boss, who fled to Lebanon in 2022, produced a medical certificate to excuse himself from a scheduled appearance earlier this month.
The inquiry continues.

articles.title: Sara Duterte's net worth grew from P7.2M in 2007 to P98.6M in 2025
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte"s declared net worth ever since she entered public office soared from P7.250 million in 2007 to P98.656 million in 2025, based on her Statements of Assets, Liabilities,…

blocks.text: Published September 15, 2026 1:59pm

Vice President Sara Duterte’s declared net worth ever since she entered public office soared from P7.250 million in 2007 to P98.656 million in 2025, based on her Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALNs).

Office of the Ombudsman Records Division officer-in-charge Atty. Karen Batu, a witness presented by the House prosecution panel, confirmed this during her direct examination on the 25th day of the impeachment trial.

“2007, madam witness, we started at P7 million, based on your testimony—P7,250,497. And in all the years of the Vice President, umakyat na ngayon sa P98 million ang kanyang net worth habang siya ay nago-gobyerno. Tama po ba based sa testimony ninyo?” private prosecutor James Bryan Alih asked Batu.

(In 2007, madam witness, we started at P7 million—based on your testimony, P7,250,497. And over the years of the Vice President’s tenure, her net worth has now risen to P98 million while she’s in government service. Is that correct, based on your testimony?)
The witness answered in the affirmative.
“Based po doon sa mga binasa kong SALN, ‘yun po ang halagang naka-declare sa kanyang mga sinubmit na SALN sa Office of the Ombudsman,” Batu said.
(Based on the SALNs I read, that is the amount declared in the SALNs she submitted to the Office of the Ombudsman.)
Based on Duterte’s SALNs, as presented by the prosecution during the trial, she declared the following net worth from 2007 to 2025:

items: 2007 - P7.250 million
2008 - P18.493 million
2009 - P18.281 million
2010 - P16.242 million
2011 - P14.271 million
2012 - P22.116 million
2016 - P34.895 million
2017 - P44.828 million
2018 - P49.699 million
2019 - P55.613 million
2020 - P56.583 million
2021 - P65.308 million
2022 - P71.658 million
2023 - P77.508 million
2024 - P88.512 million
2025 - P98.656 million

blocks.text: Alih specifically flagged the big increase in Duterte’s declared net worth from 2007 to 2008.
“Tama po, madam witness ‘no, after one year lang sa public office, sobra doble na ‘yung tinaas ng kanyang net worth, based on the records only?” Alih asked.
(Is it correct, madam witness, that after just one year in public office, her net worth increased to more than double, based solely on the records?)
Defense counsel Justin Gular objected to the line of questioning, moving to strike it off the record.
“Again, Your Honor, we move to strike those statements. Objection to those statements,” Gular said.
Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero approved to strike Alih’s specific statement off the record.

Before joining politics, Duterte briefly served as a court attorney at the Supreme Court in 2006. She was elected vice mayor of Davao City from 2007 to 2010 and became the youngest and first lady mayor of the city from 2010 to 2013.
In 2016, she was elected again as Davao City mayor and served for two consecutive terms until she decided to run for vice president in 2022. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Sara Duterte had no declared cash on hand, bank in seven years -- witness
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte did not declare any cash on hand and in bank from 2019 to 2025, based on her Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALNs), Office of the Ombudsman Records…

blocks.text: Published September 15, 2026 1:52pm

Vice President Sara Duterte did not declare any cash on hand and in bank from 2019 to 2025, based on her Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALNs), Office of the Ombudsman Records Division officer-in-charge Karen Batu said Tuesday.
During her direct examination, Batu, a witness presented by the House prosecution panel, enumerated the cash declarations of Duterte from 2007 to 2018.
Come 2019, she said that Duterte did not declare any cash on hand nor cash in bank in her SALN. She said same goes for her 2020 SALN.

“To expedite the proceedings so that we can finish this, madam witness, tuloy na lang po natin. Onwards, ano po ‘yung cash declarations ng ating Vice President after 2020, kung meron man?” Private prosecutor James Bryan Alih asked.
(To expedite the proceedings so that we can finish this, madam witness, let’s just proceed. Onwards, what were the cash declarations of our Vice President after 2020, if there were any?)
Batu answered, “For SALNs 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, and 2025, wala pong naka-declare na (there was no declared) cash on hand or in bank.”

To recall, Atty. Michael Poa, spokesperson for the Vice President’s defense team, previously explained that Duterte had no cash on hand declared in her official SALNs since 2019 because it was "lumped" under the “others” line item.
Poa said that Duterte’s cash in bank and even jewelry were also “lumped” all together under that specific line item.

Former Sandiganbayan presiding justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang on Monday said that cash on hand and cash in bank of government officials must be separately declared in the SALN and must not be lumped together with other properties. — RSJ, GMA News
