articles.title: Nato jets down drone that entered Lithuanian airspace
articles.summary: The origin of the drone is currently unknown, but authorities say it likely entered Lithuania from neighbouring Belarus, an ally of Russia.

blocks.text: Nato fighter pilots have shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace overnight, the Lithuanian president said.
Authorities said the drone likely entered southern Lithuania, near the second-largest city of Kaunas, from neighbouring Belarus shortly after midnight on Tuesday.
Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda wrote in a statement on X: "A drone that just entered Lithuanian airspace was destroyed by NATO fighter jets."
The origins of the drone are yet to be determined, a spokesperson for the Lithuanian national crisis management centre said.
Drone alerts sounded across the capital Vilnius and surrounding region earlier on Tuesday.
Lithuania's armed forces and Italian pilots serving in the Nato Air Defence Mission "showed a swift and responsible response" to the drone incursion, Lithuania's Ministry of Defence said.

Nausėda's post on social media added: "With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region. Together with our NATO Allies, Lithuania will defend its airspace."
Moscow has not commented on the incident.
Lithuania shares a large part of its southern and eastern border with Belarus, a key Russian ally.

Drone sightings were reported in Lithuania on Sunday. The crisis management centre later said an object had "likely" entered from Belarus and travelled across the country's territory before entering the airspace of Russia. The 13 September incident did not trigger air threat alerts.
Military drone incursions have become increasingly common across Europe since the beginning of Russia's full-scale of invasion of Ukraine.

Poland also announced there had been "aviation operations" in its airspace on Monday night "due to the activity of Russian Federation's jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles conducting strikes on Ukrainian territory".
These actions are of a "preventive nature" and are aimed at "securing airspace and its protection, especially in areas adjacent to threatened regions", it added.
Residents in Lithuania's capital were forced to take shelter across Vilnius in May after a drone alert was triggered, briefly grounding flights and rail travel.
Nato jets have scrambled multiple times to shoot down stray Ukrainian drones that have crossed into Baltic countries Estonia and Latvia this year.
Ukraine has blamed the stray drones on Russian electronic warfare, technology designed to change the flight paths of Ukrainian drones.

Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia all joined Nato in 2004, becoming signatories to the Article 5 provision that states "an armed attack against one NATO member shall be considered an attack against all members".

articles.title: US confirms for first time it has deployed space weapons
articles.summary: The US Air Force Secretary says the weapons are necessary to defend the country against enemy action.

blocks.text: The US has confirmed it deployed a space weapon in Earth's orbit, the first time it has acknowledged such offensive capabilities.
US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the "on orbit" weapon was necessary to safeguard US forces against hostile enemy action.
Speaking at the Air, Space and Cyber Conference on Monday, Meink said the US was ready for "evolving threats", but did not elaborate on the weapon's capabilities or when it was put into orbit.

Senior military leaders have previously said they planned to boost military capabilities in space, citing Russian and Chinese programmes developing ways to attack and disrupt US satellites in a future conflict.

The Trump administration has said that space-based capabilities - and interceptor missiles - are a crucial part of its planned "Golden Dome" defence system to protect the US from missiles and other airborne threats.

A 1967 treaty banned weapons of mass destruction in orbit. Since then, key powers including the US, Russia, and China have been exploring other capabilities outside of the treaty, such as targeting rivals' satellites - which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation.
Last year President Donald Trump issued an executive order underlining the US Space Force's role in not only defending assets, but also as an attacking force.

The US Space Force - the newest branch of the US military in more than 70 years - was launched in 2019 as a way to protect American assets in space, including hundreds of satellites used for communication and surveillance.

A US Space Force spokesperson said: "Space control encapsulates the mission areas required to contest and control the space domain – employing kinetic and non-kinetic means to affect adversary capabilities through disruption, degradation and even destruction, if necessary.
"These capabilities can be employed for offensive and defensive purposes at the direction of combatant commands."
In early February, it was revealed that two Russian satellites have likely intercepted the communications of at least a dozen European ones since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Such interceptions may have allowed Russian intelligence services to read the sensitive data they transmit, or hypothetically, even to take control of the satellites.
In 2024, the US said Russia had launched a satellite which it believed may be capable of attacking other such probes. Russia did not publicly comment on the issue.

The US Space Force says China "develops and operates space and counterspace capabilities as part of a military modernisation strategy," while Russia "views space as a warfighting domain and believes space supremacy will be a decisive factor in future conflicts".

articles.title: Gavin Newsom says he will not run for president in 2028 if Kamala Harris does
articles.summary:
In interview, term-limited California governor said running against former VP would ‘waste everybody’s time’

Gavin Newsom, the California governor, will not run for president if former…

blocks.text: Gavin Newsom, the California governor, will not run for president if former vice-president Kamala Harris does, he said in a forthcoming interview with CNN.

Newsom and Harris, both from California, are widely viewed as two of the top establishment frontrunners in the coming Democratic presidential primary. Newsom, who terms out this year as governor, has increasingly portrayed himself as a foil to Trump and is widely viewed as positioning himself for a 2028 presidential bid.
But Newsom said running against Harris would waste voters’ time and act as a “gift from God” to their political opponents, he said.
“I wouldn’t do that to her,” Newsom told Jake Tapper, a CNN anchor. “I wouldn’t waste everybody’s time.”
“The zen [sic] diagram on that, it’s pure cross over,” Newsom said. “I wouldn’t do that to people.”
Newsom said he considered running in 2024, but that he “wasn’t ready” and that he was still assessing whether he will be ready for the coming presidential primary.
“You have to meet the moment,” Newsom said. “You have to be honest with yourself. Do you represent the zeitgeist of the moment? Are you wasting everybody’s time?”
Newsom made the comments to Tapper while the two of them fly fished in the Bitterroot River of Montana, where Newsom’s in-laws own a ranch.
His apparent reluctance to challenge Harris belies his long push to gain a more prominent national profile.

Newsom has adopted a more strident tone on social media, where he routinely takes jabs at Trump. He has cultivated political “influencers” to spread awareness of his message. And he used a redistricting ballot initiative in California to help lead a national response to Trump’s attempts to manipulate the upcoming midterm elections by gerrymandering districts in conservative states to favor Republicans even more heavily.

Harris has stayed relatively quiet in comparison since losing her ill-fated presidential race against Trump in 2024, though she said publicly in July that she has yet to decide about whether to run. She lost spectacularly to Trump in 2024, in an election tainted by Joe Biden’s late exit over concerns about his apparent cognitive decline. But Harris remains a household name and a serious contender for the Democratic presidential nomination.

articles.title: Supreme Court blocks Trump's plan to restrict mail-in ballots
articles.summary: The Trump administration had asked the court to lift a federal judge's temporary block on new rules for mail-in ballots.

blocks.text: The US Supreme Court has rejected President Donald Trump's plan to restrict voting by mail before November's midterm elections, in a setback for the White House.
The justices upheld a federal judge's order that temporarily blocked the US Postal Service (USPS) from moving forwards with new requirements for postal ballots.

But it is unlikely to be the final word on the matter. Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a conservative, agreed with the ruling, but indicated he might later rule in Trump's favour as litigation in the case continues.
Trump, who argued the rules would combat electoral fraud, signed an executive order in March directing the USPS to deliver ballots only to voters on lists of citizens.
Legal challenges argued that the move violated states' constitutional rights to run elections.

Justice Kavanaugh wrote in the opinion that there was "at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service's statutory authority". But he argued that "applying the rule in the 2026 elections would be arbitrary and capricious".
Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas, also conservatives, dissented. They wrote that the challenge to Trump's order was a "Hail Mary pass" that was unlikely to be successful ultimately.
"The Postal Service has broad authority to regulate the mail," they added.
The White House did not immediately comment on the decision.
About 30% of voters, mostly Democrats, cast postal ballots in the general election two years ago.

Since returning to the White House, Trump has sought to restrict voting by mail. While he himself has voted by post, he has long claimed this method allows non-citizens to cast ballots and is prone to fraud.
In March's executive order, the president directed USPS to introduce unique barcodes on postal ballot envelopes.
State and local election officials would also be required to supply information to an online portal about voters who receive mail ballots.
Twenty-three states and Washington DC sued to stop Trump's order.
The postal workers' union also said clerks could not be trained in time for the election.
In court filings, the Trump administration maintained the new USPS rules were constitutional.

It said states "cannot choose to use the federal mails to carry out their elections but then insist that their election-related mail is somehow exempt from the Postal Service's rule-making authority, conferred by Congress".
Boston-based Judge Indira Talwani imposed an injunction on 4 September blocking Trump's order. She ruled that implementing the measures close to November's elections could disenfranchise voters.
Last week, a US appeals court refused to put Judge Talwani's order on hold.
On Sunday, another federal judge, Judge Carl Nichols, ruled against Trump's order.
Some states have already begun distributing mail-in ballots ahead of the midterm elections, which will decide which party controls Congress.
It is not the first setback on postal ballots for Trump before the Supreme Court.
In June, the justices ruled that states may count ballots postmarked by election day, rejecting the Trump administration's push to block votes being tallied when they are received after polls close.
Trump has previously made false claims that he lost the 2020 election owing to widespread electoral fraud.

articles.title: U.S. Supreme Court rejects Trump's bid to restrict mail-in ballots ahead of November midterms
articles.summary: The U.S. Supreme Court declined on Monday to let the U.S. Postal Service enforce a rule targeting mail-in ballots, dealing a setback to President Donald Trump's effort to restrict voting by mail…

image.caption: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled Monday against having the U.S. Postal Service restrict mail-in ballots. (Erin Scott/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

The U.S. Supreme Court declined on Monday to let the U.S. Postal Service enforce a rule targeting mail-in ballots, dealing a setback to President Donald Trump's effort to restrict voting by mail ahead ‌of November's midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.
8 states conduct elections entirely by mail, while all 50 allow it in some form

The U.S. Supreme Court declined on Monday to let the U.S. Postal Service enforce a rule targeting mail-in ballots, dealing a setback to U.S. President Donald Trump's effort to restrict voting by mail ahead ‌of November's midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.

The justices denied the Justice Department's request to lift a ruling by U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani in Boston that blocked the U.S. Postal Service from enforcing the measure while legal challenges by states and voting-rights groups proceed. The agency adopted the measure after Trump issued a March executive order aimed at tightening rules governing mail voting.
"The government is unlikely to succeed on the merits of its challenge to ​the District Court's preliminary injunction," the court said in its brief, one-paragraph order.

Justice Samuel Alito, ​joined by fellow conservative Justice Clarence Thomas, dissented from Monday's decision, comparing some of the challengers' claims to a "Hail Mary pass" that is "unlikely to be successfully completed," using a football analogy.
"The Postal Service has broad authority to regulate the mail," Alito added.
Mail-in restrictions would likely benefit Republicans
No other justice dissented publicly. ​The court has a 6-3 conservative majority.

Trump's fellow Republicans are locked in a tight battle to retain control of Congress in the midterms. Restricting mail-in ballots would stand to benefit Republicans, given that Democratic voters disproportionately use mail-in ballots, according ​to various surveys.

Under ⁠the new rule, states must provide ⁠lists of mail ballot recipients to the Postal Service and use agency-approved outgoing and ‌return ballot envelopes outfitted with unique barcodes. The Postal Service could then refuse to send out ballots that do not comply with the new standards or are associated with voters who do not appear on the lists.

Critics have said the plan could disrupt the delivery of thousands of legitimate ballots as the November 3 midterm vote approaches and cause chaos, given imminent plans by many states to ⁠send out mail ballots to eligible voters.

Talwani imposed ​an injunction on Sept. 4 blocking the rule, finding that it likely violated the U.S. Constitution, under which states administer elections. Talwani also said it would be impossible for the states to comply given the ⁠rapidly approaching midterms.
Another federal judge, U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols in Washington, D.C., also ruled against the new rule on Sunday.
'Testing the limits' of power
Sophia Lin Lakin, voting rights project director at the American Civil Liberties Union, which helped to represent some of the challengers to the USPS rule, welcomed Monday's decision.

"This administration keeps testing the limits of its power, as if the rules ‌governing our elections are merely suggestions to ignore when they don't suit the president's agenda. But the Constitution gives states and Congress the power to set the rules for federal elections — not the president, and not the Postal Service," she said.

"Today is a good day for democracy, the rule of law and the American people looking to exercise their constitutional right to vote," said California Gov. Gavin Newsom, whose state led one of the lawsuits against the rule.
"Trump's attacks on democracy these last 20 months ​have been nothing short of un-American."
Trump himself often votes by mail

Trump signed his executive order targeting mail-in ballots after years of casting doubt on their security, though he often votes by mail himself. Trump has made false claims of widespread fraud ‌in U.S. elections, including claims that fraud contributed to his 2020 loss to former Democratic president Joe Biden.
The administration, in a Sept. 6 emergency request, urged the Supreme Court to allow it to implement an "important federal policy to protect the mails from being used to commit voter fraud."
The truth behind Trump’s push to ban mail-in voting | About That

The 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Boston refused last Thursday to put Talwani's order on hold. The 1st Circuit said that the rule "will ⁠likely result in the disenfranchisement of millions of voters across the country while providing minimal — if any — gains in combating voter fraud."

Nichols granted ⁠a request ⁠from the Democratic Party and groups including the NAACP for ​a preliminary injunction blocking the rule. Nichols wrote that the rule could make it harder for some people to vote by mail and that it exceeded ​the Postal Service's authority.
"No statute grants the Postal ⁠Service the power to issue key parts of the rule," Nichols wrote.
All 50 states allow for some form of mail-in voting. Of those, 29 states allow voters to request mail ballots without providing a reason, and eight conduct their elections entirely by mail.

The battle over mail ballots is one in a series of efforts by the administration to boost federal involvement in voting ahead of the midterms. On Aug. 24, the Supreme Court lifted an earlier injunction imposed by Talwani in ⁠June blocking Trump's executive order, including the USPS ‌rule before it had been finalized.

articles.title: 2026 Emmy Awards launch with Hacks, The Pitt and more waiting in the wings
articles.summary: The Pitt, Pluribus, Hacks and Widow's Bay are set to compete for the top awards at this year's Emmy Awards, which launched Monday night.

image.caption: Emmys host Mariska Hargitay arrives at the 78th Emmy Awards at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles on Monday. (The Associated Press/Mark J. Terrill)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
The Pitt, Pluribus, Hacks and Widow's Bay are set to compete for the top awards at this year's Emmy Awards, which launched Monday night.
Mariska Hargitay hosts the 78th Emmy Awards
The 2026 Emmy Awards kicked off Monday night with a host of old favourites — and some up-and-comers — vying for top awards.

Medical drama The Pitt leads the pack with 25 nominations, including for lead actor in a drama series (Noah Wyle), supporting actor (Patrick Ball, Gerran Howell), supporting actress (Taylor Dearden, Fiona Dourif, Katherine LaNasa and Sepideh Moafi) and best drama series.

It already took home a number of those awards last year, leading to a surprise shut-out of competing drama Severance. This year, its already snagged four at the earlier ceremonies — nabbing prosthetic makeup and best guest actor awards — and is gunning for another strong performance tonight.
Slightly behind is Hacks, another strong performer at the seminal TV awards show. Its 24 nominations for its fifth and final season put it ahead of all comedies with a record-breaking 24 nominations.

Lead Jean Smart was, in many bettors' cards, perhaps the biggest lock of the night for best actress in a comedy — an award she won early on. Hannah Einbinder, who had a breakthrough win last year as best supporting actress in a comedy after four nominations, was be up against Kate O'Flynn, who wowed with a breakout performance in the debut season of Widow’s Bay — and who ended up taking home the prize.
The Pitt, Hacks lead 2026 Emmy nominations

And it is that series that represents what may be a shift for this year's awards: that show's first season, about a series of mysteries plaguing a struggling resort town, was a smash success in a way that hasn't been seen in years. The Emmys' track record suggests they would shower Hacks in awards for its final, send-off season. But with 19 nominations — and eight wins already — for a show with a real campaign and argument for best comedy series, its trajectory is one to watch tonight.

Fellow newcomer Pluribus, from Breaking Bad phenom Vince Gilligan, is just behind with 18 off the back of its first season. A stunningly bizarre dramedy about an alien invasion and mind control, it is similarly positioned in opposition to The Pitt. With four early wins already, the narrative has begun to circle around star Rhea Seehorn.

Given the entire show's focus on her singular performance, voters are likely to reward the former Better Call Saul star with her first Emmy after four nominations. Whether or not it earns best drama series is another story.
Seehorn's fellow nominees include Zendaya, who has won the category twice before for Euphoria.

items: How Pluribus turns the zombie genre into a philosophical masterpiece
Kimmel says interview with Democratic candidate won't air on his network show, cites FCC threats

blocks.text: Elsewhere, the limited series categories will have a diminished role at the main Emmys show after four of them were demoted to the early Emmys weekend.
HBO Max's DTF St. Louis was the big winner of those awards, taking best supporting actor and actress for David Harbour and Linda Cardellini.
Beef brings star power to the lead acting categories, with Carey Mulligan the consensus favourite for best actress in a limited series and Oscar Isaac favored for best actor.

And after another year of antagonizing U.S. President Donald Trump, the late night shows of Jimmy Kimmel and the now-cancelled Stephen Colbert are both up for outstanding variety series. The latter has nine nominations, following the news that CBS announced its end earlier this year.

Law & Order; Special Victims Unit star Mariska Hargitay is hosting this year's Emmys, off of two wins herself for documentary My Mom Jayne. She follows previous year's host Nate Bargatze, whose controversial hosting gig last year received mixed reviews.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jackson Weaver is a reporter and film critic for CBC's entertainment news team in Toronto. You can reach him at jackson.weaver@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Edmonton mayor calls for province to address release protocols after detainees dropped off in Chinatown
articles.summary: New video showing more detainees from correctional facilities being dropped off in Edmonton's Chinatown has prompted the city's mayor to call on upper levels of government to address release…

image.caption: Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack speaks about videos showing detainees being dropped off in Chinatown at a news conference on Monday, Sept. 14, 2026. (CBC News)

blocks.text: Edmonton·New

New video showing more detainees from correctional facilities being dropped off in Edmonton's Chinatown has prompted the city's mayor to call on upper levels of government to address release protocols.
Andrew Knack spoke about issue at news conference Monday

New video that shows more detainees from correctional facilities being dropped off in Edmonton's Chinatown has prompted the city's mayor to call on upper levels of government to address release protocols.

On Wednesday, CBC News reported on surveillance footage showing a provincial corrections van dropping off a former detainee in a private parking lot in Chinatown. On Sunday, CBC News received new footage, recorded Friday evening, that shows at least seven more former detainees being dropped off in a Chinatown parking lot.

At a news conference on Monday, Mayor Andrew Knack said he believes the provincial government needs to show exactly how it plans to address the issue, including what supports people receive after they leave custody.
"It's one thing to say the words that, ‘We see this problem, we've identified the problem,’" he said.
"It's something else entirely to say, ‘And here's the sequence of actions we're going to take.’"

Last week, after CBC News first reported about the drop-offs in Chinatown, a statement from Alberta’s Ministry of Public Safety and Emergency Services said the department is “reinforcing expectations with staff that releases occur at appropriate public locations and not on private property.”

items: Release of detainee into Chinatown parking lot prompts anger, calls for reform in Edmonton

blocks.text: Knack said a plan for someone leaving a correctional facility needs to include reintegration and followup.

"How are we ensuring that person is getting all of the necessary supports and care so they're not falling back into maybe a place of homelessness, that they're not falling back into issues like mental health and addictions?" he asked.
Knack said he wants the Alberta government to provide information about timelines for addressing shortages in housing, recovery and other supports.
'We have the solutions'
Knack said Edmonton has an unusually high concentration of correctional facilities, with eight such facilities. He said the city is also a northern Alberta hub for social services.
"The disproportionate pressure that our city faces due to the concentration of these services means that we need a uniquely Edmonton approach," he said.
Coun. Anne Stevenson said the city has seen at least a dozen people released into Edmonton in what she described as a state of "incredible vulnerability."
She said the city is asking the province for a "reintegration co-ordination framework," pointing to non-profit organizations already doing this work.
"We have the model, we have the solutions," Stevenson said.
Knack said the city has already made land available for affordable and supportive housing and is working toward community health hubs, recovery spaces and other supports.
But he said those efforts cannot replace provincial and federal responsibility for people leaving custody.
"We don't have the same legal tools as the provincial and federal governments," Knack said.
"This is ultimately with them on that. But we're not going to sit back and just say, 'Do it yourselves.'"
Release plans can be complicated

Kathryn Quinlan, vice-president of the Criminal Trial Lawyers' Association, said there is no single process for releasing someone from custody, and that a blanket release plan would not work because people's circumstances differ.
People can be released on bail, after serving a provincial sentence, or from federal custody through parole, statutory release or the expiry of a sentence, she said.
Quinlan said she has represented clients who were dropped off in public areas. That practice works for some people but creates significant barriers for others, she said.
Some people may have supports in the downtown area, she said, while others may have family or housing elsewhere in Edmonton or outside the city.
"It's the individuals who don't have that same access who would struggle," Quinlan said.
A person leaving custody may not have access to a cellphone, which can make it difficult to contact family, arrange transportation or access services.
Raw video shows provincial corrections van releasing person in parking lot in Edmonton's Chinatown
Quinlan said better-funded release planning could address some of those gaps.

She suggested a worker at the Edmonton Remand Centre could speak with people before release to determine what they already have in place and what they need to access those supports — potentially something as simple as bus fare or an Arc (reloadable transit fare card) card.

In a statement, the Ministry of Public Safety and Emergency Services said correctional staff work with people before release to identify available services and consider transportation, their home community, immediate needs and available supports.
The province said about 80 per cent of people in custody are on remand, meaning their release dates may not be known in advance.
In its statement, the ministry said it understands concerns raised by Chinatown residents and businesses and is reviewing practices.

"We recognize the important role Chinatown plays in Edmonton," the ministry said, adding that it will continue working with community partners to ensure release procedures balance community concerns, operational requirements and connecting people with available supports.
Knack said the city wants to see those commitments translated into action quickly.
"We need the two orders of government who have the actual levers to solve this to be the ones leading the charge," he said.
CBC News reached out to the Edmonton Police Service but the police department said it was unable to comment.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jesmeen Gill is a reporter for CBC News in Edmonton. She is a recent graduate from Carleton University’s journalism program in Ottawa and has previously interned at The Canadian Press. You can reach her at jesmeen.gill@cbc.ca.

articles.title: US Supreme Court denies Trump bid to restrict mail-in ballots
articles.summary: The court said election officials do not have sufficient time to implement the rule before the November midterms.

image.caption: The Supreme Court's decision means states are allowed to continue sending out mail ballots under the same processes they have used for years [FILE: Nov 7, 2022]Image: George Frey/Getty Images

blocks.text: The US Supreme Court has denied President Donald Trump's attempt to restrict mail-in voting ahead of the November midterm elections.
Trump had requested that the top court lift a lower court's order which blocked his bid to restrict the mail-in voting.

In a concurring opinion with the majority, conservative Justice Brett Kavanaugh said that while the Republican president's plan might ultimately prove legal, "state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections."
Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas publicly dissented from the brief order.
The Supreme Court's decision means states are allowed to continue sending out mail ballots under the same processes they have used for years.
The case has major implications because nearly one-third of the country votes by mail.
What do Trump's mail-in restrictions entail?

Trump's plan would obligate states to adopt a uniform envelope style and provide lists of mail ballot recipients to the Postal Service, which could then refuse to send out ballots that fail to comply with the new standards.

A whistleblower report has alleged that the postal system's requirements could result in millions of mail ballots never getting sent as the portal was not properly built and could therefore experience glitches.

Critics argue that the restrictions could disrupt the delivery of thousands of legitimate ballots ahead of the November 3 vote, for which states including Alabama, North Carolina and Wisconsin have already begun sending mail ballots to voters over the past week.

Democratic state officials and voting rights groups challenged the restrictions in court, arguing that the president has no constitutional authority to set election rules that would “virtually eliminate mail voting on the eve of a major election."
Lower courts have pulled the brakes on Trump's new system, which is why he had resorted to the Supreme Court.
This is a developing story. Please refresh for updates

articles.title: Supreme court rejects Trump’s mail ballot restrictions for midterm elections
articles.summary:
Decision allows states to send ballots under process followed for years even as president tried to limit system

The supreme court on Monday rejected Donald Trump’s mail ballot restrictions…

blocks.text: The supreme court on Monday rejected Donald Trump’s mail ballot restrictions for now, capping a flurry of last-minute legal action with voting in the midterm elections already underway.
The decision allows states to continue sending out mail ballots under the same processes they have used for years.

The Trump administration had asked the court, once again at the center of a roiling political controversy, to clear the way for restrictions before the pivotal November contests for control of Congress. The case has major implications because nearly one-third of the country votes by mail.

Election officials have said there was simply no way to carry out a complete overhaul in the weeks before the midterms. Indeed, Alabama, North Carolina and Wisconsin began sending mail ballots to voters over the past week while the new system was still not active.

The Trump administration plan would require states to adopt a uniform envelope style and submit lists of eligible voters to an online portal. The postal service could refuse to deliver ballots to states that didn’t comply.

A whistleblower report, though, said the postal system’s requirements could lead to millions of mail ballots never being sent, because the portal wasn’t properly built and a single bar code error could result in an entire batch of ballots being tossed out.

Democratic state officials and voting rights groups challenged the restrictions in court, arguing the president has no constitutional authority to set election rules that would “virtually eliminate mail voting on the eve of a major election”.
Lower courts agreed and blocked Trump’s plan, including a preliminary injunction issued by a judge nominated by the president.
But the Trump administration appealed to the supreme court, arguing that federal control of the postal service allows them to set rules for mail ballot handling and that compliance was possible.
The federal government won an early procedural decision at the supreme court, but the justices pointedly did not decide the legality of the plan.
Trump has long opposed mail voting and falsely blamed it for his 2020 election loss to Joe Biden, even though he often uses that method to cast his own ballot, including as recently as this year.

articles.title: US eyes Taiwan role in Luzon corridor's chip, AI push
articles.summary: Washington sees room for Taiwanese investment in chips, AI and manufacturing.

blocks.text: September 15, 2026 | 8:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The United States sees "huge scope" for Taiwanese participation in the Luzon Economic Corridor, particularly in semiconductors, advanced manufacturing and artificial intelligence, as Manila and its partners seek to draw more high-technology investment into Luzon.

U.S. Ambassador Heather Variava, a senior adviser at the State Department's Bureau of Economic, Energy and Business Affairs, said Taiwanese companies are already represented at the Luzon Economic Corridor Investment Forum in Manila.

"Given the leading role that Taiwan plays in those sectors, I think there's huge scope of opportunity," Variava said at a virtual press briefing on September 10, as transcribed, when asked about Taiwan's potential participation in semiconductors, advanced manufacturing and AI.
She added that Philippine partners would welcome greater Taiwanese investment and pointed to the existing economic and people-to-people links between Taiwan and the Philippines.
"I think there's huge scope for further collaboration and including Taiwan in the initiative," Variava said.

The Luzon Economic Corridor is a partnership of the Philippines, United States and Japan aimed at accelerating investment across Subic, Clark, Manila and Batangas. It is aimed at developing transport and logistics, energy, digital infrastructure and advanced manufacturing.

A broader goal cited is to move goods, energy, data and people more efficiently across Luzon, linking the region more closely to global markets. Variava said the corridor already covers an area accounting for about 50% of Philippine gross domestic product.
U.S. officials said the current push is on mobilizing private-sector investment rather than treating the corridor as a collection of government projects.

Among the projects under development are a freight rail system linking major corridor hubs, a feasibility study for a nickel and cobalt processing facility, improvements to Subic Bay port infrastructure and new digital connectivity projects.

U.S. Trade and Development Agency Deputy Director Thomas Hardy said the agency was nearing completion of its feasibility work on a nickel and cobalt processing facility intended to bolster the Philippines' ability to process critical minerals.

USTDA has also financed a feasibility study for a Subic-Clark-Batangas-Manila railway and announced new support for the expansion of port facilities at Subic Bay and a nationwide public Wi-Fi network.
Variava said advanced manufacturing is another focus, citing the Philippines' existing capabilities in semiconductors, automobiles and aerospace.
Taiwan role still taking shape

Taiwan's interest in the corridor predates the U.S. officials' remarks, having expressed in a 2024 report that it was considering joining the corridor. It initially identified smart agriculture as one area for cooperation. Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung said at the time that Taiwan could play a "pivotal role" in the corridor and had begun talks with the United States and other partners on possible participation.
Variava, meanwhile, said several countries had already joined the initiative, while the European Union and Spain became the latest participants.

She did not announce a formal arrangement for Taiwan or identify specific Taiwanese investments tied to the corridor. She said, however, that Taiwan's possible role around its strength in industries the corridor is trying to attract, including semiconductors, advanced manufacturing and AI.

The corridor's digital component is also aimed at building what U.S. officials describe as safe, secure infrastructure, while its energy component is intended to improve generation, grid reliability and the investment environment for new power projects.
Beyond Marcos admin
The U.S. officials also sought to play down concerns that the corridor could lose momentum after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. leaves office in 2028.

Asked whether Manila and Washington had discussed making the initiative resilient beyond the next Philippine presidential election, Variava pointed to projects and policies that had already survived changes in government on both sides.
She cited the redevelopment of the former shipyard in Subic Bay, which began under President Rodrigo Duterte and continued under Marcos.
Variava also said the Luzon Economic Corridor itself had carried over between U.S. administrations and was embraced by President Donald Trump's administration.
"So I think we do see longevity running through both the corridor initiative and many of our investments here in the Philippines," she said.
The Philippines is one of the United States' oldest treaty allies in Asia. As for trade and development, Hardy noted the agency's work with the Philippines for more than 30 years.

articles.title: Kremlin-linked Russian oligarch helped fund Trump Jr.'s wedding celebration
articles.summary: Trump's son and his wife confirmed reports that Umar Kremlev paid for parts of the festivities. Kremlev was awarded the "Order of Friendship" by Putin earlier this year.

image.caption: Donald Trump Jr. and his wife Bettina confirmed the news that was first reported by investigative website ProPublicaImage: Brendan Smialowski/AFP

blocks.text: A Russian businessman with close ties to the Kremlin paid for parts of the wedding celebrations of the US President's son, Donald Trump Jr., and his socialite wife Bettina, the couple confirmed on Monday.

The ProPublica investigative website first reported the news, saying that Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev paid hundreds of thousands of dollars for the parties which took place after the couple's wedding in May.
Bettina Trump said in a post on her Instagram cosigned by her husband that their "dear friend" Kremlev "very generously hosted two incredible nights" of festivities in the Bahamas.
What do we know about Kremlev's contribution to Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding festivities?

ProPublica said Kremlev footed the bill for the party in the Bahamas, renting a private island for around $100,000 (roughly €86,586) per night, and paying for a fireworks display which reportedly cost some $70,000.
"It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful," said the post by Bettina and Donald Trump Jr.

Bettina Trump went on to add that she was married to Trump Jr. in a private ceremony "surrounded ONLY by our family." The US president did not attend the wedding or the festivities, saying he had to remain in Washington amid talks on the Iran war.

blocks.caption: Bettina (pictured here in white next to her husband) clarified that Kremlev paid for the festivities which followed their weddingImage: Elder Ordonez/Cover-Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: "The weekend that followed had actually been planned well in advance as a fun weekend with friends. It was never intended to be our wedding weekend. When our original wedding plans changed, we simply decided to get married before it and arrived at an already planned weekend as newlyweds."
The couple then defended Kremlev's contribution to their wedding celebration.

"It's unfortunate that something so personal and happy can be recast as something political or sinister simply because of who someone is or where they come from. Friendship doesn't require a political motive. Generosity doesn't automatically come with an agenda. And sometimes a wedding gift is simply a wedding gift."
Who is Umar Kremlev?

Kremlev is the head of the International Boxing Association (IBA). The International Olympic Committee severed links with the Kremlev-led body after repeated warnings over financial governance and ethical concerns.
Russian investigative media outlet Proekt reports that Kremlev is a Tajik native who initially worked as a mid-level boxing promoter.
In April this year, Russian President Vladimir Putin presented Kremlev with the "Order of Friendship" award.

blocks.caption: Putin awarded Kremlev the 'Order of Friendship' earlier this yearImage: Artyom Geodakyan/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Both Trump and his son have been previously scrutinized over Russian ties.
During the 2016 US election campaign, Trump Jr.'s meeting with a Russian attorney was under much federal and congressional scrutiny.
A Senate Intelligence Committee report concluded that the Russian government attempted to influence the 2016 vote in Trump's favor.
Ukraine at the G7: Is Trump a bigger threat than Putin?

articles.title: Donald Trump Jr and Bettina Trump say Putin ally paid for some wedding festivities as a 'gift'
articles.summary: An Instagram post from the couple said two nights of their wedding festivities in the Bahamas were partially funded by Umar Kremlev.

blocks.text: Donald Trump Jr.'s wife, Bettina Trump, confirmed that their May wedding was paid for in part by an ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin.

A post on her Instagram account - attributed to the couple - said that two nights of their three-day wedding festivities on a private island in the Bahamas were partially funded by Umar Kremlev, a Russian oligarch with close ties to Putin.
The statement was released Monday after investigative journalism outlet ProPublica published a story detailing that Kremlev paid "hundreds of thousands of dollars" for the celebration.
Donald Trump Jr., one of the US president's sons, is a private citizen, so it's not illegal for him to accept gifts from a foreign national.

"Our dear friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding. It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful," the couple said in the statement.

But ethics watchdog groups said it still presented the appearance of a conflict of interest for the president's son to accept lavish gifts from someone associated with a foreign head of state - even if he is not a US government employee.

"People don't just give hundreds of thousands of dollars to a random acquaintance without wanting something," said Jordan Libowitz, vice president of communications for Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW).
"You can see how [Putin] would enjoy all this press about how people in his circle are cozying up to people in the president's circle."

According to the ProPublica article, the couple was married on a private island in the Bahamas, then held a two-day celebration on a separate island that rents for approximately $100,000 per night. Kremlev also paid other costs for the party, including a roughly $70,000 fireworks display, the report found.

Kremlev runs the International Boxing Association (IBA), an organization funded by the state-backed Gazprom energy company. The Olympic Committee suspended the group in part over its failure to report its ties to the Russian energy giant.
Earlier this year Kremlev was part of a delegation that visited China with Putin. The Russian president also gave Kremlev the Order of Friendship, a top state honor, according to ProPublica.
A spokesperson for Trump Jr. told the news outlet that the president's son and Kremlev were personal friends and did not have "a business relationship."
An ally of Trump Jr. referred the BBC to the Instagram statement.
In a statement to ProPublica, Kremlev's office said "Mr. Kremlev and Mr. Trump Jr have a friendly relationship." The statement said the men met a few years ago.

Kremlev attended part of the wedding, the outlet reported. Other attendees included one of the US president's daughters, Ivanka Trump, and her husband, Jared Kushner, who has worked for the US on diplomatic negotiations with Iran, Russia and in the Middle East.

The Trump campaign and family faced controversy for potential ties to Russia during the 2016 presidential election, resulting in a special counsel investigation. During the campaign Donald Trump Jr. brokered a meeting at Trump Tower with a Russian operative that was closely scrutinized during the probe.

Libowitz, of CREW, said either the president, who is a billionaire, or Trump Jr. -- who is worth $300 million, according to Forbes -- could have paid for the full wedding to avoid a conflict of interest.
"His father is worth billions he could have picked up the tab. Clearly they just didn't want to pay for it," Libowitz said. "They don't really care about the ethical ramifications."

articles.title: Romualdez moved to Payatas jail, arraignment set Sept. 16
articles.summary: Former speaker was transferred to the Quezon City jail after independent medical review.

blocks.text: September 15, 2026 | 6:50am
Then-speaker of the House Martin Romualdez speaks at the launch of Congress TV 11 in January 2024.
House of Reps / Released

MANILA, Philippines — Former House speaker Martin Romualdez was transferred to the New Quezon City Jail late Monday after government doctors found no medical need for continued hospital confinement, two days before his scheduled arraignment on a P7.44-billion plunder case.
The Sandiganbayan Third Division set Romualdez's arraignment and pre-trial for 8:30 a.m. Wednesday, September 16, according to a resolution released Monday.
During arraignment, Romualdez will be asked to enter a plea to the plunder charge against him.

The anti-graft court also ordered his immediate transfer to the Quezon City Jail Male Dormitory after doctors from the Philippine General Hospital testified that he was clinically stable and no longer required inpatient care at an acute care hospital.
Romualdez was transferred from PGH to the jail in Payatas, Quezon City at 10:09 p.m. Monday.
PGH Director Dr. Gerardo Legaspi told the court that Romualdez was "clinically stable" and unlikely to suffer an emergency medical condition if discharged from hospital confinement.
The PGH team said unstable angina was "not demonstrated" during its evaluation and found no acute cerebrovascular event, despite earlier diagnoses cited by Cardinal Santos Medical Center.
Doctors confirmed that Romualdez has chronic coronary artery disease and chronic cerebrovascular disease, but said neither condition currently requires inpatient management.
They also told the court that his response to a stress test was normal and estimated that his annual risk of suffering a heart attack over the next decade was about 3%.
Dr. Henry Fabro, chief medical officer of the Quezon City Jail Male Dormitory, assured the court that the facility could manage Romualdez's medical needs.

Fabro said Romualdez could regularly use his CPAP machine, receive prescribed medication and consult his private doctors inside the jail. He could also be transferred to a nearby hospital in an emergency.
Romualdez had sought continued confinement at Cardinal Santos Medical Center after his September 7 arrest.
The Sandiganbayan instead ordered him transferred to PGH on September 11 for an independent medical examination.

Romualdez faces plunder allegations over P7.44 billion in alleged kickbacks from contractors and other parties with interests in flood-control, infrastructure and other government projects. — with reports from The STAR / Daphne Galvez

articles.title: Republican Mitch McConnell returns to U.S. Senate after 3-month absence
articles.summary: Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky returned to the U.S. Senate on Monday for the first time since June 14, when he was hospitalized after a fall in his home.

image.caption: U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell waves at reporters outside the Senate Chamber after he returned to Capitol Hill on Monday. (Evan Vucci/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New
Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky returned to the U.S. Senate on Monday for the first time since June 14, when he was hospitalized after a fall in his home.
McConnell has been conspicuously absent since he suffered a fall June 11

McConnell's three-month absence from the Senate generated a flood of criticism and online speculation, as the Kentucky senator initially remained quiet for weeks about his condition. The 84-year-old senator eventually disclosed that he had been "briefly unconscious" due to the fall and had also been treated for mild pneumonia in the hospital.

"My recovery has been a long and often frustrating process, and the lingering effects of childhood polio haven't made it any easier," McConnell said in a statement Monday. "I'm still not quite back to 100%, but I've assured Leader [John] Thune that, as I continue with physical therapy on the advice of my doctors, I will do my best to be present for tough votes when our Conference needs me."

The concerns over McConnell's absence highlighted increasing public concern about the age of lawmakers and their capacity to carry out their duties. Speculation about his condition grew so intense at one point that Kentucky's Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear took the extraordinary step of issuing a public letter asking McConnell to update the public in a "transparent manner."
Mitch McConnell confirms he's alive; his absence, death of other senator complicate Republican power

McConnell's absence was also felt over the summer as Republicans were unable to advance a farm bill out of committee. His return could give Republican leaders a needed vote as they try to advance legislation on cryptocurrency regulation and college sports.

items: Late-night TV hosts skewer Mitch McConnell's proof-of-life photo
U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell breaks silence, says he was hospitalized after a fall

blocks.text: McConnell, who holds the distinction of being the longest-serving Senate leader, is in his final months of his four decades in office. He is retiring at the end of January after one of the most consequential careers in modern politics.
Republicans have nominated U.S. Rep. Andy Barr to replace him, while Democrats have nominated former state lawmaker Charles Booker. McConnell said he is determined to finish out his term.
History of health problems
McConnell had polio in his early childhood and has long acknowledged difficulty as an adult in walking and climbing stairs.

The physician's office in Congress in the July statement said McConnell has "experienced several falls through the year" due to his "post-polio condition." The office said his physical therapy was aimed at reducing the risk of him falling again.
"A comprehensive evaluation by a multidisciplinary team determined that he had no fractures, cardiac abnormalities, stroke, tumor, or hemorrhage," the physician's office said.

items: The U.S. Senate is in turmoil. What does it mean for upcoming midterm elections?

blocks.text: McConnell was first elected to the Senate in 1984 and was the Republican leader from 2007 until last year , serving as both majority and minority leader during that period. He has remained active as a rank-and-file senator, showing up for work when the chamber is in session, often using a wheelchair to get around.
But the senator's physical condition has visibly declined in recent years.
He was hospitalized with a concussion in March 2023 and missed several weeks of work after falling in a Washington hotel.

He twice froze up during news conferences after he returned, staring vacantly ahead before colleagues and staff. A year later, he fell and sprained his wrist while walking out of a Republican luncheon.

articles.title: Megan Stalter's Midas touch, Zendaya's Prada crystals and other stunning red carpet looks at the 2026 Emmys
articles.summary: The 78th Emmy Awards, which recognize excellence in television, are taking place Monday evening at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles. Here are the best looks from the red carpet, which is actually…

blocks.text: Style

The 78th Emmy Awards, which recognize excellence in television, are taking place Monday evening at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles. Here are the best looks from the red carpet, which is actually peacock blue this year, a nod to the host network, NBC.
Top fashion moments from television's biggest night

The 78th Emmy Awards are underway at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles, where stars of the small screen walked a red carpet that was actually blue this year, a nod to the 100th anniversary of the host network, NBC, and its stylized peacock logo.

Hosted by actor Mariska Hargitay, the event recognizes excellence in television and features a special musical tribute to Dolly Parton led by Reba McEntire, as well as an in memoriam performance of Bridge Over Troubled Water by Noah Kahan. The ceremony also celebrates the 30th anniversary of Buffy the Vampire Slayer and the 50th anniversary of Charlie’s Angels.

articles.title: Iconic winter X Games comes to Calgary
articles.summary: The X Games sports competition is coming to Calgary in February next year. WinSport's Canada Olympic Park will host the three-day event beginning Feb. 19.

image.caption: A file photo of WinSport's Canada Olympic Park. The X Games will take over the Calgary venue in February 2027. (Dave Gilson/CBC)

blocks.text: Calgary·New
The X Games sports competition is coming to Calgary in February next year. WinSport's Canada Olympic Park will host the three-day event beginning Feb. 19.
WinSport will host 3-day competition in February 2027
The iconic X Games action sports competition is coming to Calgary in February next year.
WinSport's Canada Olympic Park will host the three-day competition beginning Feb. 19, and the city will also see international musical acts Levity and Steve Aoki perform as part of the event.
The Calgary stop marks the first time in the 31-year history of the X Games that the competition will be hosted in Canada.

“X Games is one of those events you dream of hosting in your city,” said Tourism Calgary president and CEO Alisha Reynolds. “There is truly no better city than Calgary to host this electrifying event.”
The event will see some of the world's top skiers and snowboarders compete in events like Big Air, Knuckle Huck, Slopestyle and Superpipe.
Officials estimate roughly 15,000 to 20,000 spectators will attend the three days of competition.
Reynolds estimates the event will bring in roughly $25 million for the city’s visitor economy.
Canadian athletes excited to host

Calgarian Brendan Mackay, a freestyle skier with Team Canada, is excited to have the event come to his hometown. Mackay remembers what a podium finish at his first X Games in 2020 meant for his career.
“That was honestly for me a huge career-defining moment,” said Mackay. “That really set into motion what has been a really great athletic career since then.”
Growing up watching the games on TV inspired Mackay, and he says hosting could have an even bigger impact on the next generation.

items: Cal Nichols, who led community effort to save NHL hockey in Edmonton, dies at 84

blocks.text: Historically Aspen, Colo., has hosted many of the winter X Games events and therefore produced some of the sports' best athletes, says Mackay.
“So I think having that come to Calgary will be so impactful on all the young kids who get to go out and watch it,” he said.
Mike Atkinson breaks down Brendan Mackay's bronze-medal run in men's freeski halfpipe
Professional snowboarder Craig McMorris, who grew up in Saskatchewan and credits monthly trips to Canada Olympic Park for his success, is also excited for the event to finally come to Canada.
“Canada has exported the best action sports talent in the entire world — full stop,” McMorris said. "It’s finally now our time to host the X Games.”
New format for Calgary X Games
In 2026, the X Games launched a new league format where athletes compete individually but also earn points for club teams, adding a championship race that fans can follow throughout the season.
At the X Games Calgary media event on Monday, CEO Jeremy Bloom also unveiled the four clubs for the winter league, which will draft athletes later this week. They include X Games Club Whistler.
“So Canadians will have a club to root for,” Bloom said.
With files from Dave Gilson

articles.title: Raptors, Clippers agree to complete trade to send Kawhi Leonard back to Toronto: reports
articles.summary: The Raptors and Los Angeles Clippers have agreed to complete a trade to send star forward Kawhi Leonard back to Toronto, according to multiple media reports.

image.caption: Kawhi Leonard is seen as a member of the Los Angeles Clippers during a game in March. Per multiple reports, the veteran superstar is finally returning to the Toronto Raptors after the proposed trade between the two franchises can be completed following the league's investigation into the Clippers' a

blocks.text: NBA·New
The Raptors and Los Angeles Clippers have agreed to complete a trade to send star forward Kawhi Leonard back to Toronto, according to multiple media reports.
Deal involving Ingram, Dick, 5 picks has been paused during NBA's cap probe
Reports say the trade will be made official pending a trade call. Shams Charania of ESPN was the first to report the agreement.
The Raptors offered no comment on the reported trade Monday.
CBC Sports has not independently confirmed the reports.
The deal would see L.A. get all-star forward Brandon Ingram, guard Gradey Dick, unprotected first-round picks in 2031 and 2033, a 2027 first-round pick swap and two second-round picks in return.
The deal had been on hold while the NBA investigated Leonard and the Clippers for salary-cap circumvention.
The league completed its investigation on Sept. 2, fining Leonard $700,000 US but declining to suspend him or void his contract.

Although the deal had not been officially submitted to the league while the investigation was underway, Leonard, Ingram and Dick tried to participate with their new teams as much as NBA rules allowed.

Leonard sat in the front row at Kyle Lowry's July 7 news conference at OVO Athletic Centre, where Lowry announced he would retire as a member of the Raptors. Ingram attended a Clippers summer league game in Las Vegas on July 10.

items: Leonard focused on Raptors return with 'clean slate' after avoiding suspension in NBA cap probe

blocks.text: The 35-year-old Leonard averaged 27.9 points, 6.3 rebounds, 3.6 assists, 1.9 steals and 0.4 blocks per game last season for the Clippers in 2025-26.

Ingram averaged 21.5 points, 5.6 rebounds and 3.7 assists in his one season in Toronto, but was injured 11 minutes into Game 5 of the Raptors' first-round playoff series against the Cleveland Cavaliers. He underwent right heel surgery on May 8.
Dick took a step back in his third NBA season, averaging 14 minutes per game in 2025-26, averaging six points, 1.9 rebounds and 0.7 assists, all career lows.
Leonard was the central player in the Raptors' 2019 championship run, but spent just one season with the club before joining his hometown Clippers as a free agent.
Once the trade is completed, Leonard is expected to speak to reporters at the Raptors' media day on Sept. 28.

articles.title: US scraps limits on emissions from coal and gas power plants
articles.summary: The Environment Protection Agency says the move will save the country billions of dollars and reduce energy prices.

blocks.text: Rules aimed at limiting pollution from coal and gas power plants are being scrapped, the head of the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has announced.
The agency also said it would take steps to prevent future administrations from regulating power plant emissions.
The EPA said that getting rid of the majority of the climate rules from President Joe Biden's era would save $310bn (£223bn) and reduce energy prices.
But environmental groups warned it would come at a huge cost to Americans' health and the planet. The EPA's move is expected to face immediate legal challenges.

"The reality is that America produces energy better and cleaner than anywhere else in the world, and our power plants should not be unfairly targeted," the head of the EPA, Lee Zeldin, said on Monday.
Fossil fuels, which include coal and natural gas, are by far the largest driver of global climate change, according to the United Nations.
The EPA said in a statement that it found the Biden-era rules on power plant emissions had "exceeded the agency's authority".
The agency said the regulations required "control technologies that are not adequately demonstrated, effectively forcing plants to retire rather than setting standards they could actually meet".
The EPA is also seeking to get rid of all other greenhouse gas rules for the power sector.
The changes, which will undergo public scrutiny, were proposed last year by Zeldin.

He said the new rules would "ensure affordable and reliable energy supplies and drive down the costs of transportation, heating, utilities, farming, and manufacturing while boosting our national security".

The Biden-era regulations called for a major reduction in carbon emissions from power plants, as well as vehicles and industrial facilities. It was estimated that the measures would stop 4,500 premature deaths annually.
But the EPA said on Monday: "Any potential public health harms are too uncertain, conjectural, remote, and convoluted to tie specifically to the US power sector."
Zeldin told reporters that safeguards against "hazardous air pollutants" would remain in place "to safeguard human health".

articles.title: Legendary costume designer Bob Mackie dies aged 87
articles.summary: The "Sultan of Sequins" created iconic and dazzling costumes for stars including Cher, Tina Turner and Elton John.

blocks.text: Bob Mackie, who designed dazzling costumes for stars including Cher, Tina Turner, Dolly Parton and Elton John has died, aged 87.
The US fashion designer, known as the "Sultan of Sequins" for his sparkling creations, won a Tony Award, nine Emmys and received three Oscar nominations during his career.
"It is with a heavy heart that we share the news that Mr Bob Mackie passed away today," a statement on his Instagram account announced on Monday.

"He lived his 87 years to the fullest, fulfilling his dream of being a Fashion and Costume Designer, which is all he ever wanted to do," it added. "His genius and extraordinary designs will live on forever, continuing to bring beauty into this world."

Mackie was particularly influential in Cher's career and designed her iconic Mohawk outfit, which she wore to the Oscars in 1986. It became known as her "revenge" outfit, because she wasn't nominated for anything.
The showgirl-inspired costume featured a plumed mohawk headdress and showed Cher's bare midriff - a very new, and very shocking look at the time.
The costume has gone down in fashion history as one of the most outrageous and extravagant ever to appear at the awards.

"I didn't get nominated for a movie that everyone thought I would actually win for [Mask] - so was dressing that night for a kind of revenge," Cher explained in the 2024 documentary Bob Mackie: Naked Illusion.
Mackie told the BBC in 2010 that when Cher started out she "looked like no-one else in the entertainment business at the time".
"Everybody just went crazy over this woman as she could wear anything," he added.
Cher was widely reported to be the first woman to show her belly button on US television - and Mackie's designs were pivotal to that.

Mackie was also the creative genius behind several of Sir Elton John's costumes, including his now-iconic Dodgers baseball outfit - bedazzled of course - that he wore during his performances at Dodger Stadium in Los Angeles in 1975.

"Every time I put something on that Bob made, I felt very, very special," Sir John wrote on Instagram. "His costumes were works of art, and he will go down as one of the most legendary designers ever in Hollywood."

Singer Pink wore many of his designs over the years. Sharing several of the outfits she wore on stage during her Funhouse tour in 2009, she wrote "I was so lucky to be dressed by him for so long. He was loving, wickedly funny and an absolute genius."
"There are going to be some fabulously dressed angels."
Mackie was still designing up until recently - Sabrina Carpenter wore one of his designs at the MTV Video Music Awards last year.

He also designed the dress Miley Cyrus wore during her performance at the 2024 Grammy Awards. She won a Grammy that year for her break-up anthem, Flowers - perhaps it was her own version of a "revenge" dress.

items: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, "There are going to be some fabulously dressed angels," Pink wrote in a tribute to Bob Mackie. The singer wore many of his designs over the years, especially during her Funhouse Tour in 2009

blocks.text: Caitlin Cassidy
‘Multiculturalism is who we are’: Anne Aly

Multicultural affairs minister Anne Aly was also on the ABC’s National Forum panel. She said Labor was committed to bringing immigration numbers down in a “manageable way” while ensuring the system both met the needs of Australia and was “fair for those who come here”.
She pushed back at claims immigrants were harming social cohesion, pointing to an Australia she grew up in where “nobody cared what language your mum spoke”.

double quotation markThat’s the Australia that I know. And I fear that that is the Australia that we’re losing … Every time we talk about immigration, multiculturalism, it comes from a deficit point of view. Social cohesion becomes the burden of people from different countries who have come here and it is their fault, it is their responsibility to socially cohere. The fact is that multiculturalism is who we are. It is part of our identity. It’s who we are as Australia.
Andrew Hastie says Pauline Hanson hasn’t ‘had the courage’ to front media
Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie has questioned why Pauline Hanson announced One Nation’s immigration policy via a prerecorded video on social media instead of fronting the media.
Appearing alongside Barnaby Joyce on the ABC’s National Forum, he said he backed parts of One Nation’s immigration plan but was concerned about the lack of detail and Hanson’s silence:

double quotation markWe haven’t seen her at all today. And this is someone who wants to be the prime minister of Australia. And she hasn’t had the courage to front the media today and explain the budgetary, the economic and the human impact of these policy changes that she’s suggesting.

His ongoing battle with One Nation appeared to be tempered, however, with him and Joyce largely exchanging niceties, including Joyce claiming in jest, at one point, that they were “back in bed together”.
Chris Bowen downplays reintroduction of fuel excise relief amid renewed surge in oil prices
Chris Bowen has watered down any expectations that a renewed rise in oil prices will lead to the reintroduction of the federal government’s fuel excise relief.

He said Labor was continuing to look “very closely” at the spike, which was prompted after a series of drone attacks forced Saudi Arabia to close its east-west crude pipeline. But he said the federal government had been “very clear” that cutting the fuel excise was a temporary measure.
Bowen said:

double quotation markIt’s not the only cost of living measure that we put in place … At the same time, I’m very much focused on ensuring our ongoing fuel supply in this very difficult international circumstance … We’re not going to respond to every daily movement on the world oil price.
Bowen said the situation in the Middle East was “deeply concerning” and confirmed he would be travelling to Saudi Arabia next week to meet with his counterpart, Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud.

He was also asked about the appointment of the former opposition leader Sussan Ley to the board of Snowy Hydro, given the Coalition abandoned its commitment to net zero under her leadership and she had blamed Labor’s renewable energy rollout on high energy prices.
Bowen said when he saw an Australian who was “well credentialled, I don’t care how they vote”, and described her as a person of “talent and ability”.

articles.title: Former Saskatoon private school admin, pictured with paddle in 1997, testifies at former principal's trial
articles.summary: Lou Brunelle, the first defence witness at Duff Friesen's assault trial, said paddling was school policy and parents signed off.

image.caption: Lou Brunelle, then an administrator at Christian Centre Academy, photographed with a wooden paddle for a 1997 Maclean's magazine article. A copy of the photo was entered as an defence exhibit in the assault trial of Duff Friesen on Monday. (Maclean's)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan
Lou Brunelle, the first defence witness at Duff Friesen's assault trial, said paddling was school policy and parents signed off.
1997 magazine photo now a court exhibit at Duff Friesen's assault trial

A photo of a former administrator for a Saskatoon private Christian school holding a wooden paddle, published in Maclean's magazine 30 years ago, is now evidence in the assault trial of a former principal at the school.
Duff Arthur Friesen faces five counts of assault with a weapon. He has pleaded not guilty to all of them.
Friesen is accused of hitting students with a wooden paddle. The charges stem from his time at Christian Centre Academy from 1997 to 2007.
The school was later renamed Legacy Christian Academy, then Valour Academy. It's closely associated with Mile Two Church, now called Encounter Church.
Lou Brunelle, the man in the magazine photo from 1997, was the first defence witness at the trial. He testified Monday that paddling was school policy and parents signed off.

Brunelle worked at the school from 1989 to 2001, first as a supervisor and then an administrative assistant, reporting to the director and senior to the teachers. He said the role can be compared to that of a vice-principal.
He said the paddle was one of multiple methods, alongside things like demerits and detentions, that the school used to enforce discipline for things like stealing, lying or cheating.
“We would chat with the child. If warranted — three swats,” he told the jury.
He said the student and the discipliner would then pray together.

items: Former student tells jury principal struck him at private Christian School in Saskatoon

blocks.text: Brunelle also testified that none of the staff at the school at the time were certified to work as teachers. He added that the curriculum was approved and that students received Ministry of Education transcripts that allowed them to go on to university.
Crown witnesses
The Crown closed its case Friday after calling five former students, each of whom testified about being struck with a wooden paddle.
Robyn Mandell said Friesen spanked her hard enough to leave bruises for days. She said it was extremely "humiliating, shameful and terrifying."

items: Trial begins for former principal of Sask. private Christian school facing assault charges

blocks.text: Coy Nolin, who testified on Wednesday, told the jury he was called to Friesen's office during a school day after Friesen sent a letter to his mother about his schoolwork, and was told he would be taken off the basketball team if he didn't catch up.
He said Friesen told him he’d be getting paddled and sent back to class. Nolin said he then put his hands on the seat of a chair and bent over.
“He struck me three times,” Nolin said.
The trial is set for two weeks, with Justice Daryl Labach presiding.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Aishwarya Dudha is a reporter for CBC Saskatchewan based in Saskatoon. She specializes in immigration, justice and cultural issues and elevating voices of vulnerable people. She has previously worked for CBC News Network and Global News. You can email her at aishwarya.dudha@cbc.ca
