articles.title: Protesters voice concern over privatization as Carney's investment summit kicks off
articles.summary: Hundreds of activists gathered in downtown Toronto on Monday to protest against an investment summit organized by Prime Minister Mark Carney.

image.caption: The Canada Investment Summit on Sept. 14-15 is pitching Canada as a safe place for investment at a time of economic uncertainty, but some worry everyday Canadians won't see the benefits. (Michael Cole/CBC)

blocks.text: Toronto·Updated
Hundreds of activists gathered in downtown Toronto on Monday to protest against an investment summit organized by Prime Minister Mark Carney.
Activists gathered outside city hall as Mark Carney hosts over 100 potential investors Monday

The Canada Investment Summit takes place on Monday and Tuesday in Toronto and is hosted by Carney, who has invited over 100 of the world's largest investors from around the world in the hopes of securing $1 trillion in investments in some 167 projects across the country over the next five years.

At the summit, the prime minister is expected to pitch Canada as a safe and reliable place for investment at a time of economic uncertainty, but some aren't sold on outside investment yielding positive results for everyday Canadians.

Protesters, including representatives of labour unions, Indigenous leaders and climate and housing advocates, say they reject the idea of leaving Canada's economic future in the hands of CEOs and worry about the future of public services, pipelines and arms manufacturing.

On Monday evening, protesters gathered first in Nathan Phillips Square, then marched to a police barrier near the Art Gallery of Ontario, where the summit's opening gala that is closed to the public and the media is being held.

Rachel Small, an organizer with World Beyond War, a non-profit that campaigns against conflict, said Canadians are struggling to afford rent and the cost of living, and need more investment in education, transit and health care.
"Carney is doing the opposite of that," she said.
"He is selling our public resources without any guaranteed returns and at the same time growing industries that will push the world towards greater war and climate catastrophe."

items: Carney is seeking $1 trillion in investments. What will it take to land major deals at this week's summit?

blocks.text: "These billionaires make decisions behind closed doors in our city to decide our futures. Our future is not for sale," Small said.
Monday's assembly of speakers gathered under the banner "The Many vs. The Money," arguing the summit is designed to "auction off" Canadian public resources, according to its website.
What is the Canada Investment Summit? Inside Carney's investment summit in Toronto
National sovereignty and the impact of various projects on the environment was also a prominent concern throughout the speeches.
"Everybody worries about their own backyard. Our front yard is this entire planet and we must stand together to protect it." said Wet’suwet’en Nation Hereditary Chief Na'Moks.
"They're taking everything we survive on and are willing to sell it to foreign investors."
CBC Toronto has reached out to Environment and Climate Change Canada for comment.

items: NDP's Avi Lewis says Carney is selling Canadian assets to 'the captains of Wall Street'

blocks.text: Speaker Nik Barry-Shaw, trade and privatization campaigner for the Council of Canadians, which advocates for clean water, green energy and fair trade, referenced the prime minister's speech to the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland in January when he said: "If we're not at the table, we're on the menu."
"I've been looking around the table that Carney has set for this summer and I don't see any of us at the table," he said. "Does that mean we're on the menu?"

Ontario Premier Doug Ford said in a statement Sunday that he welcomes foreign investment, noting 15 major projects in the province "worth tens of billions of dollars" are set to be discussed. They range from mining to energy production and AI.
"We are building an economy that can compete with anyone, anywhere," he said in the statement. "That’s going to be my message throughout the Canada Investment Summit."
"Ontario has what the world needs and we’re going to make sure the world knows it."
Concerns over foreign investment not new: expert

Jeff Mahon, director for geopolitical and international business at consulting firm StrategyCorp., told CBC Radio's Metro Morning that concerns over foreign investment are not new, and pointed to Canada's Investment Canada Act, which reviews deals for their net benefit and impact on jobs and economic competitiveness.

"Foreign investment is really important for the Canadian economy, but there's always going to be some considerations on whether the owner or type of investment will lead to some challenges down the line," he said.

items: From pipelines to railways and AI: Ottawa pitches 167 projects ahead of Carney's investment summit
Carney's pitch to unlock trillions in global investment

blocks.text: Mahon said Canada's trade war with the U.S. is "definitely" a catalyst for the initiative, and understands the push to drive more outside funding.

"When the U.S. shuts down market access or threatens market access, that undermines investment confidence in Canada," he said. "If we don't have investment coming in then that means future economic activity is inhibited, it's going to be undermined."
"Those investment dollars lead to productive investment … that means future economic growth could be higher."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Amy van den Berg is a writer and editor based in Toronto. She often writes about human interest stories, travel and design and her work has appeared in CBC, Monocle, The Walrus, and Toronto Life.
With files from Abby Hughes and The Canadian Press

articles.title: EU seeks Arctic strategy amid growing power rivalry
articles.summary: Russia's aggression, Trump's threats against Greenland and the race for critical raw materials are pushing the Arctic to the top of Europe's agenda.

image.caption: Looking ahead: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and other European leaders gathered in Finland to discuss the future of the ArcticImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Known as the "Gateway to the Arctic," the Finnish city of Rovaniemi sits directly on the Arctic Circle. Its forests are glowing in autumn colors as European leaders gather here at the invitation of Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo to discuss a new EU strategy for the Arctic. Climate change and Russia's war against Ukraine have thrust the High North into the center of European attention.
"There is a high demand for concrete EU action in the Arctic," Orpo said. "Our security environment has changed fundamentally. The Arctic has emerged as a central arena of great power competition."
The prime minister added that the Arctic's critical natural resources are also "attracting interest."
A changing security environment in the High North

The changing security environment was a central theme throughout the summit. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas warned that Russia is reopening former Soviet military bases in the region and conducting missile exercises in the High North.
"We also see that China is increasingly more interested in the region, so we have to remain vigilant," Kallas said.

The leaders gathered at Finland's northernmost air force base, looking up into a cloudless blue sky as Finnish fighter jets took to the air for a demonstration. Security has been placed at the heart of the discussions by Prime Minister Orpo. From Rovaniemi, Finland's Air Force monitors the skies along Europe's Arctic border with Russia ― 24/7.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who attended despite facing significant political pressure at home, described the region as increasingly important to Europe's security: "This region has become a geopolitical hotspot. Russia is building up its military capabilities here and … uses its presence for hybrid activities every day."
Merz added that the Arctic is not only a security issue, but also offers major economic opportunities, particularly when it comes to critical raw materials.

blocks.caption: European leaders learned about Finnish fighter jets during the Arctic summit as wellImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Confrontation replaces cooperation
"From the Putin era onwards, Russia has been developing its military capacities everywhere, but also in the Arctic," said Timo Koivurova of the Arctic Centre at the University of Lapland.

For years Western countries still continued cooperating with Moscow on scientific research and climate issues. Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine brought that era to an end. Finland and Sweden joined NATO as a direct consequence of the war. Finland's 1,340-kilometer (833-mile) border with Russia is now also a NATO border, fundamentally changing the security landscape in northern Europe.

The European Commission plans to update its 2021 Arctic Strategy as early as October 2026. The summit's joint declaration calls for greater investment in military mobility, cross-border connectivity and critical infrastructure in the EU's northernmost regions, including transport links, digital networks and satellite technologies.
Koivurova said that Russia's current focus on Ukraine and that war takes its military capacities.

"But obviously when that war is over, and someday it will be over, there will be a lot of investments from Russia, very likely also in the northern regions, because they are so important for its overall security," Koivurova told DW.
The United States as an additional stress factor

The Arctic is also being affected by tensions among Western partners, Koivurova said. In particular, he argued that US President Donald Trump's proposals regarding Canada and Greenland have strained cooperation among Arctic allies.

"Trump's proposal to have Canada as the 51st state of the United States, or the purchase of Greenland, these are really major problems for the cooperative relations between the western Arctic states," Koivurova said. "That is a kind of additional stress factor for Arctic governance cooperation."
Veteran Arctic observer Markku Heikkilä believes the region is increasingly divided.
"In my opinion, [the] Arctic is now slowly dividing into three parts," Heikkilä told DW.
He said Russia forms one bloc, while countries such as EU member states, Norway, Iceland and Canada continue to defend a rules-based international order, climate action and Indigenous rights.
"Officially the position of the USA is now very much different from what it used to be," said Heikkilä.
Inside NATO's Arctic operation preparing for a Russia crisis
Climate change is transforming the Arctic

At the same time, climate change is reshaping the Arctic faster than any other region on Earth. Scientists expect the central Arctic Ocean to become largely ice-free during summer sometime around 2040 and 2050. As sea ice retreats, the region is gaining strategic importance with new shipping routes and significantly shortening distances between major trading centers, creating new economic and geopolitical opportunities, says Koivurova.
Yet climate policy has become another source of disagreement between the United States and many of its Arctic partners.

"Climate change is, of course, a hugely important thing in the Arctic. It's warming four times the rate as compared to the global average. So everything we do in the Arctic nowadays, one way or the other, is related to climate change," Koivurova said.

He added that the Trump administration's approach has had a significant impact on international cooperation, including within the Arctic Council: "The US is torpedoing any mention of climate change at the moment. So that was certainly a big, big change."
Orpo: 'We should strengthen Arctic resilience'
At the close of the summit, Prime Minister Orpo called for greater investment to strengthen the region's resilience.
"We should strengthen Arctic resilience by strategic investments in Arctic infrastructure, dual use transport networks, critical raw materials, icebreaking and technological innovation," Orpo said.

Rovaniemi is known worldwide as the hometown of Santa Claus. Not far from the "Arktikum" museum and science center where the leaders met lies "Santa Claus Village." It's home to the official Santa Claus Post Office, which remains open year-round. Visitors can also meet Santa himself. Whether any of the summit participants paid him a visit ― and if so, what they wished for ― remains unknown.

articles.title: Israeli minister threatens to revoke filmmakers' citizenship over Gaza documentary
articles.summary: The film accuses the Israeli army of mass civilian killing in Gaza, and Israeli officials say it could be treasonous.

blocks.text: Israel's culture minister has called for the Oscar-winning Israeli co-directors of Naza, a documentary that accuses the Israeli army of mass civilian killings in Gaza, to be stripped of their citizenship over "treason against the state".

Named for the Hebrew military acronym for collateral damage, the film speaks to 24 unidentified Israeli military and intelligence officers who outlined the AI-powered targeting systems used by the Israeli army to bombard Gaza in the war triggered by the Hamas-led attack on 7 October 2023.

Since then, more than 73,000 Palestinians, including more than 20,000 children, have been killed in the campaign by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF), according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, figures considered reliable by the UN. About 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage during the Hamas attack.

Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor say their 80-minute documentary "details the systems behind Israel's calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza" during the war, according to its official synopsis. One of the people interviewed says there was the approval for an attack to kill 500 people for "one human target", an allegation the IDF said was "completely false".

In a post on X, Culture Minister Miki Zohar said he had asked the authorities "to investigate how the materials were obtained, who is behind them, and whether in the process of obtaining or publishing them, actions were taken that amount to aiding the enemy during wartime".

In a letter addressed to Israel's Interior Ministry, he said: "The claims presented in the film are false and distorted, and I categorically reject the attempt to portray IDF soldiers and the State of Israel as perpetrators of intentional crimes." Zohar mentioned the country's Citizenship Law, saying it "allows for the revocation of citizenship due to a 'breach of allegiance to the State of Israel'". The measure, however, has rarely been applied.

There has been no immediate reaction from Abraham and Szor. The filmmakers won an Oscar last year for No Other Land, a documentary about violence by Jewish settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

Naza premiered last Thursday at the Venice Film Festival, where it received a 25-minute standing ovation, but has not yet been made available to the wider public. It won a special jury prize at the festival. Speaking then, Abraham said the reporting for the film, which was produced by the UK's Guardian newspaper, had been "rigorous" and that efforts to discredit it were "attempts to not face reality".

"It's a war that has principally been killing civilians. And I think our film is showing that this is not some mistake. It's not an accident. It's something very, very systemic. And this should have been apparent to everyone, I think, from the start. But we are showing it from the inside, with insider testimony," he told the Associated Press in an interview.

The IDF, after initially saying it "categorically rejects [the] allegations", later issued a new statement via its spokesperson Brig-Gen Effie Defrin, saying: "The film 'Naza' has not yet been released in full. However, based on what can be seen in promotional material, it presents a series of serious and false allegations regarding the IDF and its personnel.

"To enable a substantive, professional, and fact-based discussion, rather than one based on misleading portrayals, I invite the filmmakers to allow IDF representatives to view the film in full so that we can address each of the allegations it raises on merits."

Other Israeli politicians have criticised the documentary, including former prime minister Naftali Bennett, who called it a "horrific blood libel against our sons and daughters", and former defence minister Avigdor Lieberman, who described the directors as "haters of Israel".

But more than 700 members of the film industry signed a petition in support of the filmmakers, saying they were being subjected to a "campaign of incitement and vilification". Speaking to Israel's N12 channel, Israeli actor and screenwriter Shlomi Elkabetz said: "These are questions [raised in the film] that must be examined, not silenced."

articles.title: Trump seeks halt to energy attacks by both Russia, Ukraine
articles.summary: Donald Trump, under fire for record US diesel prices, claims Russia and Ukraine have agreed to stop striking energy targets. Russia said nothing, Ukraine said "we expect specifics from our partners"…

image.caption: Ukraine has been targeting Russian oil refinieries with long range drones this year, while Russia's strategy of firing on Ukrainian power infrastructure is well establishedImage: Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump claimed a breakthrough on Monday in diplomacy between Ukraine and Russia, although his unsubstantiated declaration only elicited a very reserved comment from Ukraine and no immediate word from the Kremlin.
The assertion comes amid indications from both Russia and Ukraine that they would be willing to continue with US-brokere mediations, which have been largely stagnant throughout Trump's second term.

Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelenskyy last week told DW that he would be willing to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the G20 summit in Miami in December if rumors of Putin being invited materilialized.
What did Trump say?
Trump appeared to claim that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop hitting each other's energy targets.
"Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!" Trump or his team wrote.

"The World's Diesel price is mostly caused by the Russia/Ukraine War [sic], not Iran," the Truth Social comment continued, demonstrating — as a quickfire series of agitated follow-up posts would reinforce — a desire to downplay rising US oil prices, the role of Trump's war in Iran in pushing them skywards, and economic pressures closer to home.
Donald Trump blames Ukraine for record US diesel prices
What, if anything, did Ukraine and Russia say?
There was no immediate comment on the matter from Moscow.
Ukraine's presidency declined to comment but President Volodymyr Zelenskyy issued a more guarded statement online.
He did, however, say that he had recommended seeking such an accord, as winter approaches — if Russia's cooperation could be ensured after years of it targeting Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

"Ukraine has proposed that its partners secure an agreement with Russia that would stop the destruction of critical infrastructure," Zelenskyy wrote online. "Food, energy, and other basics that sustain life must be protected, and Russian strikes are directed primarily against them."
But Zelenskyy cautioned that Kyiv "is not convinced that Russia is willing to abide by an agreement," if one could be reached.

"If our partners are ready to ensure that Russia genuinely refrains from striking our electricity system, other energy facilities, critical infrastructure, and food supply routes, then, of course, we are ready to ensure a corresponding halt to our strikes."
He said Kyiv would need assurance that this was a lasting deal and not just a bid to secure temporary relief in fuel prices in Russia ahead of elections at the end of the week.
"We expect specifics from our partners," Zelenskyy concluded, without naming names.
Ukraine has been targeting Russian warehouses, refineries amid Iran war

As Trump's war in Iran pushed oil prices to highs not seen since the immediate aftermath of Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Kyiv has started using long-range drone strikes to target Russia's refinery and petroleum supply infrastructure.
This has caused isolated shortages and price increases, even in oil-rich Russia.
Ukraine has also launched a series of high-profile strikes on Russia's best-known online retailer Wildberries, accusing it of providing logistical support to the military.

The US miltiary action of the last six months in the Gulf has also left Ukraine poorly placed to defend itself against Russian ballistic missiles, because of US Patriot missile supplies being depleted in the Middle East.

In recent winters, Russia has frequently targeted Ukraine's energy infrastructure to try to exacerbate difficulties of dealing with the cold. Last winter, as a particularly fierce cold snap hit Kyiv and other parts of the country, Trump announced a brief halt to strikes on Kyiv which only held for a few days.

articles.title: Bolsonaro 2.0: Brazil braces for the return of the far right
articles.summary:
With Lula mired in scandal, Flávio Bolsonaro is firing up his base in the bellwether state of Minas Gerais – starting at the scene of his father’s stabbing

A giant banner of Brazil’s…
articles.byline: Tom Phillips in Juiz de Fora

blocks.text: A giant banner of Brazil’s incarcerated former president Jair Bolsonaro fluttered in the morning breeze as his eldest son, Flávio, touched down at an airfield on the fringe of a city that will soon help decide the future of one of the biggest democracies on earth.

“Brazil is rudderless. Brazil has no president and Brazil needs a president – and that president is Flávio Bolsonaro,” the far-right senator declared as he waded into the flock of supporters who had gathered to welcome him to Juiz de Fora, one of the largest cities in the battleground state of Minas Gerais.

With less than a month before nearly 159 million Brazilians choose their next leader on 4 October, the election appears on a knife-edge, with the incumbent leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, neck-and-neck in the polls.

blocks.caption: Bolsonaro supporters float a giant balloon depicting the US president, Donald Trump, holding Brazil’s president, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. Photograph: Miguel Schincariol/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Bolsonaro’s campaign appears to have seized the momentum in recent weeks amid a slew of corruption scandals involving Lula’s son and the supreme court. That has prompted despair among progressives who fear their country could fall back into the hands of a radical rightwing movement that tried to grab power after the then-president, Jair Bolsonaro, lost the 2022 election to Lula.

Last September, Jair Bolsonaro received a 27-year jail sentence for spearheading that botched coup – a verdict supporters insist was unjust. But the ex-president and his accomplices are likely to be freed if his son wins power – a prospect that delights the hardcore Bolsonaristas who turned out to greet Flávio Bolsonaro wearing yellow football shirts and headbands reading: “Lula out!”

“Today is a moment of joy,” said Ulisses Lima, 50, a cybersecurity specialist with a Jesus Christ pendant around his neck. “Flávio represents change. He represents Brazil’s rescue from this socialist abyss we’ve spent so long warning about,” Lima added as supporters waited for the former president’s heir to arrive.

blocks.caption: Brazil’s president Lula at a reelection campaign rally in Curitiba on Saturday. Photograph: Rodolfo Bührer/Reuters

blocks.text: Nearby, another devotee, José Caldeira, fell to his knees and begged for divine intervention to get Bolsonaro out of house arrest. “God, free this nation! Amnesty and freedom for Bolsonaro!” Caldeira bellowed, raising his hands towards the sky.

A third man, Davi Frederico, held a banner celebrating Donald Trump, who has been accused of trying to swing the election in Bolsonaro’s favour through economic and diplomatic pressure. “Make Liberals Cry Again,” it said.

Juiz de Fora, an industrial and university city traditionally associated with the left, is also a key location for Brazil’s hard right. The city’s army headquarters was the launchpad for the 1964 coup that plunged Brazil into two decades of military rule. And it was in Juiz de Fora, on the eve of the 2018 election, that Jair Bolsonaro was stabbed in the gut while campaigning – an attack widely believed to have helped the former paratrooper seal his victory.

blocks.caption: Davi Frederico at the airport in Juiz de Fora. Photograph: Alan Lima/The Guardian

blocks.text: Bolsonaro’s shock win ushered in what, from a progressive perspective, were four abysmal years. Destruction of the Amazon rainforest and gun ownership skyrocketed, hundreds of thousands died during a Covid outbreak Bolsonaro was accused of mishandling, and the president’s authoritarian rhetoric and attacks on Brazil’s electronic voting system culminated in the 8 January 2023 riots in Brasília. The supreme court later called those disturbances part of a plot to “annihilate” the country’s democracy.
But the Bolsonaros still enjoy abundant support, and that devotion was visible as Flávio Bolsonaro’s motorcade crept towards the high street where his father was ambushed eight years ago.

blocks.caption: Street hawkers at Flavio Bolsonaro’s campaign event pay tribute to the US connection. Photograph: Alan Lima/The Guardian

blocks.text: “Let’s get the left out! Let’s get these motherfuckers out!” one elderly woman shrieked as the senator passed by on top of a sound truck stamped with the word: “Jesus”. Other fans, many senior citizens, waved Brazil flags from windows or stood on the sidewalk flashing victory signs with their hands.

“Barring some kind of leftwing trickery, Flávio Bolsonaro can already be considered president. All you have to do is take a look at the streets and social media,” claimed Nikolas Ferreira, an influential far-right congressman from Minas Gerais who has more than 9 million TikTok followers.

Alongside the enthusiasm, there were glimpses of the revulsion many Brazilians feel for the former president. One leftwinger took to his balcony with a loudhailer to taunt the Bolsonaristas as they paraded through town. “Trump! Trump! Get my daddy out of jail!” the dissenter jeered in reference to the US president’s attempts to help Bolsonaro escape punishment.

blocks.caption: Supporters gather to greet Flávio Bolsonaro at Juiz de Fora, Minas Gerais. Photograph: Alan Lima/The Guardian

blocks.text: Minas Gerais, a mountainous mining and agricultural region that is larger than France and has 21 million inhabitants, is Brazil’s bellwether state. Since democracy returned in the 1980s, no candidate has won the presidency without triumphing here. In 2018, Jair Bolsonaro beat Lula’s candidate in Minas by more than 1.7m votes. Four years later, Lula reclaimed the state by fewer than 50,000. After landing in Minas last week, Flávio Bolsonaro said he was confident of clawing back the swing state, with one recent poll putting him ahead there.

“[Lula] is a president who you look at and see the past,” the 45-year-old senator said of his 80-year-old adversary. “With Flávio you can be sure that when people look at him, they see a modern government and a government of the future.”

Thomas Traumann, a political analyst who has written a book about his polarised country, said the election was too close to call. “It’s a coin flip,” said Traumann, who believed an unexpected scandal or last-minute “black swan” event could swing the election either way. On Friday, it emerged that Flávio Bolsonaro had been placed under police investigation over suspicions of corruption involving the funding of a big-budget biopic telling the story of the assassination attempt against his father in Juiz de Fora.

blocks.caption: Flávio Bolsonaro addresses supporters at the spot where Jair Bolsonaro was stabbed in Juiz de Fora during the 2018 presidential campaign. Photograph: Pablo Porciúncula/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: For progressive voters, the vision for a Flávio Bolsonaro administration laid out during his visit to Minas is the stuff of nightmares. “I think Flávio Bolsonaro’s presidency is going to be Jair Bolsonaro 2.0,” said Bruno Engler, a Bolsonarista lawmaker from Minas’ capital, Belo Horizonte.

Engler believed a top priority would be zero-tolerance policing, with the younger Bolsonaro pledging an iron-fisted crackdown on criminals his father has compared to cockroaches. “Thugs who don’t surrender will be arrested or neutralised,” Engler vowed, predicting gun laws would be loosened.

Speaking on the street corner where his father was knifed, Flávio Bolsonaro vowed to pack Brazil’s 11-member supreme court with five conservative judges “who are against abortion [and] against drugs”. “We’re going to give the streets back to the Brazilian people … We’re going to lower the age of criminal responsibility. We are going to introduce chemical castration for rapists,” shouted the candidate, who wore a bullet-proof vest.

Those pledges prompted whoops of excitement from the crush of supporters below Bolsonaro’s truck. Dozens ofmobile phones captured the candidate’s every word. But amid the rightwing rejoicing there was fear and trepidation, too.

blocks.caption: Lennon César: ‘Brazilians have short memories when it comes to the past.’  Photograph: Alan Lima/The Guardian

blocks.text: Lennon César, a law student and leftwing activist who had come to confront Bolsonaro’s fans, voiced incredulity that less than four years after Jair Bolsonaro’s failed power grab, tens of millions of Brazilians seemed poised to vote for his son.

“We were the victims of an attempted coup – and his father was the perpetrator,” recalled César, 28. “It’s terrifying. And the thing that worries me most is that the general public doesn’t really seem to get what’s happening. Brazilians have short memories when it comes to the past.”
As a black, gay man, César felt particular dread at the prospect of a second Bolsonaro presidency, given the patriarch’s hostility to minorities.

César vowed to vote for Lula, Brazil’s first working-class president, calling him the only leader who paid attention to the poor. “If today I’m studying for a law degree it’s because one of Lula’s government programmes allowed me to achieve that,” he said, warning: “These people … might destroy it all.”
A few blocks away, a graffiti artist had spray painted their own message of disapproval on to the facade of Bolsonaro’s Juiz de Fora HQ. “Facists [sic],” it read.

blocks.caption: Graffiti on Flávio Bolsonaro’s headquarters in the city of Juiz de Fora. Photograph: Alan Lima/The Guardian

articles.title: Sydney Sweeney's 'sexualized' sports betting ad slammed by female athletes
articles.summary: U.S. actor Sydney Sweeney is once again facing backlash over an advertisement. But this time, she's enraged female athletes around the world with a nude sports betting ad — and her response.

image.caption: A composite image of screen grabs of social media posts from athletes Canadian Sophia Jensen, left, Canadian Madeline Schizas, centre, and American Gracie Kramer, posted over the Sept. 12-13 weekend in response to a new sports betting ad featuring U.S. actor Sydney Sweeney. (@sophiajensenCA/TikTok,

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
U.S. actor Sydney Sweeney is once again facing backlash over an advertisement. But this time, she's enraged female athletes around the world with a nude sports betting ad — and her response.
Canadian skier, canoeist, skater among athletes criticizing Novig ad
U.S. actor Sydney Sweeney is once again facing backlash over an advertisement.
This time, she has enraged female athletes around the world with a nude sports gambling ad — and her response.

The Novig sports prediction ad, posted online Sept. 9 and viewed nearly 39 million times by Monday morning, features Sweeney holding various pieces of sports equipment in front of what looks like her otherwise naked body, as bass music plays in the background.
"Think you know sports? Prove it," says the star of Euphoria and The Housemaid at the beginning of the ad as she holds a football in front of each breast.

In other shots, she perches on a basketball net while spinning a ball with only her hair covering her, holds a football in front of her pelvis, lies nude on a bench with a soccer ball resting on her feet and swings a golf club wearing only white underwear.

It set off a backlash from female athletes and Olympians who say the ad sexualizes women in sport and sets them back. The criticism crosses borders and a range of sports, with many posting "Dear Sydney Sweeney" videos on social media in response.

"Dear Sydney Sweeney, this is women in sports," Canadian sprint canoeist Sophia Jensen posted on TikTok on Sunday, alongside a video where the world champion competes on the water and trains in the gym.
"Hey Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like," Canadian figure skater Madeline Schizas posted on Instagram with a similar video where she competes and trains on and off the ice.
"IDK what Sydney Sweeney was doing, but this is what a woman in sport looks like," posted U.S. gymnast Gracie Kramer over a similar montage.
British sprinter Amy Hunt got a word in during a post-race interview on Sunday, after she finished fourth in the 200-metre final at the Ultimate Championship in Budapest.
"Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like," Hunt told BBC Sport, adding "hard work, blood, sweat, tears."
Australian swimmer Ariarne Titmus, the reigning Olympic champion in the 400-metre freestyle, called the ad "a kick in the face" on Instagram.
"How do we live in a world where monetizing a woman's body and sexualizing women's sport is still a thing?" she said, according to Australia's ABC News.

items: Spain's soccer federation will fund egg freezing. Is this a win for female athletes?
Women's sports are having a moment, but sexism is still holding back success

blocks.text: Novig CEO and co-founder Jacob Fortinsky praised the brand campaign for highlighting a platform that's "singularly focused on sports."
"Sydney helped bring that message to life in a way that’s impossible to ignore," Fortinsky said in a press release the same day the ad launched.
In the same press release, Sweeney called the campaign "a fun idea" that "brings that idea to life with confidence, humor and a playful edge."
Not her 1st controversial ad
If this is sounding familiar, Sweeney faced similar backlash last year over an American Eagle advertisement that was criticized for promoting white standards of beauty at best, and eugenics at worst.
In the ad, Sweeney makes a play on words between jeans (the clothing item) and genes (the genetic material).
“Genes are passed down from parents to offspring, often determining traits like hair colour, personality and even eye colour. My jeans are blue,” Sweeney said in the ad.
Some internet commentators read the ad as having eugenicist undertones. Eugenics is a discredited idea that the human race could be improved by selectively breeding for certain traits.

items: 'That’s not storytelling': Olympians hope proposed guidelines eliminate sexualization on broadcasts
Sydney Sweeney says she put her phone away during the American Eagle jeans ad controversy

blocks.text: At the time, the blond-haired, blue-eyed actor stood by the ad and downplayed the reaction, which included support from U.S. President Donald Trump, who called it the "HOTTEST ad out there."

Sweeney appeared to take a more overt approach to the backlash against her new ad, posting a series of photos on Instagram on Sunday that showed magazine covers with male and female athletes posing in little to no clothing.
What Sydney Sweeney's American Eagle ad says about the brand's marketing | Hanomansing Tonight
This move prompted even more backlash. Canadian alpine skier Cassidy Gray called it "idiotic" and "senseless."

"It's not a joke when your life is actually you being a female athlete, and you being sexualized or not taken seriously and not given the same opportunities, and then you see one of the most famous actresses in the world going and completely wiping away all the work that you have done to be taken seriously," Gray posted in an emotional video on TikTok.
Gray also responded to those who might say it's just a commercial and not meant to be taken so seriously.
"I fear you're just out of touch, because it really is that deep."
Female athletes have historically been marketed in an over-sexualized manner, with a greater focus on their appearance than their skills.

This also extends to sports coverage, with women at the Tokyo 2021 Olympics 10 times more likely to be "visually objectified" with a camera angle than men, according to a report from The Representation Project. Researchers defined visual objectification as when a camera panned across an athlete's body or focused on a specific body part in a sexualizing way.
The same study found female athletes were more likely to be infantilized by commentators, often called "young ladies" and "girls."

Another recent study from World Athletics found that female athletes were consistently targeted by online abuse more than their male counterparts at four global sporting events, including the 2024 Paris Olympics.

Natalie Stechyson has been a writer and editor at CBC News since 2021. She covers stories on social trends, families, gender, human interest, as well as general news. She's worked as a journalist since 2009, with stints at the Globe and Mail and Postmedia News, among others. Before joining CBC News, she was the parents editor at HuffPost Canada, where she won a silver Canadian Online Publishing Award for her work on pregnancy loss. articles.title: Immigrants held in small outdoor cages at 'Alligator Alcatraz' in Florida, investigators find
articles.summary: DHS inspectors say they found the immigration-detention centre violated basic standards for hygiene, medical care, food and safety.

blocks.text: In its response included in the investigation report, DHS officials said Florida - not the federal government - had authority over day-to-day operations at the facility.
The facility was established by the state of Florida through an executive order signed by DeSantis, but the federal government paid for operational costs.

In January, the OIG conducted a surprise inspection at the detention facility, which had become one of the most notorious immigration detention centres in the US. The OIG is an independent internal watchdog at DHS. The current inspector general was appointed by President Donald Trump during his first term.

In 2025, the detention facility was built over the course of eight days in the Everglades, a protected wetland known for its alligators. Trump once joked that immigrants held there would need to learn "how to run away" from the reptiles at the facility, which civil rights groups have decried as inhumane.
In June 2026, DeSantis said the facility would close as it was only meant to be temporary.

According to the OIG report, between July 2025 and January 2026, the facility kept 79 immigrants in the small metal enclosures, describing them as "calming areas" for people to "deescalate and have time alone". They were held there from periods ranging from minutes to nearly two hours, at least once as a disciplinary measure, OIG said.
"The use of such restrictive spaces is highly unconventional and does not align with standards for humane treatment," the report stated.

articles.title: Africa's richest man launches continent's biggest share sale
articles.summary: Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote says he wants ordinary people to share in the success of his oil refinery.

blocks.text: Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote has launched Africa's largest ever share sale, offering a stake in his oil refinery to the general public in a deal that could raise as much as $2.1bn (£1.6bn).
The initial public offering (IPO) is for roughly 3% of the Dangote refinery, with the billionaire saying he wanted to give ordinary Nigerians the chance to share in the plant's success.
The refinery, which started production in 2024, is one of the largest in the world and took more than a decade to complete.
It now supplies more than 70% of Nigeria's energy consumption, and many Nigerians have expressed excitement at the prospect of owning a part of it.
Among them is Isah Salisu, who told the BBC he withdrew 50,000 naira (£28; $37) from his savings to invest.
"My hope is that my small money will one day grow big. I don't want to miss out as many I know are also investing," he said.
The IPO lasts for a month and the minimum purchase is 10 shares, costing about $4.
Economy and business expert Dr Abdulrazak Ibrahim Fagge told the BBC that Monday's event was historic.
But he warned investors that the price of the shares could fall, meaning people could lose some of their money.
"What prospective buyers, especially first-time buyers, should know is that they shouldn't invest all their money or money they would need in a couple of months," he said.
"They should invest something they could do without for the next three, four, five years."
He also warned people to be wary of scammers, saying there are people who would want to take advantage of those without good knowledge of the process.
"I will advise people to only deal with the institutions that have been listed," he said.
Nigeria is Africa's biggest oil producer but until the refinery was opened, most of the country's fuel had to be imported because of a lack of refining capacity in the country.
Born in Kano, Dangote, 67, has a net worth of around $28bn, according to Forbes magazine.
He made his fortune in cement and sugar in Nigeria before expanding to 16 other African countries.
His company Dangote Cement is Africa's largest cement producer.
The Lagos refinery was first announced in 2013 with an initial estimated cost of around $19bn, but construction did not begin until 2017. It was further delayed by the Covid-19 pandemic.
The site, in the Lekki Free Zone near Lagos, required massive land reclamation, with 65 million cubic metres of sand moved.
The refinery has a processing capacity of 650,000 barrels per day, making it the seventh-largest in the world.
The money raised by the share offer is intended to help double its capacity.

articles.title: UK armed forces member killed in crash in Ukraine
articles.summary:
Ministry of Defence says person died in road incident understood not to be result of hostile action

A member of the UK armed forces has been killed in a crash in Ukraine, the Ministry of…

blocks.text: A member of the UK armed forces has been killed in a crash in Ukraine, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) said.
The MoD said the person died in a road traffic incident on Saturday.
It is understood the incident was not as a result of hostile action.
Their family has been informed and has asked for some time before more details are released.
“Our thoughts and our sympathies are with the individual’s loved ones at this difficult time,” an MoD spokesperson said.
The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said on X: “This is very sad news for the family and for those grieving with them in our Armed Forces.
“My deepest condolences go to them all.”
There is a small number of British personnel in Ukraine who provide security to diplomats and support the country’s armed forces.
British paratrooper George Hooley, 28, was killed in Ukraine in December when he watched Ukrainian forces testing a new defensive capability.
The MoD described his death as a “tragic accident”.
Russia’s full scale invasion of Ukraine is in its fifth year and the conflict continues with fresh strikes on Ukraine including at a gas works and a drone attack on a station on Sunday.
The attack hit a train at Yahodyn station, on the Polish border, shortly after a train carrying Boris Johnson had left ahead of schedule.
Ukraine’s railway operator said the attack may have been aimed at the train carrying the former prime minister, among other dignitaries.
Johnson had been returning from a major conference in Kyiv along with former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt and a number of European security advisers.
According to a translation from Ukrainian, rail operator Ukrzaliznytsia said in a post on Telegram it was “quite possible” the drone had been aimed at Johnson’s train.

articles.title: Defense questions ex-Sandigan presiding justice as witness
articles.summary: The defense panel has questioned the decision of the prosecution to present retired Sandiganbayan presiding justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang as the Senate impeachment court tackles the article on the…

blocks.text: September 15, 2026 | 12:00am
Retired Sandiganbayan presiding justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang appears before the Senate impeachment court on September 14, 2026.
SPPA

MANILA, Philippines — The defense panel has questioned the decision of the prosecution to present retired Sandiganbayan presiding justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang as the Senate impeachment court tackles the article on the alleged unexplained wealth of Vice President Sara Duterte.
In a manifestation, defense lawyer Mark Vinluan said the presentation of Cabotaje-Tang is improper.

“This is the first time that the Vice President is being confronted with Justice Tang and her testimony. For the record, she is not listed in the pre-trial order as a witness and there is no reservation for a witness with her designation or background,” said Vinluan.
“So, for all intents and purposes, Justice Tang is a surprise witness, which violates fair play and is prohibited under the rules,” Vinluan said.
“In light of the foregoing, we will move for the exclusion of the testimony of Justice Tang and will submit to this Court’s discretion as to the presentation of her testimony,” Vinluan said.

He added that the prosecution did not even furnish the defense with copies beforehand, saying that this is already the third time that the prosecution has attempted to present a witness without first furnishing the defense with the materials to be used.
“We don’t know her personal background, and we don’t know the extent of her testimony and the documents that she will identify, if any,” Vinluan noted.
According to Vinluan, the notice on Sept. 9 was only to Cabotaje-Tang’s name, previous official function and general purpose of her testimony.
He said it is the position of the defense that the presentation of Cabotaje-Tang infringes on the Vice President’s right to intelligently cross-examine her.

“And more importantly, (it) violates the Vice President’s constitutional right to due process, particularly her right to be promptly and completely informed of the nature and cause of the accusation against her,” he added.
Vinluan noted that in the Philippines, being a legal expert is not an official designation and is quite subjective.
“We don’t know the extent of her legal knowledge, her political background, whether she’s neutral, DDS, loyalista or kakampink, which is hardly distinguishable nowadays,” he noted.
Presumption of innocence
The defense maintained that the Vice President enjoys presumption of innocence as the prosecution is “hellbent” on removing her from office.
During cross-examination of Cabotaje-Tang, Vinluan stressed that it is not the prosecution’s primary duty to convict.
“The prosecution should not be too eager to convict. Vice President Sara enjoys the presumption of innocence, correct?” Vinluan said.
He said that if the prosecution fails “to discharge this burden,” Duterte is entitled to an acquittal.
“At any rate, conviction must be based on the strength of the prosecution and not the weakness of the defense,” Vinluan added.
Cabotaje-Tang agreed with Vinluan but based on the point of view of criminal lawyers.
Oral arguments
The defense is ready for the oral arguments on the two-thirds threshold to convict the Vice President.
Defense spokesman Michael Poa said they have decided who will represent Duterte during the oral arguments but will not disclose the name.

Impeachment court spokesman Reginald Tongol said the Senate impeachment court will need 11 votes from the active roster of 20 senators to overturn the ruling setting the conviction threshold at 16 votes in Duterte’s impeachment trial. — Marc Jayson Cayabyab

"The only control or ‘guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" Trump posted on his Truth Social account.

blocks.caption: Anthropic is the developer of the popular AI model ClaudeImage: IMAGO/ZUMA Press

The Pentagon previously tried to brand Anthropic's models a security risk and posed a temporary ban on one of its more advanced models.
"There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China," Trump wrote.

Anthropic boss Amodei warned against uncontrolled global AI development over the weekend saying that there's a risk of AI-led agents taking over the entire internet within six to 12 months. Microsoft published its own code of conduct to ensure human control over AI.
This led to AI stocks falling worldwide, including those of chip maker Nvidia (3.5%) and Elon Musk's SpaceX (1.7%).

articles.title: Trump says he will consider releasing more 9/11 records after families’ request
articles.summary:
Families have asked Trump to declassify records that could shed light on Saudi Arabia’s alleged role in the 2001 attacks

Donald…

blocks.text: Donald Trump said Sunday that he will look into requests from families of 9/11 victims to release records that could shed light on Saudi Arabia’s alleged role in the attacks 25 years ago.

Several families have long alleged that a group of extremist religious leaders in Saudi Arabia gained influence in the kingdom’s government and aided the hijackers. Fifteen of the 19 hijackers were Saudis, but the Saudi government has long denied any involvement in the attacks.
The families have asked Trump to declassify and release the relevant records. Asked about it on Sunday during his trip to Ireland, the president said he would consider it.
“I’m going to look at it when I get back,” Trump said just before boarding Air Force One to return to Washington after a weekend in Ireland. “I know they asked me Friday.”

The relatives of 9/11 victims have been engaged in a lengthy legal battle against the Saudis. One of them, Terry Strada, called on Trump during a remembrance in New York City on Friday to “tell the Saudis to stop lying”.
Strada, who lost her husband, Tom, on 9/11, said US presidents had chosen “to protect the Saudis instead of standing with the 9/11 families”.

Strada, who was one of the 9/11 family members who read aloud the names of victims at the remembrance on the 25th anniversary of the attacks, added that the current administration should “stand with the families, stand with the survivors”.
“It has been one betrayal after another,” she said. “President Trump can still change that.”

articles.title: Yemen's Houthis attack Saudis, seize crucial Red Sea islands
articles.summary: Iran-backed Houthi rebels have tightened their grip on a key shipping route, capturing two strategic Red Sea islands. The closure of another global transport route is the latest ripple effect of the…

image.caption: With the Strait of Hormuz already closed, Houthi control of the Bab al-Mandab passage only increases pressure on Saudi Arabia and the USImage: Osamah Abdulrahman/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Iranian-backed Houthi rebels on Monday announced they had captured Greater and Lesser Hanish Island in the southern Red Sea.
The move bolsters the group's ability to choke traffic in another key global maritime shipping route as the ripple-effect of the war in Iran grows.

The strategic advance comes as Saudi-backed Yemeni forces try to regain territory recently lost near the Bab el-Mandab Strait, an important alternative to the Strait of Hormuz — which Iran has held closed since US President Donald Trump began bombing the Islamic Republic on February 28.

The closure of the Hormuz Strait, through which roughly one-fifth of the world's oil passed before the US began hostilities, has led to a global economic and energy emergency, driving up prices around the world and forcing petro-monarchy Saudi Arabia to move its oil exports through Bab el-Mandab.
But the Houthis have declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia and last week seized strategic Mayun Island and the Red Sea port of Mokha, cutting off the alternative route.
The capture of Greater and Lesser Hanish now puts even more pressure on Saudi shipments and thus global oil supplies and prices.

Beyond putting the squeeze on Saudi Arabia — the Houthis' proxy enemy for backing the internationally recognized government in the Yemen's reignited civil war — it could also provide Iran added leverage in defending itself against the US.
Houthis seize Red Sea chokepoint: What can Saudi Arabia do?
Houthi offensive continues to escalate as Iran war expands
The Houthis pressed on with their offensive Monday, launching missile and drone attacks on Saudi military targets.
A spokesman for the group said the strikes had caused "significant damage" and had come in response to "more than 300 [Saudi] airstrikes in [Yemen over] the past five days."
Despite being a longtime backer of the Houthis as part of its anti-Israel "axis of resistance," Tehran has denied any involvement in Yemen's revived civil war.

"Iran does not interfere in Yemeni affairs," said Tehran's Foreign Ministry on Monday, with spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei telling reporters the Houthis are "entirely independent actors who make their decisions based on their own interests."

Yemen's civil war — dormant for four years until the conflict in Iran broke out — began in 2014, when Houthi rebels seized large parts of northern Yemen, including the capital Sanaa, and forced the government to flee to Aden in the south.
In 2015, Saudi Arabia led a military coalition aiding the government, launching wave after wave of airstrikes as the conflict escalated into one of the worst humanitarian disasters in the world.
Saudi oil pipeline attack could raise global gas prices
Concerning situation for US and its Saudi, Gulf State allies
On Monday, Admiral Brad Cooper of US Central Command (CENTCOM) was in Jeddah to discuss "the latest developments in the region" with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
US news site Axios reports that Cooper has been in the kingdom since Thursday, dealing with urgent coordination meetings as the situation in the Red Sea escalates.
US media outlets reported last week that President Trump had rejected a request by the crown prince for the US to directly intervene.
Despite turning down the request to unleash US firepower, Trump reportedly agreed to provide intelligence sharing and targeting assistance.
Iran war: Analyzing the Houthi blockade against Saudi Arabia
Iran blames Saudi Arabia for stalling Hormuz talks
Iran on Monday accused Saudi Arabia of delaying talks aimed at reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Baghaei called a meeting set to take place in Oman, a "real opportunity" to restore security in the region and added that an agreement between Iran and Oman on opening the passage had been finalized and would be announced later.
Saudi Arabia reportedly has concerns over the lasting implications of a deal for the Strait of Hormuz and how it might negatively impact Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries.
Tehran says Riyadh is using Yemen as a "pretext" to delay talks on how the Strait will be governed now that the status quo has been upended by the US.
Currently, the only secure routes allowing Saudi Arabia to deliver its oil to Asian markets are via the Suez Canal or around South Africa's Cape of Good Hope.
On Monday, China's Foreign Ministry called attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure "unacceptable," saying Beijing is "deeply concerned" about further escalation.
No sign of end to US-Iran conflict after six months

articles.title: Ukraine, Russia set for new round of US-mediated talks
articles.summary: New trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US could begin in October, according to Kyiv and Moscow. Few expect a breakthrough, but Ukraine is seeking a partial de-escalation to help it get…

image.caption: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has offered to meet with Vladimir Putin face-to-faceImage: Office of the President of Ukraine/B66/Avalon/Photoshot/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ukraine and Russia have signaled their readiness to resume trilateral talks under US mediation.
"We're preparing. For October," said Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Ukrainian president's office.
Similar signals came from Moscow: "We do not rule out such a possibility. We are talking about the foreseeable future," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner aimed to revive trilateral talks to end Russia's war in Ukraine, visiting Moscow and Kyiv in the first week of September.

The last round of trilateral talks took place in January and February 2026 in Abu Dhabi and Geneva, without producing a breakthrough, as the issue of territory control in eastern Ukraine remained unresolved.
Territory remains a difficult subject
Vladimir Putin still demands more territory than Russia currently controls, Kushner confirmed on September 12, speaking online at the YES security conference in Kyiv.

"President Putin [has] laid out his line of what he wants to achieve. If Ukraine wanted to withdraw to that line, then obviously we have the rest of the deal set up and put together. Ukraine right now does not want to do that," the US envoy said.

The Ukrainian government has indicated it is willing to freeze the fighting along the current frontline in exchange for security guarantees. Such a step could be supported by 60% of Ukrainians, according to a poll by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology conducted in summer 2026. A similar majority of respondents rejected giving up territory that Russia hasn't been able to conquer. 33% said Ukraine should give up territory that Putin demands.
Russia's air superiority is a problem for Ukraine
Few expect a breakthrough anytime soon.

"For there to be a negotiated end to the war, there has to be parity. Right now, there's a stalemate on the front lines and not much is changing there, but in the air war, unfortunately, Russia currently has a significant advantage," Volodymyr Fesenko, a Kyiv-based political scientist, told DW.

Ukraine is running low on interceptors for Russian ballistic missiles. Russia has also stepped up attacks with new jet-powered drones, which fly faster than older gasoline-powered models and are harder to intercept.
Russia turns to jet-powered drones to wear Kyiv down
Russian airstrikes are increasingly targeting Ukraine's economy, including warehouses, energy facilities, gas stations and railway infrastructure.

The Kremlin has accused Ukraine of opening a "Pandora's box" by targeting Russia's economy and fuel and energy facilities with deep strikes since the summer. Ukraine says the attacks are intended to force Russia to the negotiating table.
Ukraine is worrying about the winter
Ukraine's supporters say Kyiv's strategy is working.

"The escalation ... is not a problem. It's a sign of success," said Jonathan Powell, the United Kingdom's National Security Adviser, speaking at the Yalta European Strategy conference in Kyiv on September 11. "Of course [Putin] doesn't go straight to negotiations, he tries to escalate in the ways that he can."
The West must "keep its foot on the gas" to make Putin negotiate in earnest, Powell said.

Such optimism contrasts with concerns in Ukraine about the upcoming winter. In 2025, Russian attacks on energy infrastructure caused extended blackouts and left people without heating in freezing temperatures.

"We anticipate a very difficult winter in terms of both critical infrastructure, which is being destroyed every day by Russian attacks, but also in terms of overall economic conditions in the country," said Ukraine's Economy Minister, Oleksandr Kravchenko.
Zelenskyy calls for partial de-escalation

Russia rejected the idea of a ceasefire during the upcoming talks. Ukraine is now calling for a de-escalation of attacks on energy infrastructure and the unblocking of grain exports via the Black Sea instead.

"What can bring us to any kind of negotiations? So, energy and grain. This is step number one. What we can achieve," Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told DW in an interview aired on September 12.
Zelenskyy backs Putin meeting at Miami G20: 'Results matter'

Political scientist Fesenko says an agreement on grain exports could prove the easier task: "In the Black Sea, both Ukraine and Russia are facing major problems. Grain exports have been blocked; ports have been shut down and therefore both sides have a stake in the matter."
An energy truce, however, remains elusive, as Ukraine's vulnerability in the winter gives Putin leverage he would not give up easily, Fesenko said.
At the same time, the US is increasing pressure on Ukraine to halt its attacks on Russian energy facilities.

"Mr. Zelenskyy has to do one thing: He has to ‌stop ⁠knocking out diesel fuel in Russia," Donald Trump said on Sunday, September 13. "There are plenty of other targets. Don't hit diesel fuel. That's hurting the world."
Kremlin rejected Zelenskyy-Putin meeting
The Kremlin has already rejected another of Zelenskyy's proposals: a meeting between the Ukrainian and Russian leaders in December on the sidelines of the G20 summit in Miami.

"Putin doesn't want to negotiate with Zelenskyy. It's been obvious since last year that he wants to reach an agreement with Trump," said Fesenko. "If Trump insists, Putin may agree to a meeting between the three leaders. But he has no intention of negotiating with Zelenskyy."
If negotiations start in October as expected, negotiating teams rather than the leaders themselves will conduct them. But Ukraine insists that only the presidents can decide the territorial issue.
"The territorial question remains a pressing one... Complex issues such as this are only resolved at the level of leaders," Zelenskyy said during the US envoys' visit to Kyiv.

articles.title: Women's Basketball World Cup: Can Germany harness a boom?
articles.summary: Germany thrilled fans at the Women's Basketball World Cup. But even if this sparked a boom in the women's game, the infrastructure simply isn't ready for it.

image.caption: Leonie Fiebich and her teammates thrilled German fans at the Women's Basketball World Cup in BerlinImage: sampics/picture alliance

blocks.text: The world's best players showcased their sport at the Women's Basketball World Cup in Berlin, which wrapped up on September 13.

Germany, led by Leonie Fiebich and Nyara, improved with every game throughout the preliminary and intermediate round of the 10-day tournament. In the quarterfinals, Germany beat European champions Belgium, delivering what was arguably their best-ever performance.

The final weekend though, revealed the team still isn't quite ready to compete with the world's elite over a full 40 minutes. Germany lost to France in the semifinals before losing to Spain in the match for third place. Despite their disappointment, the Germans still saw the tournament as a huge success.
"We simply aren't good enough yet," said Fiebich after the Spain match.
"We played the tournament with a lot of euphoria and beat the European champions, Belgium. But it's hard to keep overperforming. Still, we will get better."

The World Cup marked a climax of the positive development seen in German women's basketball in recent years. In 2024, the team qualified for the Olympic Games for the first time, where the women also won a surprising gold in the 3x3 basketball. At the 2025 EuroBasket, Germany's women finished fifth. The next women's EuroBasket is next year and if Germany qualify, they should be medal contenders.
"I think it's important to harness the pain the players are feeling right now," Germany head coach Olaf Lange said.
"Because in our day-to-day work over the coming months and years, we need to improve individually. That requires a lot of motivation, and this pain acts as fuel for improvement."

The support from Germany fans could hardly have been greater. A total of around 230,000 tickets were sold for the World Cup and although visiting fans were present, the crowds were made up primarily of Germans.
Only three play for German clubs
While the national team is just a few steps away from establishing itself among the world's elite, Germany's top women's basketball league (DBBL) lags well behind the international competition.

Most players from the World Cup squad play abroad. Fiebich, Nyara Sabally and her sister Satou, who missed the tournament due to injury, as well as Luisa Geiselsöder and Frieda Bühner, play in the WNBA. Team captain Marie Gülich is moving to a club in Australia after the World Cup, having previously played in Taiwan. Emily Bessoir, Lina Sontag, and Alexis Peterson-Smalls play in Spain. Clara Bielefeld currently plays US college basketball.

blocks.caption: Frieda Bühner and the other Germany players enjoyed the attention of the Berlin fans Image: Tonhäuser/BEAUTIFUL SPORTS/picture alliance

blocks.text: Only three Germany players; Alexandra Wilke, Emma Eichmeyer, and Britta Daub, play for DBBL clubs, although both Eichmeyer and Daub have previously played abroad.
In Germany, they simply can't earn a living from playing basketball. Wilke, for example, works as a teacher at a secondary school.
DBBL level 'semi-professional'
Lange, who was a coach in the league from 1995 to 2002, describes it as "semi-professional," and says it has gone downhill since he left.
"Back then, the top clubs had better structures than they do today—and we are in 2026. That says it all. Things are really going backwards," he lamented during his post-tournament press conference.

blocks.caption: Olaf Lange's day job is as an assistant coach of the WNBA's Toronto TempoImage: Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: "I have to ensure that our top players go abroad. As long as nothing changes in the league, it will be difficult to sustain this success."
Professionalization efforts

Changes are needed to ensure the national team's continued success. Ireti Amojo took over as DBBL president in March. The former Germany player is a TV pundit and podcaster and has also worked in management of the women's program of top men's club ALBA Berlin. She has introduced several measures aimed to professionalize conditions at DBBL clubs.
"We aim to hire full-time youth development coaches. We also want to increase arena capacities," Amojo told daily newspaper TAZ prior to the World Cup.
"Currently, some venues hold a maximum of 600 spectators, and if interest grows – as it is now – we will need larger arenas."

blocks.caption: DBBL President Ireti Amojo is seeking to professionalize the leagueImage: Alexander Trienitz/nordphoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: 'Too late to capitalize on a World Cup boom'

However, the top division is not the whole story; even if the Women's Basketball World Cup were to trigger a surge of young girls taking up the game in Germany, most clubs would be ill-prepared to handle them. This is partly due to a shortage of coaches, but also because there is a lack of basketball facilities, making court time scarce.

"We should have started five years ago so that we could say now: 'We are capitalizing on the momentum of the World Cup and ensuring that all these kids who have become basketball fans can play the sport in clubs across Germany,'" Amojo told Magenta Sport after the World Cup final.

"We are too late. We lack the structures to harness this interest and provide all the children fascinated by basketball with the opportunity, under perfect training conditions, to develop into the next Leonie Fiebich or Nyara Sabally."
Still, Amojo thinks the World Cup may just prove to be a much-needed spark for future development.

"It was the kind of proof we all needed, because people are quick to dismiss it, claiming that no one in Germany is interested in women's basketball. Now we've seen that people in Germany are interested in women's basketball," she said.
"We already have a few levers we want to use to work on the structures. And this certainly shouldn't be the end of things."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: CBS’s 60 Minutes accused of peddling pro-Iran war propaganda in segment
articles.summary:
Critics say segment on US rescue operation in Iran was made to boost public perception of Trump’s unpopular war

A US airman has spoken of climbing a 7,000ft ridge with a broken back, arm and…

blocks.text: A US airman has spoken of climbing a 7,000ft ridge with a broken back, arm and shoulder after he was shot down in Iran – and of being rescued by a team of American special forces as hostile locals closed in on him.

The air force colonel, identified only by his codename Bravo, appeared on camera Sunday night on CBS’s 60 Minutes in a segment some critics have labelled Pentagon propaganda to boost public perception of Donald Trump’s unpopular war.

Pete Hegseth, the president’s defense secretary; Dan Caine, chair of the joint chiefs of staff; and Brad Cooper, head of US Central Command; all appeared on the show to talk about the rescue operation. “Alpha”, the co-pilot of the downed F-15 fighter jet, declined to take part, despite reported pressure from the Trump administration to do so.

The airmen were recovered in April in an operation involving thousands of military personnel, including the elite Army Delta Force, Navy Seal Team Six, and a CIA decoy operation to distract and deceive Iranians chasing a bounty for their capture, the 60 Minutes segment said.

Bravo, who was reportedly also initially hesitant to take part, told interviewer Norah O’Donnell that his aircraft was struck by an Iranian shoulder-fired missile – and he realized his parachute was damaged after he and his co-pilot ejected.

“When I looked up and saw no parachute, that was the most terrifying thing I’ve ever seen,” the weapons system operator said. “So I paused, right then. And I prayed: ‘Lord, your will be done. But if I’m getting through this, I need help.’”
Bravo said he was unable to fully untangle his chute and hit the ground hard.
“Based on my description and the injuries that I had, the professionals think I hit the ground, going somewhere between 70 and 100 mph,” he said.
In addition to the broken bones, Bravo said he also sustained a sprained ankle in the hard landing, and serious wounds to his head and face.
“I had injuries, but we all train to adapt and overcome the things that we’re faced with,” he said. “I moved as quickly as I could, despite the injuries, away from the place that I landed.”
Bravo said he managed to hike and climb up the 7,000ft ridge with only a pistol, a communication device and a tracking beacon.

Declassified video broadcast by 60 Minutes showed a “risky” daytime raid by US forces to rescue Alpha, who landed about 5 miles away from his colleague. More than 20 helicopters took part in that operation – and the video showed two of them under fire.

“It was a gun fight all the way in and all the way out,” Hegseth told O’Donnell. “But they got Alpha back. And then we began to, immediately, I mean you’re celebrating that Alpha’s back, but you realize the job’s only half done.”
While Alpha was retrieved about six hours after they were shot down, Bravo’s ordeal lasted about 50 hours.

“As soon as I found a spot that I felt provided some concealment, I started working toward communication,” he said. “When I got to the moment where I could review and think about all that I’d gone through, I sent: ‘God is good,’ as a recognition of all that he had brought me through.”
Cooper said a plan to rescue him was accelerated as soon as it was clear he had survived.
“There was a: ‘I’m hurt, I’m moving,’ and there was a ‘God is good’ message that came in there,” he said. “Now we knew he was alive. He’s moving. OK, let’s keep planning.”

US bombers and drones hit Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces nearby, according to CBS, which showed separate video of those attacks. Two large search and rescue planes with special forces troops and small helicopters landed on a makeshift desert airstrip several miles from where Bravo was hiding.
His first glimpse of the US soldiers was, he said, “one of the greatest moments of my life” – and came with about 1,500 Iranian personnel inside a 10-mile radius, Cooper said.
The extraction did not conclude without incident. One rescue plane became lodged in the desert sand, was abandoned and then bombed to avoid it falling into enemy hands.
Cooper said more than 90 Americans were involved on the ground, supported by several hundred more in the air, and up to 5,000 people involved overall.
“What you need to know is we would have sent more to go get the back-seater,” he said.

CNN reported on Saturday that getting the airmen to appear on television was a priority for Hegseth, who was eager to present a success story in Trump’s ongoing war that has killed 18 US troops, wounded more than 800 and sent oil and gasoline prices soaring.

In a statement to CNN, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell called that story “a complete lie”. He said the decision about whether to participate in the 60 Minutes interview on Sunday “was each pilot’s alone, because it is their story”.

“As CNN notes, one pilot decided to participate and one did not,” Parnell’s statement said. “Additionally, the [Pentagon] took great care to ensure operational security, sources, and methods were protected. To suggest otherwise is to denigrate every member of our military who participated in and supported the interview.”

CNN further reported Bari Weiss, CBS News’s editor-in-chief, who has been criticized for perceived favoritism towards the Trump administration, put pressure on Hegseth for exclusive access to the story.

A backlash to the airing of the segment was reported on Monday by the Daily Beast. One analyst, Zeteo News media commentator Justin Baragona, posted on X that a CBS staffer told him: “Norah [was] absolutely willing to play the part of dimwit reporter used as a propaganda tool.”
