articles.title: Africa's richest man Dangote's IPO out of reach in Nigeria
articles.summary: Dangote seeks $1.6 billion from investors to finance a $14.3 billion expansion and thus double the oil refinery's capacity. The offer could give millions of Nigerians a stake in the company. But who…

image.caption: "Of the people, by the people, for the people" — or rather a market-driven strategy_Image: Sodiq Adelakun/REUTERS

blocks.text: The industrialist Aliko Dangote is turning to Nigerians to help finance the next growth phase of his oil refinery: The richest man in Africa announced that he is seeking to attract about $1.6 billion (€1.4 billion) by going public.

This initial public offering of Dangote Industries is intended to help support a $14.3 billion expansion, which would more than double the refinery's production capacity. In absolute numbers, it would increase capacity from 700,000 barrels per day (bpd) to 1.4 million bpd.

It would also include new petrochemical and refining units designed to reduce Nigeria's reliance on imports of some petrochemical products while also allowing the plant to produce different grades of diesel.
This plan would make the refinery one of the largest single-site refining complexes in the world.

Dangote's ambitious plans also include the launch of a processing plant in Kenya to extend his reach from the Atlantic to the Indian Ocean, which is planned to be launched in partnership with governments in eastern Africa.

blocks.caption: He might be the richest man in Africa, but it appears that Dangote is banking on public support to expand his operationsImage: Noushad Thekkayil/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: African success story

Since it began operations in 2024, the Dangote Petroleum Refinery has started to reshape Nigeria's fuel market and has become one of the few businesses in the world to benefit from the ongoing supply disruptions caused by the war in Iran.

The refinery has become an important supplier of petrol and other fuels domestically and abroad; in fact, it made Nigeria a net exporter of refined fuel for the first time after reaching its full capacity in early 2026.
The refinery reported making an after-tax profit of $1.82 ​billion in the first half ​of 2026, following ⁠a $476 million loss for all of 2025.
Things appear to be on the up-and-up for Dangote — so, why is the company seeking public investment now?
Why is Dangote going public?

Ayodele Oni, an energy analyst and partner with the Bloomfield Law Practice in Lagos, told DW that the public offering could be a "game changer," as it alters the role of who could stand to benefit from Dangote's expansion drive.

Oni said equity invested by potentially millions of Nigerian and international shareholders would shield the corporation from having to rely solely on expensive dollar debt "with permanent Naira capital, which matches a business now earning heavily in Naira."
This could also unlock additional long-term investment as any "listed company answers to ... its shareholders every quarter."
"That transparency is precisely what long-term lenders and international partners want to see before the next billion is committed," Oni said.
He said this would turn into a sustainable model for Dangote, as the approach would be designed to permanently "lower its cost of capital for every future phase."
Why Nigeria's largest refinery is importing US oil
For 'the people' of Nigeria

Oni summarized the potential of the deal by referring to it as a restructuring of both who bears the risk — and who stands to share with the reward, with "the people" being the greatest beneficiaries of the IPO, at least to his mind.
Opening up the ownership of the refinery business to ordinary Nigerians does not automatically mean that many can afford it, however.
The pricing of the initial offering is indeed priced at an affordable 525 Naira (€0.34/$0.39) a piece for each of the 4.1 billion ordinary shares, and a minimum of just 10 shares.

At the signing ceremony in Lagos, Dangote said the company was trying to "make sure that the majority of … our drivers, our cook, our servants, our managers, everybody will have an opportunity to have a stake in the refinery."
Nigeria cost-of-living protests turn violent
Nigeria: Deep inequality, deeper pockets

In a country where almost two-thirds of the population is struggling with extreme poverty, according to Nigeria's National Bureau of Statistics, that figure can translate into 10% of the minimum wage — for people who are fortunate enough to have a job.

Entry-level employees and workers who perform menial tasks at Dangote are fortunate enough to earn almost four times the minimum wage in Nigeria, according to media reports — though this still translates to only about $150 a month in a country that has been witnessing steep inflation, especially in petrol prices. For most, seeing any personal benefit by investing in Nigeria's oil remains a pipe dream.

Charles Asiegbu, a policy and economic analyst who has worked as a consultant for various Nigerian organizations, told DW that Dangote's description of the offer as "for the people" could still qualify as a "psychological masterstroke" for those who can afford to invest.
Asiegbu said broader ownership could bring a large number of Nigerians into one consolidated platform, changing how they view the refinery.
"With millions as shareholders, it would shift from a private enterprise to a national asset in the public consciousness," Asiegbu said.

blocks.caption: Dangote's current success is linked to the ongoing crisis in the Strait of Hormuz — but what happens when the Middle East returns to normal?Image: Majid Asgaripour/WANA/REUTERS

blocks.text: IPO excites investors
Nigerians who can afford to invest in Dangote appear to quickly be adopting that mindset.

Olamilekan Oladehinde, a Nigerian retail investor, told DW that he is "excited" to partake in the launch and buy shares. He said Dangote was now much more than just a private enterprise: It has become a key national asset that addresses direct social problems in Nigeria — including fuel shortages.

"They're trying to expand, and that's something I am very proud and happy to identify with," Oladehinde said. "The fact that it's also owned by a Nigerian makes me more than happy, and that's why I will be buying a stake in the company," he said about the richest man in Africa.
Risks and opportunities

Oladehinde said he had no concerns about investing in Dangote — despite the fact that various market experts have cautioned investors to be mindful of potential risks, especially because refining is a cyclical business.

Oni said Dangote was riding a wave during the current situation across the Middle East; however, fortunes could change — especially when the tensions around the Strait of Hormuz eventually ease. A return to steep competition in oil prices from those Middle Eastern countries could then saturate markets.
Africa's fuel crisis: Is Dangote the answer?

Dangote's strengths were a mitigating factor, Oni said: "The Middle East disruption showed that a refinery on [Nigeria's] Atlantic coast can supply Europe and the Americas faster than the Gulf can — and, at 700,000 bpd, the plant has already proven the model, so the expansion is about scale on an existing site, which is the cheapest capacity anyone can build."
Oladehinde said this was exactly the outlook that he will be betting on. "I believe the time has come for us," he said. "We can't lose this the momentum."

articles.title: Wild dogs record 2,500-mile trek across Africa in search of a mate
articles.summary: Scientists say the record-breaking journey by three brothers offers hope wildlife can survive growing pressures.

blocks.text: A pack of African wild dogs has completed a record-breaking 2,485-mile (4000km) journey across the continent.
Scientists say it is the furthest recorded distance for any African land mammal searching for a mate, offering hope that wildlife can travel across vast distances despite growing human pressures.
The three brothers zigzagged across Zambia, navigating a landscape increasingly shaped by people and avoiding obstacles including major cities.
However, other wild dogs tracked with GPS collars in the study died in illegal snares, underlining the dangers they face.
Three sisters almost completed an equally epic journey, but stopped when one became trapped in a snare.
African wild dogs are among Africa's rarest predators, with only about 6,000 remaining in the wild.
They live in highly social packs, hunt together and are known for their vast roaming in search of new territory and breeding opportunities with other packs.
They cannot breed within the pack they are born into, so they either wait and may eventually inherit their pack, or set off at the age of two or three in search of a mate.
The brothers covered about 260 miles in a straight line over the course of eight months, but travelled nearly 10 times that overall while crossing through a broken-up landscape.

These sorts of journeys are known as dispersals - travelling one way in search of a mate, which is a behaviour distinct from migrations, where animals move back and forth with the seasons in search of food or habitat.
The UN Convention on Migratory Species identifies Africa's longest migrations as wildebeest moving seasonally between Tanzania and Kenya in search of grazing and water covering more than 400 miles.
Globally, caribou undertake the longest single land migrations of any animal - travelling 839 miles in a round trip, while grey wolves have been recorded travelling more than 4,350 miles over a year.
Perhaps even more significant than the distance itself was the route the wild dogs took through Zambia.
They moved between wildlife strongholds, skirting areas containing major human obstacles, including the capital, Lusaka, and heavily developed industrial areas.
The findings suggest wild dog populations across eastern and southern Africa may remain more connected than conservationists previously believed.
Professor Scott Creel of Montana State University, the paper's lead author, who has been studying African wild dogs since 1991, said the study provides cautious optimism.
"It's plausible to believe that every major wild dog population in eastern and southern Africa, other than fenced ones, are potentially connected," he said.
But he said, in conservation,"the glass is half empty and the glass is half full", highlighting the threat of poaching snares.
While the three male wild dogs successfully completed their extraordinary journey, two of the three females died.
Researchers identified a pattern in which surviving pack members repeatedly returned to the same location, a behaviour that often signals the death of a companion.

The research, published in the journal, Ecology, external, adds weight to calls to create strips of natural land outside protected areas that connect separate wildlife areas broken apart by roads, towns, or farms.

Bruce Ellender, one of the paper's co-authors and Kafue Conservation director for the environmental charity, The Nature Conservancy, said species that roam over large areas, such as wild dogs and elephants, need connected landscapes if they are to survive into the future.
"We can't see these protected areas as islands and expect them to be functional in the long term, we need to think much broader than that," he said.

articles.title: The London hospital funded by donors who invested in the slave trade
articles.summary:
St Barts is one of many UK institutions whose benefactors were involved in the trafficking of enslaved Africans

Inside the Great Hall of St Bartholomew’s North Wing, alongside stately…
articles.byline: Written by Morgan Ofori and David Conn; Animation by Alexander Purcell; Photography by Wayne Crichlow

blocks.text: Inside the Great Hall of St Bartholomew’s North Wing, alongside stately portraits of the apostle from whom London’s oldest hospital takes its name and King Henry VIII, extravagant commemorative boards adorn the walls.

The Great Hall was a grand, formal space where governors weighed their philanthropic donations and drafted their wills, many while investing in the stock of companies built on the trafficking of enslaved Africans. Today, many of those donors are commemorated in acrylic gold paint on the boards.

The Register of British Slave Traders, a joint venture between Lancaster University, the University of Manchester and University College London, includes biographical data on every known investor in Britain’s transatlantic trafficking of enslaved African people from the 16th to 19th centuries.

It reveals how wealthy individuals, often enriched by the proceeds from racialised chattel enslavement, donated to hundreds of church parishes and helped to fund schools, hospitals and charities across the country.

Prof William Pettigrew, who led the project, said the register had established connections with roughly 900 organisations. “Most of those organisations sought to improve the lives of ordinary Britons,” he added.
The register reveals at least 50 people with deep financial ties to St Barts who are directly linked to this history.

Among the names etched on to the boards in the Great Hall is Sir Jeffrey Jeffreys, a London merchant who left an unspecified sum to the hospital in his will. In 1694, the Jeffreys-funded ship Hannibal, commanded by Capt Thomas Phillips, docked in Barbados. This concluded a harrowing journey in which only 372 of the 700 enslaved African people bought at Whydah (Ouidah in modern-day Benin) survived the Atlantic crossing.

blocks.caption: The grand Hogarth Stair, which leads to the Great Hall, adorned with paintings depicting healing. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian

Ornate boards adorn the walls of the Great Hall in St Barts, where governors recorded their philanthropic donations, many while investing in the companies built on the trafficking of enslaved Africans. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian
The church of St Bartholomew the Less, in the grounds of St Barts hospital.  Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian
A portrait of King Henry VIII in the Great Hall of St Bartholomew’s North Wing, surrounded by the boards commemorating the hospital’s benefactors. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian

blocks.text: Phillips’s journal, one of the few surviving records of the voyage, details the horrors onboard, where captives were subjected to branding and calculated psychological cruelty. “Then we marked the slaves we had bought in the breast or shoulder, with a hot iron, having the letter of the ship’s name on it,” he wrote. The Africans on his ship, he recorded, held “a more dreadful apprehension of Barbadoes than we have of hell”.

Phillips recalled using African overseers, who were enslaved themselves, to keep order, whipping any plotters of mutiny. There were grave consequences of the squalid conditions on the ship; many who died on the Hannibal were killed by smallpox, dysentery, starvation and suicide. Some were thrown overboard when dead or dying to prevent the spread of disease and to protect profits.
The voyage’s mortality rate was close to 50%, cementing its place as one of the deadliest crossings in the history of the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans.

blocks.caption: A diagram of a ship showing the cramped conditions in which enslaved Africans were trafficked. Composite: Guardian

blocks.text: The 1694 Hannibal crossing was one of 13 to which Jeffreys was financially linked. The London merchant was a director of the Royal African Company from 1684-86, and from 1692-98. His latter term coincided with the end of the company’s royal monopoly on trading enslaved Africans, from which he profited handsomely. He also inherited a fortune from his tobacco-trading uncle, John Jeffreys, in 1688. During Jeffrey Jeffreys’ time with the RAC, the organisation made 170 crossings.

Others commemorated at St Barts have links to the trafficking of enslaved Africans. Edward Colston, whose statue was toppled by Black Lives Matter protesters in Bristol in June 2020, appears in the register. William Prichard, once president of St Barts and a leading City merchant, bought £600 of RAC stock in January 1678.

Sir Robert Geffrye, who left money to the hospital and other philanthropic causes in his will, was a substantial investor in the trafficking of enslaved Africans, selling £1,600 (the equivalent of £350,000 today) of RAC stock on 5 January 1692 alone. Diane Abbott, the MP for Hackney North and Stoke Newington, has called for the removal of Geffrye’s statue at the Museum of the Home in Hoxton.

These connections run through the heart of the City of London’s political structure, with several lord mayors commemorated in the Great Hall. Sir William Humphreys, who left legacies to three London hospitals including St Barts, sat on the RAC’s court of assistants from 1683-85 and from 1688-90. In 1711, he attended Board of Trade hearings on the company’s operations on the west African coast, three years before he became lord mayor.
His predecessor, Samuel Stanier, who also left money to St Barts in his will, sold off most of his substantial £4,000 holding in the RAC in February 1698, before his lord mayoralty started in 1713.
After the British crown was restored in 1660, the trafficking of enslaved Africans became more formalised and was a lucrative source of funds for merchants.

blocks.caption: Several leading City merchants who invested in companies linked to the enslavement of African people are commemorated in the Great Hall at St Barts. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian
After the British crown was restored in 1660, the trafficking of enslaved Africans formalised to become a lucrative source of funds for merchants. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian

The Great Hall’s baroque ceiling carries its own coded message. Its botanical motifs – oak leaves for strength, laurel wreaths for triumph and palm branches for peace – are tied to themes of healthcare. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian
The stairwell leading to the Great Hall was restored last year and rehung with William Hogarth’s The Good Samaritan and The Pool of Bethesda. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian

blocks.text: The private banker Sir Robert Vyner (also known as Viner) became a central figure in the City and was lord mayor of London from 1674-75. He first invested in the Company of Royal Adventurers in January 1663; by August, his holding had grown to two shares, worth £800. In January 1665, he bought a further £1,200 from the Countess of Chesterfield, and was elected to the company’s board where he served from 1667-70.

He continued attending board meetings, without formally serving, from 1671 until the company’s dissolution. This positioned him to invest heavily in the RAC, the Adventurers’ successor, subscribing with £5,000 (the equivalent of £1.18m today) and serving as an assistant from 1672-74. During his involvement with both companies, they undertook 81 crossings. Vyner left a portion of the remainder of his estate to St Barts after his death in 1688.

Like St Thomas’ hospital in Lambeth, south London, St Barts provided free medical care to the city’s sick and poor people, sustained by charitable donations from City merchants and rental income from land and property across the capital.

Last year, the stairwell leading to the Great Hall was restored and rehung with William Hogarth’s The Good Samaritan and The Pool of Bethesda. The hall’s baroque ceiling carries its own coded message, its botanical motifs – oak leaves for strength, laurel wreaths for triumph and palm branches for peace – all tied to themes of healthcare.

St Barts has acknowledged its links to slavery: Barts health NHS trust archives produced an official research guide in 2024 setting out the known history and how to investigate it further, though the trust has not commissioned a stand-alone enslavement report.

A spokesperson for the trust said it was “well aware that some notable individuals historically associated with our hospitals profited from the transatlantic slave trade”, and they were identified in the Great Hall because of their donations.

“As further information comes to light we are discussing with Barts Charity and Barts Heritage, which manages the listed building, how we could most appropriately acknowledge the full story behind these historic links.”

A spokesperson for Barts Charity, which supports the trust, said that, previously, “detailed research has not established whether, or to what extent, particular gifts can be traced into the assets managed by the charity today. We are reviewing the new findings with Barts Health and Barts Heritage and considering any appropriate next steps.”

In 2023, the Scott Trust, the Guardian’s sole owner, published research showing the founder of the Manchester Guardian and his backers profited from the enslavement of African people in Jamaica and the US. In response, the Scott Trust launched the Cotton Capital series and the Legacies of Enslavement programme, a ten-year restorative justice initiative.

articles.title: Far-right AfD puts pressure on German aid to Ukraine
articles.summary: Emboldened by its win in Saxony-Anhalt, the far-right Alternative for Germany wants the government to change its Ukraine and Russia policies. Berlin is staying the course, but support is fading —…

image.caption: AfD leader Alice Weidel is calling on Merz to stop assistance to Ukraine in its fight against the Russian invasionImage: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS

blocks.text: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is standing firm on military aid for Ukraine in its war with Russia.
"We support Ukraine, and we will continue to support her, because she is also defending our freedom," Merz said on September 9 during a debate in the Bundestag, Germany's lower house of parliament.
He was reacting to Alternative for Germany (AfD) co-leader Alice Weidel, who had urged him to "finally start pushing for peace talks, like the US is doing."
US President Donald Trump has indicated that he would make far-reaching concessions to Russia at such negotiations; critics in Germany have described that as dictated peace.
On the topic of high energy prices in Germany, Weidel said, "We need cheap natural gas from Russia. That is what we will work toward."

She insinuated that the Ukrainian government was responsible for blowing up the Nord Stream gas pipelines between Russia and Germany in September 2022. "They continue to reward the suspected masterminds of the attack in Kyiv with billion-dollar payments at the expense of Germany." A Ukrainian sabotage team is suspected to be behind the attack.
Merz and Weidel clash in parliament after AfD election win

How pro-Russia the AfD is, despite its invasion of Ukraine, was shown clearly by its lawmaker Jürgen Koegel during the debate. He spoke of "valued President Vladimir Putin," who posed no threat of war to NATO.
East-west division in Germany over Ukraine aid

The AfD's position on the war in Ukraine is nothing new. However, since winning the state parliament election in Saxony-Anhalt on September 6 by a large margin, gaining almost 44% of the vote, it has expressed it even more vehemently.

Combining the votes for the AfD, the socialist Left Party and the populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), about 60% of voters in Saxony-Anhalt chose parties that either oppose support for Ukraine or are skeptical of it.

According to one survey, citizens' concerns about peace in Europe influenced their votes. Those surveyed named this topic as their second-most important, after "social security" and far ahead of "immigration" or "environment and climate."

In addition, there is the result of an ARD Deutschlandtrend survey conducted shortly before the election. It showed an east-west divide on the question of military support for Ukraine. About 39% of western Germans (from the area which was West Germany prior to reunification) thought military assistance went too far, while it was 54% for eastern Germans — that is, people who live in the area which used to be the communist German Democratic Republic (GDR/DDR).

"The course that the German federal government is taking on Ukraine does not have majority support in the east," Johannes Varwick, a political scientist at the Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg in Saxony-Anhalt, told DW.
"I would not describe that as 'pro-Russia'; it comes from the desire to focus more on diplomacy rather than delivering ever more weapons to fuel a war which Ukraine cannot win."
Fear in Germany of Russian threats
On September 2, the German government blamed Russia for a failed attack with an armed drone in early August at Leipzig airport, a key hub for military aid to Ukraine.

Putin spoke of a "grave error," Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov even called the accusation the "start of a real war." The exchange of verbal blows marked a new level of escalation in an already tense relationship.

According to the latest ARD Deutschlandtrend survey, most Germans (56%) see themselves currently either strongly or very strongly threatened by Russia. But it also showed that eastern Germans and AfD voters feel less threatened by Russia. The election results in Saxony-Anhalt also seem to reflect this.
Political scientist Sven Leunig from the Friedrich Schiller University Jena in the state of Thuringia has his own take on the reaction of eastern Germans, especially after the Leipzig incident.

"It is less a fundamental rejection of support for Ukraine, more a reaction based on fear," Leunig said. "They want to keep out of the conflict, so as not to be drawn further into it. That of course strengthens parties like the AfD, BSW and Left, who accommodate these sentiments."

Support for Ukraine is also coming under pressure for another reason. According to the AfD and BSW, the money Ukraine receives could be better spent on Germany's stretched social services. AfD lawmaker Gottfried Curio, for example, accused the German government of cutting social benefits and raising taxes "to keep on giving billions to foreign countries," to finance "foreign wars" such as in Ukraine.
Germany seeks extradition of Nord Stream 2 bombing suspect
Support for Ukraine is crumbling, but slowly

Chancellor Merz still believes he has political and public backing for his course. During the Bundestag debate, this was his response to the AfD's suggestion of resuming energy deliveries from Russia and ending German support for Ukraine: "This path that you depict is not supported by the majority in the German parliament and it is also not supported by the majority of the population of the Federal Republic of Germany. We will defend our freedom, also in the future."

But support for Ukraine, as shown in ARD Deutschlandtrend surveys over the years, is becoming less favored by the public. The share of people who think military support goes too far is growing, slowly but steadily, and is now 42%.

Leunig thinks the German government is not yet under pressure to reconsider its Ukraine policy: it still has "clear support" for the current course. "Plus, the threat coming from Russia is also becoming widely recognized. Of course, if public support weakens in the long-term, the government will have to react to that."
Is Ukraine 'another Afghanistan'?

His colleague Johannes Varwick, on the other hand, advises a course correction now, but not so much due to the mood in Germany: "Yes, we should stand with Ukraine, but standing by Ukraine does not mean fueling a futile war of attrition without a viable political strategy. That runs Ukraine into the ground, even if it is portrayed as 'pro-Ukraine'."
Critics have drawn parallels to Western intervention in Afghanistan, which after 20 years, billions of dollars spent and about 3500 western soldiers killed, ended with the Taliban retaking power.

But Leunig sees it differently. "I think both cases are not identical. In Afghanistan there was a direct military intervention by Western countries with ground and air forces. In Ukraine, the support is supplying weapons. But the public fear that the war will drag on for a long time, in this there is of course a parallel to Afghanistan, and that in the end Ukraine might still have to give up."

So far, however, there is no sign that the German government is rethinking its position. During a recent (September 10) visit from NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Berlin, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said, "Germany will stay the course during this time," despite the domestic debate.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: The Crusades: How a medieval Holy War still shapes politics
articles.summary: In 1095, the Catholic Church launched the Crusades, wars that left millions dead and whose legacy still shapes political and ideological conflicts.

image.caption: Crusaders sewed blood-red crosses onto their garments to symbolize their commitment to Holy War. They are depicted here in defeat after Saladin recaptured Jerusalem in 1187Image: akg-images/picture alliance

blocks.text: "The present moment is much like the 11th century ... We don't want to fight, but, like our fellow Christians a thousand years ago, we must." Those are the words of United States Secretary of War Pete Hegseth in his 2020 book "American Crusade: Our Fight to Stay Free."

Hegseth has repeatedly used the biblical language and symbolism of the Crusades to frame both domestic and foreign policy, from the current war in Iran to the "fight" against the "scourge of leftism."
Nearly 1,000 years have passed since the cold November day in 1095 when Pope Urban II delivered the fiery speech that would ignite centuries of warfare and change the course of history.
But Hegseth is only the latest in a long line of politicians and extremists to reference to the Crusades, from the Ku Klux Klan to US President George W. Bush and Osama bin Laden.
Why do the Crusades remain such a powerful source of inspiration for contemporary leaders?
Princes and peasants promised eternal salvation

The history of the Crusades is long and complex. But it can be summarized as an extraordinary example of how religion can become a powerful tool for political goals, helping leaders to unite people, justify wars and mobilize support on a massive scale.

In the mid-11th century, Muslim Seljuk Turks conquered vast swathes of territory in the Middle East. In the early 1070s, they took control of Jerusalem, the most important holy site in Christendom. Rumors spread that pilgrims and Christians living in the region were being persecuted, and holy sites desecrated.

blocks.caption: At the Council of Clermont in 1095, Pope Urban II used the words that would become the battle cry of the Crusaders: 'Deus vult!' ('God wills it!')Image: Fine Art Images/Heritage Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: The papacy in Rome at the time was locked in a bitter power struggle with Holy Roman Emperor Henry IV over who really held the reins of power in Western Christendom. When Byzantine Emperor Alexios I Komnenos appealed to Pope Urban II for help to defend against the Seljuks in 1095, it presented the papacy with an opportunity to demonstrate its power by bypassing Henry to rally Europe's nobility for nothing less than Holy War.
Urban believed that a major Christian cause would strengthen his authority by uniting Western Europe towards a common external enemy.
War was the status quo in medieval Europe, which had been hit by a series of droughts, famines and plagues. Belief in the "end times" was widespread.

In this context, Urban's call for a Holy War to "liberate the Church of God" was persuasive: He demonized Muslims and promised Crusaders complete forgiveness for all past sins, as well as eternal salvation.

"If you think about what a Crusade is, it's asking people to go into the unknown, thousands of miles into an unknown land," explains Jonathan Phillips, an expert on crusading history at Royal Holloway University in London. Their chances of dying were about 35 to 40%, notes the expert. So they had "to be driven by something. Religion has to come at the top," he adds.

blocks.caption: Crusaders murdered thousands of Jews, whom they believed to be 'enemies of Christ,' during the Rhineland Massacres in 1096Image: Fine Art Images/Heritage Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: Urban's call to Holy War was taken up by men and women from every level of society, from "princes to peasants," explains Phillips. A "tabby cat army," as he describes it, composed of peasants, low-ranking knights and nobles, and led by preachers, set out for the Holy Land in 1096.

This would later become known as the People's Crusade, which claimed its first victims in the Rhineland, where they massacred Jewish communities in one of medieval Europe's earliest outbreaks of antisemitism.
A better organized army of European upper nobility was eventually assembled in Constantinople between November 1096 and April 1097.
Unprecedented bloodshed
The Holy Land, located between what is today Turkey, Syria and Egypt, was a polyglot society divided among Sunni Seljuk Turkish warlords and the Shi'a Fatimid Caliphate.

blocks.caption: Godfrey of Bouillon, a Frankish knight, led the bloody siege of Jerusalem in 1099Image: Ken Welsh/UIG/IMAGO

blocks.text: It took some time for locals to understand that this wasn't just another raid, explains Mohamad El-Merheb, an expert on the premodern Islamic Eastern Mediterranean at SOAS University of London: "It takes maybe at least a decade for some people to see it as an ideological project to convert and take the Holy Land."
"Some of the cities are well defended, some are not. But it is all in the context of very fragmented political power," says El-Merheb.

The Crusaders had what El-Merheb describes as a series of swift conquests in important cities like Edessa and Antioch. Despite these early victories, life fighting a Holy War was grueling. The majority returned home, or died of disease, hunger or sheer exhaustion.
When they captured Jerusalem in 1099, Crusaders massacred thousands of Muslims and Jews because they couldn't tell them apart.

blocks.caption: The Crusades remain a fixture in the popular imagination through symbols, stories and films like 'The Crusades' (1935), a historical drama directed by Cecil B. DeMille Image: Everett Collection/IMAGO

blocks.text: Many historians consider the fall of the city of Acre to Mamluk warriors in 1291 to be the end of the Crusades in the Holy Land.

However, later crusades were also called, for example to block the advance of Ottoman Turks in Eastern Europe in 14th century, while "Reconquista" Christian military campaigns aimed to retake the Iberian Peninsula from Muslim rule into the late 15th century.
The Crusades meet the culture wars

The legacy of the Crusades remains a powerful and polarizing cultural touchstone. In both the East and the West, the historical memory of these medieval holy wars is frequently repurposed to frame modern identities, politics and conflicts.

In 2001, US President George W. Bush caused uproar when he described the so-called "War on Terror" as a "crusade," a term already used by Osama bin Laden to frame US-led wars as religious wars intended to destroy Islam.

blocks.caption: Saladin, depicted here receiving the English Bishop of Salisbury in 1192, successfully united fractured Muslim territories from Egypt to Mesopotamia Image: GRANGER Historical Picture Archive/IMAGO

blocks.text: In his propaganda to legitimize his global jihad, bin Laden also invoked the legacy of Saladin, a legendary Kurdish commander revered to this day as the hero who recaptured Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187.

"As of the 19th century, Saladin specifically becomes a symbol of fighting Western colonialism and imperialism," says El-Merheb. "Throughout the 20th century, a lot of Islamist groups also start referring to the Western powers as Crusaders, so this becomes part of political nationalism on the state level and also on a more popular level in films, for example. This is happening in the West now in the opposite way."

Crusader symbolism has long been used by far-right movements in the US and Europe to promote narratives of civilizational conflict. The Latin phrase "deus vult," or "God wills it," has been used by figures including far-right mass murderer Anders Breivik and Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, while France's far-right party Reconquête draws its name from the Reconquista campaigns. US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth famously has "deus vult" tattooed on his arm and a Crusader cross on his chest.

blocks.caption: In his book 'American Crusade,' US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth described the Crusades as a 'defensive' and 'existential' war launched to defend the Europe against Islamic expansion Image: Sra Madelyn Keech/DoD/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: But El-Merheb believes that such references often reduce the Crusades to a simple clash between Christianity and Islam, "which really was never simply the case."

This framing, he explains, ignores "how the Crusades were from the start very antisemitic projects, or violent projects against other Christian communities in Europe such as the Cathars in France, against Byzantium and the Islamic world and ignores the many cross-religious alliances between Muslims and Crusaders."
Along the way, he adds, these politicians are also forgetting how violent and destructive these historical campaigns were.

articles.title: Africa’s richest man aiming to make $23bn from continent’s biggest-ever IPO
articles.summary:
Public offering of Aliko Dangote’s Nigerian oil refinery business could swell his net wealth by two thirds

The fortune of Africa’s richest person could swell by two thirds to nearly $60bn…
articles.byline: Eromo Egbejule in Abidjan and agencies

blocks.text: The fortune of Africa’s richest person could swell by two thirds to nearly $60bn (£44bn) after his refinery in Nigeria listed publicly in the continent’s biggest-ever initial public offering.
If Monday’s flotation of Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals on the Nigerian exchange goes to plan, then Aliko Dangote will add a further $23bn (£17bn) to his $35bn net worth.

Dangote, who has framed the offering as “an IPO for the people”, hopes it will draw in a broad mix of institutional and retail investors with a minimum subscription of just 10 shares at a cost of 5,250 naira (£2.94). The share purchases have a month to complete, with the process finishing on 13 October.

The IPO has been marketed to young Nigerians in particular, through banking platforms and fintech ventures, as a way of building wealth and growing the economy. If completely subscribed, the refinery’s value is expected to rise to about 65.22tn naira (£36.5bn).
That would be a big win for Dangote, who has financed several successful presidential campaigns in Nigeria, where policymakers have granted him a near monopoly in his chosen sectors.

Responding last year to criticism of his political influence, he said: “We have chosen to build here, to employ here, to produce here. Let us not use the cry of monopoly to stall growth. No one is prevented from investing.”

Dangote, 69, made his fortune in cement and sugar. He started his company in the late 1970s with a loan from his maternal grandfather, who was a member of one of west Africa’s all-time richest families, the Dantatas.

His recent move into the petroleum sector led to Nigeria becoming a net exporter of refined fuel for the first time. Prior to the opening of the $20bn Dangote refinery on the outskirts of Lagos in January 2024, the country had relied on exporting crude and importing refined petroleum for domestic use, while expending billions to subsidise fuel costs and inject life into its colonial-era refineries.

The Dangote refinery now has a capacity of 700,000 barrels a day and is expected to double that by the end of the decade. This year, it has benefited from disruptions in supply across the globe as a result of the war in Iran. The Brent crude benchmark touched $108 a barrel on Monday, after attacks on Saudi Arabia’s east-west pipeline.
after newsletter promotion

Dangote has said he will use profits from his Lagos oil refinery to spur continental growth and curb Africa’s reliance on foreign goods. His ambitious plan is to build a $100bn industrial empire centred on heavy manufacturing and regional infrastructure. Key to this is a planned $17bn energy complex in the Kenyan island town of Lamu with an oil-refining capacity of 700,000 barrels a day, to boost the region’s energy security.

“We, as Nigerians and Africans, must be bold and lead the change to develop our economies,” Dangote said at an IPO signing ceremony in Lagos on 7 September. “Only then will the others take us very seriously, only then we’ll be in a position to negotiate and walk away with terms we deserve, not those terms that are given to us.”
After the ceremony, Dangote’s fellow Nigerian billionaire, the banker Tony Elumelu, called the IPO “a landmark moment for Nigeria and a huge milestone for Africa”.

articles.title: EU leaders urge unity after Russian strike on train
articles.summary: Russia's drone attack on a train near the Ukraine-Poland border has triggered EU calls to up support for Kyiv. Allies of Ukraine should show they "are not scared," said the bloc's top diplomat, Kaja…

image.caption: Top EU diplomat Kaja Kallas was among those to call for unity after Russia's attackImage: Britta Pedersen/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Several top EU politicians have called a Russian drone strike on a passenger train ​on Ukraine's border with Poland a bid by Moscow to intimidate Kyiv's allies that should be met with even more resolution.

In the incident, a drone hit the train's locomotive at a railway station in the Volyn region, some 2 kilometers (1.24 miles) from the border, shortly after a diplomatic ‌train carrying former British ​Prime ⁠Minister Boris Johnson and other ⁠European ​diplomats had been at the station.

blocks.caption: Russia carried out two drone strikes at the Ukraine-Poland border on SundayImage: Sylwester Uchanski/REUTERS

blocks.text: What did EU leaders say about the train attack?
"It [the attack] is clearly meant to scare Western countries from supporting Ukraine, from going to Ukraine to show support," the EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said.
"I ​think we should act the opposite. ​We should show that we are ⁠there ​for Ukraine ​and we are ​not scared," ‌she told reporters in ​Finland, ⁠where she attended ⁠a ​summit on Arctic strategy.

Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo, who was also at the meeting, said the attack demonstrated Russia's growing aggression and called both for more support for Kyiv and for harsher penalties on Moscow.

"For me, it means that we have to [...] do even more to help Ukraine, to support Ukraine. And we need more measures against Russia, more political measures, more sanctions, and make it clear that this is strong strategy," he said.
"We are united here in Europe," he added.
Amid Russia's war Ukraine, Poland reconcile painful past
Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda said the attack showed that Russia was "challenging all of us."

"We should not talk about concrete geographic regions, because Russia's goal is much more ambitious: to test the rule of law, to test our style of life, to test democracy. And I think they will put additional efforts to do it," he said.
French Foreign Affairs Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said the attack had a "very clear goal, which is to intimidate Europeans, discourage them and, above all, drive a wedge between them."
Barrot said Russian President Vladimir Putin had constantly stepped up pressure on the EU and NATO over the past five years.
"Why? Because he knows that our strength lies in our unity, and that as long as we stand together, nothing can intimidate us," he said.
Germany warns against escalation with Russia
German Foreign Minister Boris Pistorius, for his part, called for caution.
"I take the drones that were approaching trains near the (Ukrainian-Polish) border very seriously, but we must not be forced into an escalation," he said.
The Kremlin has commented on the attack only by saying that the Russian army operated across all Ukrainian territory and would continue to do so.
Speaking about the incident on Sunday, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga has said Putin considered Russia to be "de facto" at war with Europe.
"Putin's terror is literally knocking at the door of the European Union and NATO," Sybiga said.

articles.title: China criticises idea it is in 'malicious competition' over AI
articles.summary: It follows the Anthropic CEO 's calls for a slowdown in AI development, in a way that China doesn't pull ahead.

blocks.text: China has hit out against what it has called "threat narratives" over AI governance and warned against "engaging in confrontation and malicious competition".
It follows Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's calls for a slowdown in AI development - but in a way that prevents China from pulling ahead in the AI race.
Over the past week, industry insiders at the leading US AI labs have been warning in extremely stark terms about the potential threat AI poses, with some saying it could wipe out humanity.
But US President Donald Trump has said his priority is making sure the US develops the tech faster than China.

China's foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters on Monday "narratives of threat, confrontation, and malicious competition serve only to disrupt the process of global AI governance and are not in anyone's interest".
"All parties should work together to advance AI in a manner that is open, inclusive, beneficial to all, and oriented toward the good," he added.
His comments highlight the difficulties in getting agreement between the world's two leading AI powers.

An agreement between the US and China to regulate AI development is "next to impossible", says Chang Jun Yan, an assistant professor with the military studies programme at Singapore's S Rajaratnam School of International Studies.
"As part of each state's core national security interests, cooperation in taking things slower and more safely in relation to AI, is very, very unlikely."

AI now sits at the heart of the US-China rivalry as the world's two largest economies seek to gain an edge in advanced tech. Despite US export bans on critical chips, Chinese AI innovation has been expanding, driven by open-source technology and Beijing's backing.
Many experts believe the US is still ahead, and Chinese firms are trying to catch up as they struggle to raise the hundreds of billions of dollars that investors are ploughing into American AI.

But Beijing, including Chinese leader Xi Jinping himself, has also spoken about the risks posed by AI. China must "balance development and security", and introduce and improve relevant laws and ethical guidelines, and strengthen prevention of risks, to "safeguard the interests of the people and national security", state security minister Chen Yixin wrote on Sunday.
He warned of the dangers of "hostile forces" such as foreign intelligence using AI and called for international cooperation.
"There are strong signals that Washington and Beijing share an understanding of frontier risks," Kenton Thibaut, a senior resident China fellow at the Atlantic Council, wrote recently.
China has "technical reasons" to work with the US, she argues, because its developers would be able to see how their models are deployed outside China, and detect and undertsand vulnerabilities.

In July, China set up the World AI Cooperation Organisation, which aims to shape global AI governance. And speaking at the Brics summit in India on Sunday, Xi proposed creating a community for open-source AI.

All this comes as calls for AI regulation grow louder in the US, especially after a former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxson said last week that "there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future" if the current pace of development continued.
Since then top industry bosses, such as Amodei, have called for a slowdown and more regulation.

"We need ways to ensure that alignment and safety techniques stay ahead of progress in model capabilities," Open AI's chief exective Sam Altman wrote on X on Monday, which was echoed by Microsoft boss Satya Nadella who said AI development "cannot be controlled by a handful of entities".
But US President Donald Trump downplayed the risks, saying that he wanted to keep the US's lead over China "because whoever wins AI, wins".

The competition is fierce. The former Anthropic employee Coxson told the BBC that there needed to be "some sort of coordinated slowdown with China, if we're going to avoid a race at an international scale".
As Trump prepares to host Xi at the White House next week, the two sides are trying to include AI on the agenda, South China Morning Post reports.

It is also likely to be part of the talks between US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng, who are trying to meet before next week's summit, the paper said. Vice-Premier He runs the agency that oversees the country's economic planning, including AI development.
While collaboration between the US and China is important, experts say the nstakes are high for both countries.

"If China establishes a durable lead in frontier AI, this will not be viewed in Washington as losing a technology race," says Chasen Nevett, managing director at Hong Kong-based firm, Forani Investments.
"It will be viewed as losing part of the strategic infrastructure of the next industrial era."
Additional reporting by Osmond Chia

blocks.text: Key events

items: 18m agoTrump's mail-in voting restrictions blocked by a second judge

blocks.text: Trump's mail-in voting restrictions blocked by a second judge
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
A second ⁠federal ⁠judge has prevented ⁠Donald Trump’s administration from implementing ⁠a ​new ‌US ‌Postal Service ‌rule that would tighten mail-in voting requirements.

However, ‌the US Supreme Court is ​still weighing the administration’s ⁠request to ​overturn a separate ​order ​blocking the ​rule. Late on Sunday, District Judge Carl J Nichols in Washington, DC, handed down a similar hold on the rule, which was issued 21 August.

“Plaintiffs have demonstrated that, absent an injunction, there is an increased risk that a significant number of otherwise appropriate absentee or mail-in ballots will ultimately not be counted in the upcoming elections,” Nichols wrote in issuing the preliminary injunction.
“The public has a strong interest in ensuring that doesn’t happen.”

Nichols in May had refused to issue an injunction because he ruled the lawsuit seeking one was brought too early. That was the high court’s reasoning late last month when it lifted an earlier freeze by Talwani.

But because the administration had just issued its rule to move ahead with Trump’s plan, the plaintiffs in Boston and Washington, DC, refiled their lawsuits. Talwani was nominated by former president Barack Obama and Nichols was nominated by Trump.

The new Postal Service regulations stem from an executive order Trump issued earlier this year. Election officials say it would be impossible to implement the changes this close to a general election.
In other developments:

items: Trump on Sunday called on Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries and other infrastructure used to produce and distribute diesel, saying the attacks are causing a global shortage. He spoke after diesel prices in the US hit a record on Friday, soaring past $6 a gallon on average.

British ministers face calls to act after US authorities secretly flew out of the UK a diplomat accused of possessing indecent images of children. US officials reportedly raided the diplomat’s London flat in August before taking him to an American airbase and flying him out of the country, without warning the Metropolitan police.

A newly unveiled statue of the rightwing activist Charlie Kirk was vandalized at the Turning Point USA headquarters in Phoenix, Arizona. The statue was found with red spray-paint. A nearby poster memorial in front of the statue was vandalized with red paint as well.

A coroner in Pennsylvania announced the death of a 40-year-old woman associated with the state’s ongoing measles outbreak. The death appears to mark the third in the US state’s ongoing outbreak. Two previous deaths in the state were in infant children. In one case, the infant was born with a genetic defect that made her vulnerable to infection. The second infant child was infected with measles, and died of a ruptured spleen.

A Republican congressman said he had to swim to safety after a plane he was traveling in made an emergency landing in a lake late Saturday. Representative Tom Tiffany says he was returning from the La Crosse county Lincoln Day Dinner when the light aircraft lost power as it approached Wausau downtown airport. The pilot made an emergency landing in Lake Wausau. They both ended up in the water and swam to safety.

Barack Obama urged Democrats to prioritize a “public conversation” about AI management and safety in a closed-door Manhattan fundraiser last week. The comments by the former US president reportedly urged the party to create a sweeping framework for everything from a safety “slow-down” to domestic job losses and children’s wellbeing.
