articles.title: As climate change warms the Himalayas, disasters like the Nepal floods are becoming more frequent
articles.summary: KATHMANDU, Nepal (AP) — When a wall of water, rocks and mud tore through her remote village in Nepal, Pema Tamang and her neighbors fled uphill to a Buddhist shrine that had been rebuilt the previous…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU, Nepal (AP) — When a wall of water, rocks and mud tore through her remote village in Nepal, Pema Tamang and her neighbors fled uphill to a Buddhist shrine that had been rebuilt the previous year after a 2015 earthquake.
FILE -In this June 20, 2013, photo, the Kedarnath shrine, one of the holiest Hindu temples, and other buildings around it are seen damaged following monsoon rains in northern India. (AP Photo, File)

The steep mountain folds of the Himalayas, already prone to earthquakes, have seen more frequent flash floods as high mountain glaciers melt, redrawing rivers at sometimes terrifying speed. Residents have had little time to rebuild from one disaster to the next, raising concerns over whether their communities can endure as climate change accelerates.

“We were able to rebuild the stupa only last year after it was destroyed during the earthquake,” Tamang told The Associated Press, referring to the shrine. “Sheltering in it was how we saved our lives from the floods,” she said in a makeshift shelter at a monastery in Kathmandu.

The Aug. 26 floods in Nepal and neighboring China have killed more than 1,000 people and left thousands missing, including hundreds feared trapped in tunnels at hydropower projects. The floods were triggered after a collapse of bedrock and glacier ice sent debris and water surging through multiple Himalayan rivers.

Scientists say it is too early to directly link Wednesday’s catastrophe to global warming. But as Earth’s temperature rises at a faster rate because of the burning of oil, gas and coal, the chances of such disasters increase, especially in the Himalayan mountains, which are warming considerably faster than many other parts of the world.

“Climate change has been playing a large role in the Hindu Kush Himalayas, causing these kinds of complex disasters which have really impacted downstream communities and investments,” said Saswata Sanyal, a disaster risk resilience expert at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development based in Kathmandu.
Global warming’s effects are heightened in the Himalayas
Sanyal said the region is increasingly confronting hazards that trigger one another.

Warmer temperatures cause high mountain ice to melt, leading to more frequent rockslides, avalanches and floods. An avalanche can dam a river before unleashing a flash flood. Heavy rain after an initial disaster can compound the destruction.

Flash floods last year in the same region in Nepal claimed nine lives and caused millions of dollars in damage. Across the wider Himalayan region, the 2013 Kedarnath floods, the 2021 Chamoli disaster, the 2023 South Lhonak glacial lake outburst flood, and other recent landslides and floods, have killed thousands of people and caused hundreds of billions of dollars in damage.

blocks.caption: A drone view shows rescue workers inspect the area and damaged structures following recent flash flooding along the Trishuli River in the Devighat area of Nuwakot district, Nepal, Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. (AP Photo/Rajesh Kumar Singh)

blocks.text: A drone view shows rescue workers inspect the area and damaged structures following recent flash flooding along the Trishuli River in the Devighat area of Nuwakot district, Nepal, Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. (AP Photo/Rajesh Kumar Singh)
People in Nepal were still recovering from last year's floods, Sanyal said, “and before they could fully adapt, the next one came.”

The Hindu Kush Himalaya stretches across parts of Afghanistan, Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Myanmar and China, and contains the largest concentration of ice outside the polar regions. River systems originating in the mountains support nearly 2 billion people.

Glacier ice loss has accelerated sharply since 2000, according to Sanyal's intergovernmental climate research group. Another risk is thawing permafrost — ground that has remained frozen for long periods — that can weaken mountain slopes.

Satellite imagery of the glacial collapse last week indicates that a huge mass of bedrock and glacial ice plunged into a valley below, sending a wall of water and mud several stories high through communities many kilometers (miles) downstream.
Adaptation has limits in the mountains

Climate experts say that in some places the danger may become so great that rebuilding is no longer viable, forcing residents to move. Climate change could also have implications for efforts to develop the region through the construction of roads, bridges and hydropower plants.
“The adaptation threshold has been crossed in some areas,” said Manjeet Dhakal, a Nepali climate policy expert and United Nations climate negotiator.

blocks.caption: FILE -A man tries to recover a vehicle submerged in mud in a flood-affected area along the Teesta river in northeastern India, Oct. 8. 2023. (AP Photo/Anupam Nath, File)

blocks.text: FILE -A man tries to recover a vehicle submerged in mud in a flood-affected area along the Teesta river in northeastern India, Oct. 8. 2023. (AP Photo/Anupam Nath, File)

When an earthquake destroys a house, belongings can sometimes be recovered, he said. A catastrophic flood can wipe out not only the house, but the land beneath it, along with roads, water systems, schools and electricity. He said future resettlement would have to incorporate climate risk from the beginning.
The consequences can be mitigated by stricter land-use rules, better assessments before infrastructure is approved, stronger cross-border monitoring and early warning systems.

Still, Sanyal said that of the 670,000 people who received text alerts about the Aug. 26 floods, some were visitors or migrant workers who could not understand Nepali while others downplayed the risk. Other systems designed to measure rivers were overwhelmed or washed away.
Chanda Lal Chitrakar, a 62-year-old resident of Nuwakot in Nepal, told the AP that he paid little attention to warning messages. As the waters rose, he ran uphill to save himself.
Nepal suffers from the much larger emissions of wealthier countries

Sanyal said such warnings need to provide more information on what actions to take. He also suggested prioritizing development in less-dangerous areas, assessing infrastructure for multiple hazards and incorporating the knowledge of Indigenous communities into disaster planning.
Dhakal, the climate negotiator, noted that Nepal has emitted less than 0.1% of the greenhouse gases that cause global warming, even as it grapples with some of its most severe effects.

“We should blame those who are responsible for increasing the global temperature, those who have benefited from the fossil fuel economy for such a long time,” he said. “We can at least use this devastating example as an inspiration to urgently reduce carbon emissions.”

articles.title: Trump claims AI poses no real risk — but even some of his allies disagree

image.caption: Pages from the website of artificial intelligence company Anthropic are displayed on a computer screen. U.S. President Donald Trump is dismissing dire predictions about AI's potential risks as a hoax and rejecting calls to regulate the industry. (Patrick Sison/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·Analysis
Fresh warnings that artificial intelligence models could go rogue and wipe out the human race appear to have jolted some U.S. politicians into action, but not President Donald Trump.
Public and bipartisan pressure are mounting amid dire warnings from experts

In a flurry of posts to his Truth Social platform on Monday, Trump dismissed AI regulation as something that would drive the industry "into oblivion and bankruptcy" and claimed that the economic engine of AI "will not be stopped" while he is president.
"AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX," Trump declared in one post.
"The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" he said in another.
Trump's posts come in response to dire predictions about the technology's potential risks and mounting calls from executives and researchers to rein in the industry.

Last week, engineer Jacob Coxon thrust AI safety into the public spotlight by announcing his resignation from his job with Anthropic in a social media post that warned: "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade."
Anthropic CEO calls for AI development to slow down
While Trump is the most powerful voice in Washington opposing calls to rein in AI, he is far from the only one.

More than 260 bills have been introduced in Congress containing provisions to address the risks from AI since 2021, yet only two have become law, according to the Brennan Center's AI legislation tracker.
However, experts in AI policy see some encouraging signs in the past few days that the political momentum could now be shifting in favour of regulation.
'Full speed, no brakes'

Chris MacKenzie, vice-president of communications at Americans for Responsible Innovation, a non-profit advocacy group in Washington focused on AI safety, says one of the biggest obstacles to regulation has long been the amount of money stacked against it.
"We have a lot of money on the other side of this issue, a lot of money and lobbyists who do not want to see AI regulations," MacKenzie told CBC News.
"They want innovation at full speed, no brakes."
But as the public outcry grows for Congress to take action and the issue becomes a campaign talking point in the U.S. midterm elections, MacKenzie says he's confident there will be some movement.

"At the moment, what we see is a real window of opportunity where lawmakers and the public are mobilized around these issues and there's a clear desire to pass guardrails that will protect people from AI's risks," he said.

One event that helped fuel that desire came in late July, when OpenAI revealed that hundreds of its AI agents had gone rogue by independently breaking out of their secure testing environment and hacking into the servers of Hugging Face, an online platform of AI development tools.
Warnings about the risks have accelerated in the past week, kicked off by Coxon's post stating that AI "could kill us all." They include:

items: Thursday: Anthropic, which makes the chatbot Claude, said it had banned some accounts linked to foreign governments and military actors for using its AI models to try to develop weapons.
Thursday: Former U.S. president Barack Obama told top Democrats to make AI safety policy a priority. "If we don’t get on top of it, I think can be dangerous," he said.

Saturday: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a 3,800-word essay urging a slower pace of AI development to manage the risks. His rivals Elon Musk, chief executive of X, and Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, supported his call.
Monday: Microsoft published its code of conduct to ensure human control of AI.

blocks.text: While plenty of Democrats lined up on the weekend to call for stricter AI regulation, even a few prominent Republicans expressed openness to tighten oversight. They included Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and the party's candidate for the Senate in Michigan, Mike Rogers, a former chairman of Intel.
"I believe we must slow down development of AI in order to allow the government and its partners to catch up and put stricter protocols and guardrails in place," Rogers posted on X.
Superintelligence is 'an adversary,' says AI researcher

With major AI companies and an increasing number of Republicans agreeing that something needs to be done, Trump will likely need to compromise, says Nita Farahany, a Duke University professor who studies the legal and social implications of emerging technologies.
"I think it's going to be hard for the president to stay in the camp of 'No, let's go full speed ahead,'" Farahany told CBC News.
"I think you're going to see a shift, probably within the next 72 hours, out of the White House about what their tune is going to be on these issues."

items: Trump decries critics of AI, saying they're 'negative forces' with exaggerated concerns
Could AI really 'kill all humans'? Breaking down the dire warnings about the technology's existential risk

blocks.text: Trump has long resisted AI regulation. Last December, he signed an order aimed at forcing states to drop their efforts at regulating the technology.

The top Republican in the U.S. House of Representatives, Speaker Mike Johnson, says Trump may meet with AI company executives at some point in the next two weeks, but he's making no promises about the outcome.

The meeting would be "a deliberate discussion about the responsibility of the companies to maintain safety, and what role, if any, the government has to play," Johnson told reporters on Capitol Hill on Monday.

One sign that regulating AI appeals across a wide range of the political spectrum is the eclectic list of people slated to attend the launch of the Pro-Human Assembly, a new coalition that says its mission is "charting a better path for AI."
Among the speakers at the event Tuesday in Washington: Steve Bannon, Trump's one-time chief of staff and a prominent MAGA voice, along with Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, a darling of the left.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Mike Crawley is a correspondent for CBC News, based in Washington. He began his career as a newspaper reporter in B.C., spent six years as a freelance journalist in various parts of Africa, then joined the CBC in 2005. Mike reported on Ontario politics for 15 years. He was born and raised in Saint John, N.B.

articles.title: What we know about Carney's push for a 'unique alliance' with the EU

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney takes part in a news conference during a Canada-EU Summit in Brussels on June 23, 2025. Carney has said Ottawa is looking for forge a 'unique alliance' with the European Union. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Prime Minister Mark Carney has said Canada plans to begin discussions on a "unique alliance" with the 27-nation European Union that will be based on shared values but be short of a full membership. Conservative MPs have replied that Canadians should be concerned about becoming the "28th EU state." Here's what we know so far.
Details sparse as PM set to address the European Parliament on Thursday
Prime Minister Mark Carney said Sunday that Canada plans to begin discussions on a "unique alliance" with the European Union.
Carney was responding to a Wall Street Journal article that said Canada was seeking to become an "associate member" of the 27-nation bloc.
That report included this quote from Finnish President Alexander Stubb: "Wouldn’t it be lovely if Canada was the 28th state of the European Union rather than the 51st state of the United States?"
In response to the article, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre and other MPs in his party said on X on Sunday that Canadians should be concerned about becoming the "28th EU state."
Here is what we know about the Canada-EU partnership as Carney prepares to deliver a speech to the European Parliament on Thursday morning.
Is Canada planning to join the EU?
No, Carney says. The prime minister reiterated at the Toronto International Film Festival on Sunday that that is not the plan.
"We're not looking to become a member of the European Union," Carney said, adding that officials are instead looking to begin discussions on a "unique alliance."
"We share the same values, we have the same priorities, and we have very complementary strengths," he said.
Canada looking into 'unique alliance' with EU, not membership: Carney
Has the idea of full EU membership been floated?
Not officially, but the idea has made the rounds among media and some people in power as Canada seeks to become less dependent on its relationship with the U.S.
One public instance was a comment by French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, who said in March that "maybe Canada at some point" could sign up for the political and economic union.
Barrot's comments at a European conference in Berlin generated laughs and applause at the time, though Carney has consistently said, as early as June 2025, that membership is not on the table.
He said then that he wants to "co-operate much more clearly and broadly to our mutual benefit."
"Not as a member, but along that continuum."
What is an 'associate' member?

Saturday's Wall Street Journal article said Carney is pushing his team to take Ottawa's relationship with the EU "to the next level" — including having Canada take on a new title: "Associate Member of the European Union."
"Associate member" is not a legal designation.

A senior Canadian official, who offered information to CBC News on a not-for-attribution basis, said the "associate member" label is one of a few that have been considered and that Canada did not propose it.

items: Canada and Europe should get ‘creative’ in forging closer ties, EU ambassador says
Finland's president on why he believes Canada could — eventually — be part of the EU

blocks.text: The official added that the government is still examining what the relationship could look like, and hopes to more clearly sketch it out at the EU-Canada summit at the end of October.

The official said they did a deep analysis of the EU's relationships with non-members Norway, Switzerland, the U.K. and Georgia and said none of those would work because the Canadian government does not want to give up independence in return for access.
What do we know about deepening ties between the EU and Canada?
Carney and the EU's ambassador to Canada, Geneviève Tuts, have both used the same word: "unique."
But there have been few on-the-record details beyond a willingness on both sides to work something out.

Carney said on Aug. 22 that the two sides would talk this fall about building a "much stronger and deeper" security and economic partnership. This is on top of their only partially applied free-trade deal (CETA) and the non-trade Strategic Partnership Agreement, as well as the Security and Defence Partnership they signed in June 2025.
Tuts said what that looks like is still being worked out.
Canada will 'not become a member of the EU,' Stéphane Dion says
The Wall Street Journal report says Canada and the EU are "eyeing ways" for Canada to move closer on energy, AI, critical minerals and defence.
The Canadian official said they're aiming for more options on where Canadians study, travel, do business and retire.
What are the possibilities?

Tuts said she expects only discussions about any new partnership at this point, possibly with more detail from speeches by Carney on Thursday and by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday.
Achim Hurrelmann, co-director of the Centre for European Studies at Carleton University, says it seems the new agreement is being put together in a hurry.
He said the plan might include things like collaboration on a European stockpile of critical minerals, university student exchanges through the Erasmus program and a digital trade agreement.

items: No longer taboo, Canada's defence industry steps into Europe's spotlight
European Parliament to open Ottawa office as Carney seeks 'unique alliance' with EU

blocks.text: Hurrelmann said this all might amount to a series of agreements instead of a major pact, or a grab bag of ideas assembled under the label of "co-operating on strategic capabilities."

"There are lots of initiatives, but they don’t at this point really amount, from what I can see, to this systematically new step in the relationship," he said. "I’m not really sure if the substance will actually justify the new label."
With files from The Canadian Press and CBC's Ashley Burke

articles.title: Zelenskyy's comparison of Canada to Ukraine is imperfect — but it matters

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy walk together in Banff, Alta., last week. The Ukrainian leader urged Canada and the United States to keep talking, offering a stark warning of how bad things can get between neighbouring countries. (Todd Korol/Pool/Reuters)

blocks.text: There was something extraordinarily refreshing about listening to Volodymyr Zelenskyy say the quiet part out loud.

Asked to comment on the deteriorating relationship between Canada and the United States, the Ukrainian president described it as "strange" and "very dangerous" before drawing — arguably — an imperfect comparison with his country and Russia.

"It's very dangerous that there are some problems between neighbours. We are the example," Zelenskyy told CBC's chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault in an exclusive interview at the end of his visit to Canada last week.
It's well known Zelenskyy has little patience for diplomatic euphemism and he has made something of a habit of dragging the unspoken into the open.
U.S. threats to annex Canada 'dangerous,' Zelenskyy says
But is it a fair and accurate comparison?

Talk to most Canadians and many are inclined to agree with the analogy at least on the surface, especially with the collapse of trade talks where Washington introduced last-minute demands — including a veto over Canada's third-party trade deals and a weakening of domestic cultural protections.
There is an important distinction, of course.
Russia invaded Ukraine.
The United States has not threatened Canada militarily and no American divisions are assembling at the border. There is no Canadian territory that's been annexed.

The Ukrainian president was quick to urge Ottawa and Washington to keep the dialogue going to work out their differences, but three times referred to the ongoing trade war and the associated rhetoric as "dangerous."
You won't find a Canadian political leader or senior official making the same comparison, at least in public.

items: Zelenskyy describes Canada-U.S. tensions as 'strange,' draws comparison to Ukraine and Russia
Canada, Ukraine forge 100-year pact built on drones and defence

blocks.text: In some of his language, Prime Minister Mark Carney alludes to it, saying how U.S. President Donald Trump "wants to break us, so he can own us."
But he never completes the thought the way Zelenskyy did.

Former deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland, who remains an economic adviser to Zelenskyy, has described the Trump administration as an "existential threat" to Canada's future, but never crossed into the territory of comparing the plight of her ancestral homeland with Canada.
Even former prime minister Jean Chrétien, in his fiery, "we bow to know no one" 9/11 speech last Friday, didn't make the link.
One of the prominent Canadian voices to make the comparison is former vice-chief of the defence staff, retired vice-admiral Mark Norman.
Writing in the National Post during the early 2025 annexation controversy, Norman posed the question: "Are we as Canadians any different than Ukraine is to Russia or Taiwan to China?"

items: U.S. interest in Alberta separatism raises red flags over what might come next
What if the U.S. invaded Canada?

blocks.text: In a subsequent interview with CBC's Front Burner, the former commander of the navy used his initial argument as the jumping-off point to examine what Trump's threats meant for Canadian sovereignty.
His message was: While an American invasion is not imminent, the annexation rhetoric and the way the trade war has unfolded should force Canadians to reconsider their assumptions.
What happens when you live beside a vastly more powerful neighbour that starts to treat your sovereignty as conditional?
Can Canada actually win a trade war with the U.S.? | About That
Interestingly, outside Canada, the comparison between Canada and Ukraine has been considerably more explicit.
In a March 2025 analysis story examining Trump's 51st state rhetoric, The Washington Post asked outright: "As Putin sees Ukraine … Trump sees Canada?"
The argument was that Russian President Vladimir Putin's relationship with Ukraine provides a disturbing parallel for Trump's rhetoric toward Canada.

A subsequent Post commentary put it even more directly, and argued that Trump talks about Canada much as Putin talks about Ukraine: as though it were a wayward province rather than a fully separate country.

The comparison resurfaced just recently with an article in The Atlantic, which described Trump's approach to Canada as reflecting a worldview in which sovereign countries can be treated almost as properties to be controlled. The article explicitly drew a parallel between Trump's apparent disregard for Canadian sovereignty and Putin's attitude toward Ukraine.

items: Amid Trump trade war, Canada's exports to China up 30% in first half of 2026
Will the U.S. midterm results affect Trump's tariffs on Canada? Democrats think yes
Canada's oil windfall may yet wipe out its losses from tariffs

blocks.text: Trump has threatened to force Canada into the union through economic coercion.
Canada built its postwar prosperity around extraordinary integration with the United States, including supply chains, energy, defence production, intelligence and continental security.
Carney is attempting to untangle that by diversifying trade, especially with Europe.

Dominique Arel, chair of Ukrainian studies at the University of Ottawa, said you can draw some parallels in the sense that Ukraine was extraordinarily dependent on Russia for energy following the collapse of the Soviet Union and has been "with a gun at its head" since the 2014 annexation of Crimea trying to change that.

"Everybody's learning the hard way that basically overdependence is actually a great security risk," said Arel, who noted that the recent collapsed trade talks between Canada and the U.S. looked very Russian-like, but it's tough to know what was in Trump's mind.

"What was demanded by the United States was a direct attack on Canada's sovereignty. But is that just a negotiating tactic to put massive pressure without long-term consequences? It's a bit early to know that. But clearly, it's not much of a negotiation. It's basically an ultimatum, which you could draw parallels with Russia, of course."
Moscow viewed Kyiv's economic overtures toward the European Union as opening the door to security concerns and the possibility that NATO would be parked on its doorstep, Arel said.
For years, Moscow's proposition to Kyiv was essentially: You may technically be sovereign, but your sovereignty cannot be exercised against Russian interests.

Matt Schmidt, an associate professor and national security expert at the University of New Haven in Connecticut and former instructor at the U.S. Army War College, also said there are similarities, but important differences.
U.S. effort to make Canada a 'vassal state' lacks clear strategy, security expert says
"What's driving this isn't rational economic thinking. What's driving this is an irrational belief that Canada is not a real nation," said Schmidt.

"Putin knew what he wanted and he was trying different different pathways to get it. I don't think that the president [Trump] knows what he wants. He's really just blurting out a sort of psychological impulse — a pressure in his mind — where he has to act like the big dog in the room.
"And so he pops out with whatever is in there and then the rest of the administration races around and says, can we turn that into real policy?"
He said the idea of dominating Canada doesn't have broad appeal among Americans, whereas in Russia the opposite is true where Ukraine is concerned.
He also said, militarily there's a big difference in that Russia wants to swallow Ukraine whole, while the U.S. is more interested in pulling the strings of its neighbours, including Canada.
Russia, Schmidt argues, is also more organized and focused about what it wants out of Ukraine.
"I don't think there's a clear idea that goes beyond the Oval Office itself that says we have X goal in mind for Canada. We want to make it the 51st state," said Schmidt.
"I think most people in the administration think that's crazy. And so there's no broader strategic plan to say, well, let's do this economically and let's make this threat militarily."
